TO-DAY AND TO-MO Old Time is the drollest of wags, And puzzles the world with his rules; Be gives all to-day to the wise, To-morrow he promised the fools. At first he made naught but to-icy, With its joys, its successes and sorrow; Then, to keep on good terms with the world, He promised he'd make a tc-storrotc. The idle rejoiced at the news, Pot their hands in their Dockets and slept, Believing the promise of Time Would be most religiously kept. They never conceived that the rogue Had promised to-morrow in fan, So quietly went to decay. Leaving all to-day's work to be done. At last they woke up, but to find To-morrow was really a myth, And thought what they'd do, when too late, If they had the time to do with.

An industry hitherto unknown in the Canadian North. West is about to be started in Winnipeg by the establish• ment of a linseed oil mill. 'The growth of flax has, up to the present time, bee= almost exclusively confined to the Russian Menonites on their settlement in Manitoba. Hun- dreds of thonb.nds 6: -acres of the seed have been cropped with success on the newly-turned sod, during the past five or six years, throughout the Western States of America, notably in Minnesota, lowa, and Nebraska, and it is gene- rally admitted that by its use the emigrant may secure a crop in his first year. Exrexir Cerra:: TRADE OF CANADA.—The Canadian Minister of Agriculture, in his annual report, refers as fol- lows to the remarkable growth of the cattle trade of the Dominion during recent years :—The export trade of cattle from Canada, during the year 1883, shows a large increase over the previous year, being 55,825 cattle agairet 35,378 In 1882; and -the increase in the number of sheep exported is very striking, viz., 114,352 against 75,905 the preceding year. The cattle trade of Canada has now ceased to be an experiment. It has grown to be one of.the greatest lines of trade of the country, and hundreds of thousands of dollarl have been invested in it by shrewd and practical men. It is an established fact, too, that Canada is destined to be- come one of the most important cattle-raising countries of the world, pcssessing, as it does, every facility for the con- duct of an enormous trade. The grazing lands are ample and rich, fodder is comparatively cheap, labour is reason- able, and the means of transport are unsurpassed. Within the last two yews the value of our exports of live stock ,has been not lese than $3,500,000 annually, while the total value of the cattle shipped from Canada six years ago was little more than $38,000. Every inch of space that could be pro- cured by the St. Lawrence route during the past season-was taken up and filled with Canadian cattle. Be loving, and you will never want for love; be humble, and you will nevec want for guiding. The tary and the industrious can never live happily to- gether; the lazy despise the industrious too much. An Anirrican girl wrote to her lover: "Now, George, don't you tale to be at the singing-school to-night." George wrote bank: "There's no such word as tale." Ah, how wonderful is the advent of the spring !—the great annual miracle of the blossoming of Aaron's rod, re- peated on myriads and myriads or branches!—Kavanayb. To mormur against death in petulant defiance, Is never for the best, To will what God.deth win, that is the only science That gives as any rest—Lonyfellow. div.head: 4.OYAL COMMISSIONERS' REPORT ON AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION. NO. 111.
div.p: THE 4.OYAL COMMISSIONERS' REPORT ON AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION. NO. 111.

After giving examples of the farming schools of Ger- many, Mr. Jenkins, the Royal Commissioner, points out that the great majority of the directors, although having a general opinion aa to the influence which their schools have already lead upon the farming of the districts in which they are Situated, state frankly that they have not been established long enough to enable them to give a precise answer to his questions on this point. In one case—the school of Riesenrodt—the director seems tolerably certain that advances have been made along the whole line of march of progressive agriculture in his district, and this he attributes to the insnence of the theoretical and practical teaching which has been given at his echool for many years. The opinion of the Commissioner is that some of these schools, when their organisation has been suitable to their surroundings, have done an immense amount of good. In a

div.head: 11TE EXAMINER SATURDAY. JUNE 21, 1884.
div.p: 11TE EXAMINER SATURDAY. JUNE 21, 1884.

communication- sent to Mr. Jenkins by Dr. Dumkelberg, Director of the Agricultural Academy at Poppeladorf, the learned professor says that in general people have aban- doned the idea of improving the sons of peasants, small farmers, and farm labourers, both practically and theo- retically, in the lower farming schools because it has been found that work in the field and farm buildings can only be foNo wed at the expense of theoretical instruction. Such schools are inadequately frequented, he says, by the sons of small proprietors and tenant farmers, and the expense which the State inners for their education is out of all proportion to the success achieved in the distribution of knowledge and of better methods of agriculture in those districts where I small farming prevails. He goes on to contend that it has been proved that agricultural instruction does not properly belong to elementary schools, but only to those specially or- ganised for it. The Association of Rhenish Prussia de- veloped the institotion of agricultural travelling lecturers, .appointiog aspiring young agriculturists thoroughly com- petent both in practice and science. These gentlemen travel about the Rhine provinces and elucidate the most im- portant agricultural questions of the day at the assemblies of farmers convoked for the purpose. After the lectures follow discussions and the exchange of views and -expe- riences which are instructive and stimulating. Schools are opened at which the young are educated, and in the summer months, when the teachers go oat as the travelling lecturers among the farming communities, it is found al mdiSt imposaible to separate the winter schools from the travelling lecturer. The function of the former was to continue the school edu- cation of youths after the termination of the ordin try school periods daring the almost dead season of the agricul- tural year throughout Germany, while the function of the latter is to draw the attention of established farmers to the newest discoveries of science and the most successful appli- cations of them to practice. Though the system of winter schools cannot in the opinion of Mr. Jenkins be adopted in their entirety in England, it is worthy of very serious con- sideration. He proceeds to give a somewhat detailed ac- count of the organisation of the winter schools in Rhenish Prussia ae a type of she whole class in the south-west of thel empire with the exception of Wfirtemberg. Nearly all the winter schools for agricultural education are to be found in she eolith and the west of Germany, where small fawns, generally occupied by their proprietors, predominate. The buildings used for the winter schools were always more or less of the nature of cottages, but the accommodation WAS generally in accordance with the requirements of the .school. The physical and chemical apparatus was in all cases sicciale, but apparently sufficient and well chosen, and there was always a microscope. Agricultural, zoological, and botani- cal diagrams were to be seen upon the walls, and a small museum of natural history objects was generally the pride of the director and the " curatoriqm." In one school—that of Gumbinnen—the pupils pay 24. for one winter's course, and an additional 3s. as an entrance fee. There are pecan teachers atd the director, who is the travelling lecturer of the district. The provincial administration of East Prussia gives a subvention of £6O annually, and the Prussian Mulls. ter of Agriculture adds £l5O a year, while the local agricul- tural society votes £25 per annum. making £235 a year, or £8 per pupil, in addition to the 275. each which the pupils themselves pay. The salary of the travelling lecturers vary from £6O to £lOO per annum.

Rogers Bey, as secretary of the Committee for the Pre- servation and Restoration of the Monuments of Arab Art, has presented a report to the Khedive, which includes a list .of 34 mosques and other buildings which have been strengthened, repaired, or restored in 1862 and 1883. The expenses incurred in these works and in the establishment of the Museum of Arab Art in the mosque of Al-Hakim have amounted to rather more than £l7OOO. ..Steps are to be immediately taken for enlarging the ob- servatory at the summit of Ben Nevis, which has rendered ~.-rood service to meteorologicalscience since its opening in October last. The observers have hitherto been greatly cramped in their single apartment, and it is now proposed to erect three additional rooms and a tower, which latter will contain space for the instruments in use. Shelter will be provided for tourists who may climb the mountain—a task rendered comparatively easy by the construction of a road, available for horses, from Fort William to the sum- mit. The Athmount says memoir of the late Dr. Humphry Sandwith, C. 8., compiled by his nephew, Mr. T. Humphry Ward, will shortly be published by Messrs. Cassell and Co. The book, which will be in one comparatively short volume, will be founded upon the ample autobiography left by Dr. Sandwith for the use of his children. It will describe his - early struggles as a medical student, his life at Constanti- nople and in Mesopotamia, his-adventures on the Danube and at Kars, London society in 1856, and his subsequent career as a politician and as an agent for the various socie- ties for succouring the sick and wounded during the wars of 1870, 1876, and 1877. , PREntsmitac TUMCILL—In "ilardwicke's Science Gossip" is an interesting account of a very rich find by Professor P. W. Norris, Assistant United States Ethnologist (mark the title! Who -is the British ethnologist, and where is his assistant?) of a prehistoric city near Charlestown, contain- ing not only the usual remains of Daleolithic or neolithic implements or vestiges of the beginning of the use of metals, bat these and the skeletons of the men who used them. Dealing with to wer agricultural education in Wurteraburg the Commissioner gives a brief sketch of its present psis tion, and observes that in Wurtemburg such technical ins structioo, espscially in the lower grades, has received a larger and more continuous impulse than in any other part of Germany. Including the Farming Scho Is attached to the liotienheim Institute, there are four of such institu- tions in Wurtemburg—one in each of the administrative distriats into which the kingdom is divided. They are organised for 12 pupils, who must be at leazt 17 years of age. The pupils pay nothing for instruction, and are bound to go through the three years' course. They also receive lodging at the school, and the cost of their board is put. against the value of their labour according to an official scale. During the steamer the pupils generally work ten ' hours a day, and in winter eight, but daring haytime and harvest the working hours are prolonged, and no lessons given.. At other periods of the year toe lesson hours range from 12 to 17 hour, per week. The teacher at the village school gives the necessary lessons in general subjects, and in the event of wet or other inclement weather preventing-field work, the time is immediately utilised for the further in- struction of the pupils in the schoolroom. In connection with the school at Ellwangen the farm consists of about 310 acre, of which 165 are arable and 77 meadow. There is an ' experimental garden of 24. acres, a hopfield of 6,000 hil- locks, and an orchard. The live stock consisteof six horses, 17 draught oxeo, eight young oxen, one boll, 443 COW 3 and calves, 18 feeding beasts, 300 sheep, and 10 feeding pigs. Bee-keeping is largely eneougaged, and the number of h:ves vary from 48 in the winter to more than 70 in the summer. Every boy in Wurtemburg is compelled to remain at a school of some kind until he is 14 years of age. If he leaves a regular echool at 14 he is compelled to continue his educa- tion until he is 18 years of age by attending a school estab- lished by the communal authorities for this special purpose. In connection with the obligatory winter schools just named there was formed a series of voluntary improvement schcols, where theoretical agriculture is also a leading feature. These schools are frequented by youths above 18 years of age, who have acquired a thirst for knowledge capable of practical application during their compulsory attendance at the win- ter school, and even by older people, whose first notions of agricultural theory have been obtained at them. The Stele grant towards the expenses of these schools is £l,OOO per annum. In addition to these winter schools there are .28 farmers' clubs, with 924 members; 57 reading societles, with 2,173 members, and 904 parish libraries, containing 159,2E9 volumes.

The other ekele tone, their arrangement, the ornaments and weapons found with them, render this discovery of comparable value to that of the Viking ship at Sandefjord a few years ago under the mound long known as " The King's Hill." The Charlestown remains were under similar mounds.—Gentleman's Magazine. CHOLERA Gsams Awn BORIC Aorao.—Dr. Koch appears to have at last discovered the. specific. germs of cholera. He

describes them as comma-lie bacilli, always found con- nected with this disease, but nowhere else. One of their very serious properties is an aptitudo to develop in a moist soil, and therefore they are not necessarily destroyed by burial. As a set.off to this he finds that they only survive and mpltiply in fluids that are alkaline or basic. The pre- sence of free acid destroys them. This fact has an impor- tant bearing on the question raised in a previous note con- cerning the effect of boric acid when taken into the human system. Will this acid destroy these germs and others of a like nature? I am told that boric acid is an effectual specific against diarrhcea, and if so its action probably de- pends upon its destruction of the bacilli or bacteria, which produce the disturbance. I may inform my London readers that moat of them are daily consumers of boric acid; the Practice of adding "glacialine," or some such boracic com- pound, to milk intended for the London market, is becoming almost universal. My attention was 'first directed towards this use of glacialine by an instructive incident. I was seeking for a missing parcel at a railway station, and ob- • served a stray can of milk waiting for identification. I asked a porter how long it had been there. "Above a week," he replied. When I spoke of the probable condition of its contents, he told me that they hod had milk standing thus for about a fortnight, and none the worse. I believe this to be quite true, and that glacialine is the preservative agent generally used.—Gentlentan's Magazine.

In Germany there are a•large number of schools where Borne special branch of knowledge connected with agricul- ture is taught, eithlr theoretically, or practically, or both, and either separately or in connection with a coarse of general education. For instaa le, there are 18 dairy schools in Germany, the most celebrated being at Hades, near Lalendort. There are two large veterinary colleges, viz, at Berlin and Hanover; in additi at to the Vete,.inary Insa-

At the Widen dairy school, the course of in- ..stractlon extends over sia months, and is given entirely to young men. They must be 18 years of age, of good char- acter, and already possessed of some knowledge of dairying. The dairy instruction gives demonstrations in all matters of a practical nature, in.duding the making of whole-milk cteese on the Gruyere and other systems. Theoretical in- struction is given daily for an hoar•by a professor. Great attention is paid to bookkeeping, and to the principles of breeding and feeding, as well as at dairying. At Hein- •richsthal, the Commission visited a •dairy school where 10 •to:12 young women were taught the theory and practice of batter making and cheese making. The farm consists of MO, acres of arable land, grass, and wood. Twenty-two IDotch milch cows are kept, the total stock being 30 bead. The young women are taught the technical management of a dairy,incliading bookeeping; the.fcediag and manage- ment of cows, fatting calves and piga ; instruction in cook- ing.; housekeeping in general; management of poultry, according to season; and management of tte kitchen garden. it acme of the improvement winter schools of Germany there is given a course of instruction on drain. age and irrigating grass land. There are also in Germany sugar making, brewery, and distillery schools, formed largely with the object of giving the managers and chemist: of such factories an opportnnity of learning the cheseiatry of the proc ems em?loyed which are gone through in the laboratories of these institutions on a small scale.

SEASONABLE HINTS. It is a mistake to suppose that growing chicks do best if permitted to run amongst long grass, for when it is wet, as we have been having it of late, it is very injurious to them, and causes diseases of various kintis, especially those affect- ing the respiratory organs. In very dry weather the chicks may be allowed to wander where they like amongst growing crops, but not in wet Iseasons. Those who keep feather. footed birds for show will do well to have the grass regu- larly cut. If not it breaks the foot feather, which, of course, greatly mars the beauty of this kind of birds. Some exhinitors keep the runs cut as closely as any lawn, and this is the eecret why their birds are so good in the feet. It is also necessary when the hot sunny weather comes to keep white and light plumaged fowls sheltered, or the Bun will tan their plumage—always a great drawback. Old birds do not need this care as they will moult out; but young ones will retaia their drat adult feathers until next year.

WHERE THREE COUNTIES Mt—They took the down- ward path and I the upward, and as I climbed, the ,silence deepened, till it was broken.onlY by the tinkling rills falling from roe% to rock and the reiterated bleating of one eolitary little fell-lamb whioh had lost its dam. Still upward by a zigzag path, now pasaing behind a bold rock and now coal- ; ing out again into full view o the valley-head, while more than oncez. sharp shower folic wed by a burst of sunshine seemed to sat the mountain all aflame and to turn the little rals to streams of molten lava. Higher still, till a rush of cold wind told me that I was almost at a level of Wrynose ac,p, then straight ahead with Black Crag upon the right and Wetside Edge upon the left, and here at last is the "Three.ShireStone," where Cu aiJeriand, Lancashire, and Westmoreland clasp hand in hand. A tiny trickling thread issuioc; from a peat-bog tea. that is now left of the Brathay; but from the same bog there issues another little rill which after afew hesitating twists and turns decides to run in the opposite direction and proves to be one of the many stream- ids which go to form the far-famed Duldon. Bcfore night- I fail I hope to follow that little river past Cockley Beck with its " cottage rude and grey," of which Wordsworth sang in one ,of the sweetest.cf his sonnets, past Birks Brig with its FaCrie Chasm, and Seathwaite with itsmemories of Wonder- ful Walker, and Ulpha Kirk, and Broughtown Tower, and many another classic rpot ; but for the present I pause, and, climbing to a point of vantage, turn to look back upon the Brathay valley. There it lies—the whole valley from Lang- dale Tarn to Wiadermere--'• beautiful as a wreck of Para- dise"—(or why not beautiful as Paradise itself? I for one desire no fairer)—with its rich foliage glowing in the morn- ing sun, and the little river winding adown its length, like that "river which went cut of Elea to water the Garden." Looking down upon it thus, in its completeness and its beauty, the heart instinctively rises in gratitude and worship to Him who' "sendeth the springs into the valleyS which run among the hills."—Good Words.

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

. A great deal has been said on the question as to whether ' poultry keeping will or will not pay that any contribution ' to its solution is welcome, especially that which is practical rather than theoretical. That poultry does pay, and the production of eggs too, we have no doubt, but it is not where much noise is made, but where the business is carried • on quietly and unostentatiously. Recently we were speak- sag with the manager of one of the largest London dairy companies, and, he told us that where -five years ago his company sold one dozen eggs, now they sell a hundred • dozen,—guaranteed new laid eggs these are—and that farmers in all parts of the country were Ending it to their advantage to send him regularly, in some cases daily, in others three times a week, the produce of their hens. They were paying greater attention to breeds, to the feeding of the fowls, and he hopes are as many more years are over • that he will be able to obtain thousands where he now gets tens. His deotapd for undoubtedly fresh eggs is practically unlimited, and at present it is only restricted by the supply. The following letter, which appeared some time ago in the Li:ve Stock Journal, will show what is being done in a quiet corner of Yorkshire:—" So much has been said and written," • nays the writer, "upon the vexed question of ' Will poultry pay?' that the account of a visit recently made by me to a .farm where the staple return is from the hens, may be of interest. In the middle of Yorkshire, at the picturesque village of —, surrounded by a beautiful scenery of 'heather, moor, hill, and rushing brown stream, lies the farm , to which I refer. Mr. and Mrs. W— are the only occu- pants of the cosy little stone farmhouse, and, preferring to perform all the work of the dairy and poultry. yard them- selves, are therefore satisfied that it is well done. I should mention that the exceptional size and beauty of the eggs which I saw in a grocer's window in the market town led ,me to inquire whether they were a specimen basketful or no, and being much etteck with the reply that these were 'only part of a -coneignment received that day," I begged permission to visit the farm which supplied them. A short journey of half an hour brought me to the village, where I was most kindly received; and Mrs. W— at once gave me fall par- ticulars as to her method of feeding and managing the hens. In the morning, about six, they receive a good meal of small round maize. Directly afterwards they go roaming all over the grass fields, always returning punctually at noon for their dinner. This second feed consists of the best Indian meal, mixed with a fourth part of very superior Scotch oatmeal, sweet and fresh; a sprinkling of spice is added, and the mixture made with boiling water. This they eat ravenously, and then -rush off again to the fields. About 'Eve o'clock a duplicate meal is given them, after which they go to roost. Mr. W-- has not over 200 hens. The breeds are mixed. In some I could see Andalusian blood; in others the nodding tuft and speckled plumage of the Houdan was apparent; Cochin and Brahma, as well as Dorkingoharacteristics might be observed in others. From these SOO hens Mr. W--- has obtained, from May Ist to September, Ist, £6O worth of eggs, the highest price ob- tained being Is. for seven, and the bravest is. for seventeen. In April and May he several times collected 1,000 eggs per week. The average yield during May and Jane was 100 to 130 eggs per day. At this moment he is bringing to market from 350 t 0.420 eggs weekly, the heat laying daily from 50 to 60 eggs. Fifty eggs daily in September from 200 hens in deep moult, is a ,raost eztraordinary return ; of course, a very large proportion are not laying at all at this moment. The eggs are quite over the renal size, els of them when selected turning the scale at a pound; but they average seven to the pound picked up haphazard from the nest. Mrs. W. initiate upon the food, given to the birds being of the best quality, and distributed most punctually. She oc- casionally, In the winter, makos a pailful.cf sound barley quite hot, by baking slowly for an hour, and considers it to • 'ee a great stimulus to laying. The hens are many of them in their fourth year, at the commencement gf which they 2./3 killed. Mr. W.'s experience eatisfies him that birds bred from laying straine do not reach the height ef their powers till the completion of their soO'cnd year. Green corn he conciders the worst of food for laying hens, and has ob. served that, if al/owed access tc the ricks at.this season, they cease laving, He thinks it (being sweet and new) f atteno, but lacks the stimulant -contained in Bound and thoroughly dried earn. Referring .to the ravageg hens are supposed to commit in their rangicg, Mr. W. spe::e highly of the benefit contoured by poultry on grass lands, by de- vouring insects and manuring the tooil. He informed me that when he began to farm his presont tenement, thirteen years ago—consisting of sixteen acros—he could not make enough hay to winter three cows, but that now he keeps ten with ease. tis evident that In this case the "eye of the master fattens the steed," as the old proverb has ii; but Mr. W— gives much of the credit to his poultry. Butter.milk forms another article of diet in the chicken- yard ; this or sweet milk is given en troughs, and especially during the autumn and winter months forms a valuable heat producer. On inquiring as to what method Mr. W— pursued in breeding his laying birds, he replied, "Whenever I see a good layer, I buy her, and set a few clutches of her eggs, and always, when sitting from my own birds, select the eggs of those which' lay the largest ones, and that most frequantly." The cocks are of the same mixed breeds as the hena. I think I eaw about twenty in all. The soil is dry—a mixture of loans and sand, with here and there a good deal cf limestone. The fowls' houses are of the most simple description, and they have a free run over the grass fields. I left Kr. farm with a feel- ing of real pleasure. It is delightful to have found even , one English farmer that allows that poultry will pay, and 'who demonstrates it so practically. All around, his neigh-

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

TURNMS.-Our earliest sowing of these—the Early Munich variety—are now nearly two inches in diameter, and are consequently fit for palling for flavouring broths, &c. To have turnips sweet and tender during the summer months we find it best to make frequent sowings, regulating the quantity according to the demand. Much may be done to secure succulence and sweetness by selecting a cool, moist position, or such as is screened from the mid-day sun. We are about to sow our third crop, which will consist of Veitch's Red Globe and Snowball, and if we wished for a yellow one we should use the Preston Yellow. In tho above the grower will find three distinct kinds, and their names indicate the colour of their skin, though Veitch is more of a purplo than a red. If the grower is an exhibitor he will find it advantageous to be in possession of three varieties instead of one, because one may be in better form than another at a certain time. The distance between the rows must bo more than for earlier sowings, and if it is I-Cin. the plante in the rows can be regulated so as to give ample space for each root to develop. The turnip has many ene- mies, but the most troublesome is the turnip flea, which has in some seasons perforated the young leaves in entire fields to sueli an extent as to necessitate another sowing. Over such an area there is no practical remedy, but the cottager with his' small patch may do much by dusting the plants with soot and lime. A fresh-tarred piece of net stretched over the bed would catch numbers by their alighting on it or coming in contact with it in their rapid movements. The insect rises but a short distance above the soil, and farmers have taken advantage of this peculiarity, and have drawn a piece of light tarred cloth over the rows, eight or ten of which may be done at once, and as rapidly as two active boys can walk, who have the two upper corners attached to sticks which can rest on their shoulders as they proceed, and adjusted so that the lower edge of the cloth barely touches the surface of the soil. Against this canvas the lies must come sooner or later.

Tim FRONT GARDEN.—Many of the annuals are now sufficiently advanced to require thinning, an operation best performed when the soil is moist, because they not only come easier out of the ground, but they do not disturb the roots of those left behind to the same extent as when the ground is dry. All should be thinned so as to leave a space of 3in. or 4in. between each plant, excepting, perhaps, Virginian Stock when used for an edging, as the object in that case is te get a dense miniature hedge in the shortest time, but after that is attained they also may with advan- tage be reduced in number. •There are very few annual plants that grow less than 6in. in diameter, and vet we see half & dozen left to occupy that space with the ,result that after the first flush of flowering the plants decay at the bot- tom, and this soon spreads through the whole row or patch. We therefore say thin, and continue thinning,either by pulling some up or slightly reducing the dimensions of the ethers. Many plants, after being so treated, put forth fresh shoots and produce a succession of flowers. There are others that will not do this, and their habit must be ob- served before they are submitted to a severe reducing pro- cess.

TEM WINDOW.—MOSS FOR PLANT GROWING.—It is well known to those engaged in plant culture that many plants will root freely in several kinds of 0103 S, bat it is only re- cently that attention has been directed to its adaptation for ordinary plant culture. To a Frenchman named Et umesnil is due the credit of improving the fertilising properties of moss by a method which he at the time patented. The prepara- tion was not generally approved, though many spoke well of It. Captain Thompson found it defective, and after. several experiments he has produced an article which has given far better results. The .Garden states that—" A novel feature, and one that attracted some attention at the Regent Park Show, London, was some baskets of plants said to have been grown in prepared moss and entirely without soil. The ex- hibitor was Captain Raiford Thompson, who claims to have discovered a new method of growing plants." If this article is sold at a reasonable price it will be a boon to plant growers in towns where they have a difficulty in procuring soil suitable for plants in pots.

div.head: IMPORTANT LICENSING PROSECUTIONS.
div.p: IMPORTANT LICENSING PROSECUTIONS.

. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Mcnday, before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, and Mr. John Fairclough,John Hill, Rowley-lane, Warrington, was summoned that he, og the Bth of June, being the occupier of licensed premises to sell by retail, did unlawfully keep open the said house and premises for the sale of beer during the time that the premises were revired to be closed, the said day being Sunday. Three men named Thomas Cartwright, Griffith Griffiths, and James Maidely, were summoned for aiding and abettiAg in the offence.—Mr. A. Browne prose- cuted on behalf of the police, and the defendant Hill was represented by Mr. Davies.—Mr. Browne said that the defendant Hill was licensed to sell beer to be consumed off the premises at a house and shop in Howley-lane, Warring- ton. Owing to complaints received by the police, on Sun- day morning, the Bth inst., two inspectors of police pro- ceeded to watch the house. They arrived in the neigh- bourhood at about seven e'clock in the morning, and from that time until eight o'cl.)ck they saw no less than eight persons go to the back door of the house in question, try it, and, finding it fastened, go back again. From eight the watch was continued until twelve o'clock, and during that peried sixteen persons called at the back door of the house, Barna of them going in and remaining a few minutes, sod others receiving a jug full of bear or other liquor over a wall, admittance being gained by getting into the yard of the defendant Graffithe, which adjoined, and knocking with a churn stick against the back door of Hill's house. The beer was then supplied, and something which was believed to be money was seen to be received. Money was appar- ently received no lees than four times, and the churn stall was used three times for the purpose of gaining admittance. iln the cellar of the house the'inspectors found a pint jug half full of freshly-drawn beer, and also several measures with the fresh foam in thom.—lnspector Berry was then called, and said that in consequence of 'instructions received from the chief constable, be, in tom- puny with Inspector Spinks, went on Sunday morning week hear to the premises of the defendant Hall, in Howley-lane, and there took observations. „Between 7-30 and 8 o'clock, ' eight persons called at the house, but the kitchen door was lacked. At eight o'clock the defendant Cartwright came end it appearing that the servant was up he was admitted and,remained five minutes. Shortly afterwards Maidely was admitted. Witness then told in detail the nature of his ob- servations, noted down at the time, which shewed that dif- ferent persons went to, and returned from, the house during the morning, and in certain instances jugs were handed over the wall into Griffiths' s yard, and that money was to all ap- peatances.received in exchange. In the cellar of the house he saw ajag in which was some newly drawn beer, and ves- sels with foam at the bottom. Mrs. Hill was then in the house and she said "1 ,am very sorry for it, I wish I had not done it." Witness went to Griffiths's house and aseere tamed that a number of men had been in the house. Defen- dant Cartwright admitted having bad some beer, and Maidely said that he had been to tell Hill something about a cow that was out at grass.—At this point Mr. Davies con- tended that a man with an off-license could not be charged with keeping open during prohibited bours.—The Clerk mentioned that there was a second summons that would apply if the one now being heard was not considered a pro- per one.—Mr. Davies: I admit that he may be charged under the second summons; he has only a right to sell beer to be drunk off .the premises.—lt was then decided to pro- ceed with the ease, and Mr. Davies cross-examined Inspec- tor Eerry ss to his evidence. In reply Mr. Berry stated that he and Inspector Spioks secreted themselves in the bedroom of an empty house, a abort distance from the house of the defendant, whence they took their observations.—lnspector Spinks gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Browne at this juncture withdrew the charges against Cartwright and Maidely; the former of whom at the beginning of the case said that the beer he bad had was given him and was not paid for by him.—ln defence Mr. Davies said that the in- spectors were confined in the bedroom of an empty house and he should ask the Bench whether he believed their evi- dence as against the evidence of parties who must know what took place, and who were in a better position to give evidence. The defendant himself was away at the time and knew nothing whatever about the matter. Ile contended that the jugs which the police supposed to contain beer only contained milk, the defendant being a dealer in milk, and further that if any beer was sold, it must have been by a lit- tle girl who was in the house, named Thornley. He sub- mitted that there was no evidence against his client, and said that he should prove that if anything was done that was wrong the defendant knew nothing about ,it.—He then cal- led Mrs. Hill who swore that no beer was sold and that the

jugs passed over the wall ,contained milk and buttermilk,— The little girl Thornley, the defendant's neice, also gave evi- dence to a similar effect, but in cross-examination by Mr. Browne she utterly broke down, and admitted that one of the jags contained beec.—ln answer to the Mayor it was stated that the watch on the premises had been made in con- sequence of numerous complaints that had been received. —The Mayor said that the Bench had it ia their power to indict a penalty of £lO and to endorse the license, but, hav- ing discussed the matter they were inclined to lean upon the merciful side of the question and would only inflict a penalty of £5 and costs upon Hill. In reference to Grif- fiths he would be fined 40s and costs.—Mr. Davies asked the Bench not to order the license to be en- dorsed, remarking that it was a first offence that the defendant was a very respectable mail and that whatever had been done had been in his absence.— The Clerk said that in serious cases it was customary to en- dorse the license, but if the Bench SAW circumstances of mitigation it WAS open to them not to take that course.-The Mayor said that they were disposed to be merciful, as they had been in the matter of the penalty, and under the cir- cumstances that the jlefendant was not himself present, though that did notliffect the legal question, they would make no order as to the license. At the same sitting of the magistrates, George Bradburn, provision dealer, Folly-lane, the holder of an off license, WU summoned for illegally selling beer to be drunk on the highway near his premises, and Ralph bale was Summoned for aiding and abetting.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the police, and Mr. Davies defended.—Mr. Browne charac- terised the case as a serious one, inasmuch as off licenses, if people were allowed to take the liquor into the road to drink, the houses would have the same power as an ordin- ary licensed house. On Saturday morning, the 9th mat, a constable wifk on duty in Folly lane when he saw a man named Dale go into the shop of the defendant Rradburn and immediately come out again with a pint pot of 'beer, drink the beer straight off, and take the pot bank again into the shop, leaving it there.—P.C. Johnstone proved seeing defendant Dale fetch the beer and drink it when afew yards away from Brasiburn'e door, and then take the vessel back. He ascertained that the pot belonged to the defendant's wife who said that they often supplied beer in that man- ner if it was drunk off the premises.—It being stated that Dale, though only a short distance from the house, took the beer into a field and was not on the highway when he drank it, it was thought advisable to withdraw the sum- mons, Mr. Browne intimating that a summons would pro- bably be taken out in respect of another case in which a constable saw beer supplied in a similar manner and drunk jun outside Bralburn's shop. On Thursday, George Bradburn, the defendant in the last case, was again summoned before Captain Litton (in the chair) and Alderman Webster for serving beer ton a person unknown which was drunk on the highway near his pre- mises, on the 7th of June.—Mr. A. Browne again represented tbe police, and Mr. P. Davies appeared for the defendant.— Mr. Browne said that the action WAS taken under the sth section of the Licensing Act, 1872, which stated that if any person sold drink on premises licensed for the sale of beer by retail to be consumed off the premises and allowed the same to be drunk on the highway close to, with his. privity and consent, was liable under that section. On the date,in ques- tion P.C. Smith WAS on duty in Folly-lane, and saw two men home out of the house of the defendant with beer. One drank his beer in a field close by, and the other, whose name was not known, . drank his beer on • the highway.—P.C. Smith deposed that oh the 7th June he was near the defen- dant's Shop and was in plain clothes, when he saw two men go in and speak to the defendant. One of them was served with a pint of beer, which he drank on a grass platt near by, and then took the ing back to the defendant. Witness went into the shop, where he SAW another man. There was a qpart jug of beer on the. connter, Mid a vessel was bang tilled. ln answer to witness defendant seid that he was in the habit of supplying drink to be drunk outside, and did not know that he was doing anything wrong; he should be. glad to know. Witness told defendant he should report hint and left. The person whom witness saw in the house then . came out with a vessel of beer, proceeded to a traveller's rest stone on the highway close by, where another man was awaiting him, and drank the beer. The stone was ten or twelve yards from the house.—Mr. Davies said that they were summoned for serving a person unknown • why did not the police brin.g forward the person?—Randall Hynaston, labourer, LongfOrd wire works, was then called, and posi- tively affirmed that the constable spoke to him when he was drinking his beer in the field.—Tbe Chairman said that the Bench had. conoluded that the defendant had committed an illegal offence. They should, however, as defendant said he was ignorant Of offending, only fine him in the amount of the casts. If any ether case of the same nature were brought before them their decision would probably be more severe.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING. SIR GILBERT GREENALL AGAIN ON FISHING
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING. SIR GILBERT GREENALL AGAIN ON FISHING
AND FLOGGING.

On Monday evening i iTaiTeii;i-o-i-the Conservatives of north-east ward was held in St. Peter's schoolroom, John street, Warrington. The chair was occupied by Councillor Francomb, and there were also on the platform Sir Gilbert Green ill, Capt. Reynolds, Councillor Schott (Manchester): Meagre. T. V. Taylor, H. Greenell, John Burgess, Jas. Richards, R. Isherwood, Jno. ,Roberts, George Cropper. Joe. Berry, and others. There was only a thin attendance at the commencement of the proceedings. The CHADINAN said he had been sorry to call them toge- ther that evening, but his excuse.for so doing was that be believed the:, should very soon have a general election, and he felt confident that at that time they would not like to be caught napping. At the last election, he believed, the con- servative party had been very careless and indolent, and they found out that if they wished to meet with success, they must certainly work hard. (Hear, hear). He believed the working classes of this country thought seriously, and were not going to be carrie& by the Birmingham Caucus, or any- t ing else. They would think for themielves, and they would turn Mr. Gladstone's slavish majority into an abject , and miserable minority. (Applause). Mr. nitwit then moved "That this meeting pledges Itself to do all in its power to .return Sir Gilbert Greenall, bart., to Parliament, as member ,for Warrington at the next election." It was, he said, a source of greatest possiole satisfaction to him to be able to propose the resolution. He thought it was a good thing to be able to assist a gee- ,tleman who had devoted, be believed. nearly 30 years of his "life to the services of this Mifflin Parliament. They had heard lately from the Radical candidate that they must not vote for the man, but for the principles. That was qui:e true,but when, in an exceptional case like the present one —when-Sir Gilbert Greenall had devoted so much of his time to the services at this town, they went further, and said that the setvices of such a man demanded their sup- pert. , (Hear, hear.) Some most discreditable remarks and charges had been made against Sir (filbert by some Radical wireepullers in Warrington. They had heard of lately and no doubt had seen a print which was most indus- triously cieculated. He had one placed in his hands a few days ago and he flaw that some remarks that Sir Gilbert Greenall made at some of the local meetings had been twis- ted in every possible kind of way; and misinterpretations had been put upon them to his discredit. With regard to Sir Crilbert's presence at these local ward meetings he did not attend these meetings so much for the purpose of expres- sing his political opinion, because he considered his services to the town for 30 years ought to make known his political opinions without his speiking upon them there. (Hear, hear.) His presence at these meetings was not so much to express his opinions as to encourage other younger mem- bers of the Conservative party in Warrington to say what they thought on the burning questions of the day. There- fore he considered the attempts which had been made to twist Sir Gilberee remarks in these extempore small speeches and to attempt to place them before the public of Warring- ton as the best efforts he could make' he (Mr. Taylor) thought was certainly most disgraceful.. He had no doubt himself that Sir Gilbert Greenall would not stoop to answer such things, but he (Mr. Taylor) thought that if the whole of the Conservatives were to remain in absolute silence re- specting some of these charges, their political opponents would then take it that by their silence they acquiesced in these charges which they did net do. He wished to refer to a print which had been circulated in which the writer hid placed three words together in an alliterative fashion to make fun to the discredit of Sir Gilbert Greenall. These words were "Flood, Fishing, and Flogging." (Laughter.) It sounded very well no doubt, and no doubt at some of the Radical meetings it would take when this was mentioned. He thought, however, a little explanation would take away any sting that might be left f!I it. With regard to the first they were told—probably on the authority of some speaker at the recent meeting of the Warrington caucus—that a gentleman of the name of Flood dared to have some political views of his own, and in furtherance of these singular poli- tical views he thought tit to make a most disreputable at- tack upon Sir Gilbert Greenall, an attack which would not have been noticed but for the fact that the writer said that Sir Gilbert had done nothing for the working-men of War- rington, and that he had placed work out of their hands, which he (Mr. Taylor) could say was an utter untruth. As regarded the miserable question of fishing he saw that something had been said about it. Some little time ago he believed that nearly everybody fished at the reservoir. The pond was nearly emptied and if I it had not been that Sir Gilbert placed some restrictions on fishing there would not only have been no fish but not a germ of a fish. Therefore it was only wise and reasonable that the fish should have a close sea- son. Now, Sir Gilbert bad made inquiry as to the fish, and he had thrown it open with one reservation., He su4gests that some slight charge should be made, and this charge banded to the Warrington Infirmary. (Applause.) The third of these F's, which the Radicals were determined to celebrate so much, was with reference to the flogging busi- ness. This journalist had industriously gone through the Parliamentary records and bad found—at least he asserted he bad found, and they would take his assertion for granted —that Sir Gilbert had voted against the abolition of flog- ging in the army. Let them consider what the subject of Flogging was. It simply meant a severe punishment for the disreputable characters in the army. He thoullat it was merely an expression of opinion on the part of an bone.st man; and he thought the Liberals had least of all to sly on this subject, for he believed it was they whe introduced the flogging of civilians when garotting came up. He (Mr. Taylor) then referred to the recent iteech of Mr. Crosfield, and said it was evident from that speech that Mr. Cros- field was a sympathiser with Mr. Bradlangh owing to his exclusion from Parliament. (Applause.) From Mr. Cros- tield's recent speech it seemed that he also bad been takiog for granted that the recent utterances of Sir Gilbert at these, ward meeetings had been regular speeches such as he 'should have made at a large political meeting. Mr. Gros.

field had also said that Sir Gilbert appeared to have no opinions on foreign politics although at each of the meet- ' ings at which Sir Gilbert ad been present there had been . plenty said about foreign politics. Referring to what in the course of his speech he called " the wretched Franchise Bill," Mr. Taylor said he had never found out any great cr.dY for this change in the franchise; and in conclusion said that they as Conservatives ought to be thankful that the House of Lords existed to give them an opportunity of say- ing they did not approve of the measure in its present form. (Applause.) Mr. BURGESS seconded the resolution. He said he had been born at Warrington on the other side of the bridge, and the name of Greenall was a household word with bun. and always had been. He was reading The Examiner last Saturday and found in it a letter from a person signing himself " A Young Radical." He told them that Warring- ton must do its duty at the next election, and he (Mr. Burgess) hoped it would do its duty by returning Sir Gil- bert Greenall. (Laughter.) He got up that night 10 support Sir Gilbert Greenall, because by returning him the! would not be returning a man who would say " ditto " 10 Lord Salisbury or Lord Randolph Churchill, or anybodY ales; but if theYsent Mr. Crosfield he would say " ditto to the "grand old man." (Laughter, and hear, hear.) Mr. Jos. BERRY supported the resolution. Mr. ROBERTS also supported the resolution. Sir Gilbert, he said, had been thoroughly true to them as working men. Ha was a large employer of labour, and be did not know whatever they should have done if they had not had such gentlemen as Sir Gilbert Greenall at their back. They eV' tainly could not be too fully alive to what they had read in one of the local papers within the last few weeks. It had ridiculed Sir Gilbert Greenall in a manner which he con- sidered Sir Gilbert never was nor never would be deserving of. He was sure that those gentlemen who sent those letters for publication never could have for one moment thought of what they were doing or what they intended to do. It had simply been that they were alive to the facet that the Conservatives had been putting their spurs on, and that when the general election took place they meant action. He remembered their sending a pamphlet out a fortnight or three weeks ago with something about fishing and the rest in it. He could tell them without any denial that he wan asked by several prominent Liberals to write to Sir Gilbert and ask him for the privilege for the workingmen of War- rington of fishing at Walton again. (A Voice "He would not let you have it.") Sir Gilbert said at one of their meetings that when the proper time came—when the fish i° the reservoir was in a fit state—fishing would be allowed. After 'that this pamphlet came out and threatened Sir , Gilbert that if he allowed this when the next general ' election came they would bring him up for bribery and cor- ruption. (Laughter.) He asked them if.they would hear such threats as these—that if he is returned to Parliament they would try to above him out. These very men said this • without a consideration of what they themselves did in < 1880. (Applause.) Mr.lsnEawoon thought that Sir Gilbert was like him- self. He treated with utter contempt the remarks that bad been made by a certain paper. The best thine they could , do was to treat this language with silent contempt, and when the time came to support Sir Gilbert Greenail. They did not ask them to do what he saw done at the election in 1880, , or he should be ashamed of owning he was a Conservative, or ever associated with them. He would tell them this : tbey never drilled them in chapel; they never asked theta • down to the forge, and from the forge they did not ask theta to the school, and from the school they did not ask them to the public-house, and say, "There is a good breakfast before you go to vote," and then take them like a regiment of , children or Sunday school scholars, and see them all vote the ininle way. That he saw himself. He saw it in the .wad which he realty believed was th'e ward that carried , Mr. Mchilnnies into Parliament. He was not like a speaker . at one of their meetings who said he liked beer, and he had it. (Voice: "Aw could do wi' a pint.") He never had , beer and he Was not going to have it, so they saw that all of Own did not agree on that point. They did not ask them to let a gill of beer lead them; they did not ask them , to go to a breakfast; they did net ask them to go to a.dinaer, I but they simply told them they had the franchise and to exercise it. (Applause.) Sir GILBERT GREEWALL said: Mr. Francomb and gentle- , men, accept my bast thanks for the very kind manner in , which you have accepted that resolution. I value your • friendship; 1 value your support: I earnestly hope that your support will be efficient. I shall earnestly strive and hope that I shall never disappoint you in any expectation I you may form of me. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Francoinb, heard your speech with very great pleasure. You touched ; upon a great many subillects. With many of them we are familiar and we are acquainted. We do not say, lam sure, you speak without knowledge on the subject upon which you spoke, and we must cordially thank you for your utteranceee and we accept from you very gratefully the things which you have communicated. Mr. Taylor, you also spoke, and very kindly, but somehow or other you placed me utterly and entirely in the dark. Now, what The Examiner says I do not knew. (Laughter.) I will assure son, gentlemen, I I bear things to night which I certainly never should think I of reading, and mally and truly never heard of them. As • far as The Examiner is concerned—l am not at all savage ; about The Examiner. The Examiner is a roll of paper Per*- : fectly indifferent to me. Ido not read the lucubrations of The Examiner, and, believe me, I never talk about The Examiner. (Laughter.) Well now, with respect to the fishing. (Re- newed laughter. I do not fish: no man has a right to 01 to me there is a .man there with a long stick ; there is a . worm alone end—look at the fool at the other. (Laughter.) ) Well now, my friends, you perceive no blood has been drawn from me by that little bark and grump put cruelly upon me, but let me confeea I never intended to have opened my lips . again about fishing—(laughter)—about the fool and the , grub. I never intended to say a word about it but I must tell you my -crime about fishing. Now, really, I will tell you my crime. Before I had the power to permit fishing, fishing was carried on and permitted by the previous owners . of these fish; the fishing was permitted to those who paid • for it. Now, listen—to those who paid for it. When the fishing came to Gilbert Greenall he let everybody,-1 realty think he would have let the editor of The Examiner I fish. (Laughter and applause.) He really allowed every- body to fish who asked and they did fish; they fished and , they took all the fish. Well, now then, am Ito find the , fish ? If I undertook to find fish, I should be a regular fool at the end of the fishing-rod. I cannot find fish and there is no fishing. Now, there are no fish worth fishing. You ask me what my feelings are. My feeling and my in- tention is this—if the fish breed and they are in sufficient quantity Isbell never hesitate to give permission to fish (applause and a voice 'But notto Radicals ")—to any respec- table man who asks for a day's fishing when the fish is there. That is clearly understood isn't it ? I will pass on now from the subject of fishing. With respect to various mat- ters I have no political secrets; I have nothing to conceal from you; I have neve; done anything of which I am ashamed. (Hear, hear.) I hate, I abominate flogging. If I ever voted upon the subject of flogging it was in mitiga- tion of the punishment and not to increase it. (Hear, hear.) I have not voted for this severe infliction of punishment— I have voted and shall vote always for the mitigation of severity. (Hear, heat.) Don't for one moment believe that the question of 114gging will ever arise again. It won't arise again. Flogging is odious to the English chrracter, and flogging will never be perpetrated with the sanction and will of Englishmen. If flogging is ever resorted to the of- fence committed will be very extensive indeed to involve such a punishment and very rightly. Now, wills respect to my own speaking about various subjects. Foreign politics! We have enough of foreign politics—we rather know too much of the manner in which the present Government deal . with foreign subjects. England does not stand too high in the estimation of other countries. Let us raise her; let us lift her ; let England retain her true and rightful position. Let England—l will say in few words—let England be just let Eagland never fear. Those are my politics—let England be just and England then will never have cause to fear. (Hear, hear.) As the other gentlemen who are near to me have said time is quickly passing away. Here, to night, we have met again with feelings and objects and motives as we base met on previous occasions. Let us make these meet- ings useful ; let these meetings be an opportunity of our meeting together in a friendly way; and let them be special occasions made useful and made valuable by the determina- tion of our action when the day and the hour and the time of contest comes. (Applause.) Mr. CROPPER moved "That in the opinion of this meet- ing the policy of the present Government as regards Egypt has been one long record of blunder, bloodshed, and be- trayal, and consequently the authors of such a policy are not fit to be trusted to carry on the affairs of this great empire."

Councillor ScHou (Manchester) seconded this resolution, and in the course of a somewhat protracted address referred to the question of Free Trade. He said that at the present time they had not Free Trade in England, but simply had a system of free impOrts whilst our own goods were shut out from other parts of the world. The Government of the day would act very wisely were they to institute an inquiry into the causes of the present depression of trade. (Hear, hear.) Ho believed himself—though he only spoke for himself and did not wish to commit the Conservative party of Warring- ton—that to a large extent the depression of trade was really to be ascribed to the influence of the foreign tariffs, which might to some extent be mitigated by counter action on our part. (Applause.) C‘ptain RHYNOLDS moved a vote of thanks to Councilor Schou. Referring to the question of bad trade, he said no harm could come from a Government inquiry into its causes, and much good might arise from it. He did not wish to say anything harsh, for he did not believe in ill-feeling being brought about in a not very large borough, and he was there- fore rather shocked at the want of taste shown by Mr. Crosfield when he said anything of their late member—a man who had been respected so long. (Applause.) Mr. CAWLEY moved a vote of thanks to the chairman, and in doing so said that until they put a duty on foreign goods they should never do any good. (Applause.) Mr. JA3DIS RICHARDS seconded the vote of thanks, which was carried, and the Chairman having responded the meeting terminated.

Mr. Hallam Tennyson, son of the Poet Laureate' will be married to Miss Boyle at Westminster Abbey on Wedne3- day. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 21, 1884.

EXPLOSION OF A BOMB AT MADRID. MADRID, WRDNIRSDAY, 3-16. A.2ll.—An explosion occurred at about two o'clock this morning in the Calls .Sevilla, one 'of the principal thoroughfares of this city. On a search being subsequently made at the spot, it was discovered that a petard or bomb containing some explosive substance had been placed inside the doorway of one of the houses in the street. Great damage WWI caused to the building. Two large holes were made in the door, which was closed at the time, and several windows were broken. The explosion create 4 great alarm, bat no one was injured. No nine has been discovered as to the authors of the outrage.

The annual conference of visit'og. justices and other gentlemen interested in prison management was held on Wednesday in London, Sir U. K. Shuttleworth presiding. The Australians gained a remarkably easy victory over Cambridge University on Wednesday, winning by an innings and 81 runs. Hampshire beat Kea by three wickets.

Three of the Judges on Wednesday heard an appeal from a decision by the Judge of the Liverpool County Court, re- fusing to confirm a scheme of aDrangement hetNeen a debtor and his creditors. Their lordships held that the scheme was not one calculated. to benefit the creditors, and dismissed the appeal. The Liverpool City Council, at a special meeting on Wednesday, unanimously confirmed a recommendation from the Finance Committee that Mr. W. F. Prudence, deputy registrar of the Court of Passage, should be removed from his post. This action was rendered necessary by the dis- covery of grave flaancial irregularities in Mr. Prudence's department. There is a deficit, so far as ascertained, of nearly £6OO. PARDON OF A CONDEMNED MAN.—A full pardon was received at Durham on Weclnesiav for Siddle, the man cbn• demned to death for the Butterknowle murder. Siddle, who expressed great joy at the news, was liberated at half•past nine, and, accompanied by the Rev. William Batev, Primi- tive Methodist, the minister who has been in corwant at- tendance upon him, left the gaol, followed by a large crowd. He looked but little the worse for his incarceration.

' THE POISONING BY TINNED MEAT.—At an adjourned in- quest, held on Monday, on Sarah Dewin, 51, and her son Frederick, 21, who died on the 22nd ult., after partaking of a supper of tinned salmon, the report of Drs. Ballard and Clinn, Local Crrvernment officers, who had analysed the contents of the stomachs of the deceased, and the remaining portions of the salmon, attributed the deaths to the diseased condition of the fish, which was ascribed to the defective character of tbe tin, admitting atmospheric air. THE WHALLEY WILL SUIT.—In the Probate and Divorce Division, on Monday, Sir James lianuen gave his decision in the Whall-y will suit, Priestman v. Thomas and Gunnell. The plaintiff, being the illegitimate son of the testator, sought to set aside a will which has been the subject ot various suits, and by which the testator left his property to the defendant Thomas, excepting -4.:5,000 left to the plain- tiff. He sought probate for a will dated April, 1851, giving him the bulk of the property. The court gave judgment for the plaintiff en all the issues, with costs. MORMONISM.—A large body of recruits for Mormondom, left Liverpool on Saturday in the Arizona. The party num- bered about 500, and was accompanied by upwards of 20 "elders," who have been engaged on "mission " work in Europe for some years. Irishmen will read with satisfac- tion that their country furnished no recruits to the Mormon cause. Scandinavia supplied by far the larger part of the, 500, and there were contingents from England, Scotland and Wales. The two previous shipments this year via Liverpool numbered between 600 and 700 persons. THE SUICIDE OF A Cuendvarst.r.—At the inquest held on Saturday 'on the body of the Rev. F. Shepherd, vicar of Stoke-under-Hamdon, who committed suicide by hanging on Friday, it was shown that tbe death of his wife had preyed on the mind of the deceased, and that he was much affected by the suicide of ths Dean of Bangor. Indeed, he expressed a conviction that he should have a similar end. He was also under the impression that he was pecuniarily embarassed, which was proved by the Rev. M. Howe, viear of Bromley, to be a delusion. A verdict of "Suicide while Ins state of unsound mind" was returned:

NATIONAL LIBERAL Cl:cit.—The National Liberal Club have finally settled the question of a site for a new club- house, and will straightway set about building. The situa- tion is exceedingly favourable, being at the lower or ern- bankment end of Whitehall-place, with a corner looking on Whitehall-avenue. Between it and the Embankment are the pretty little gardens to be overlooked by' the private terrace of the club. It is estimated to cost L 200,000. The position of the club is very remarkable, and fully justifies this great outlay. At the end of 'April, when the first annual report was presented, the total number of members was a little under 4,000 Since then it has increased by 400, being at the rate of more than 200 a month.

-- AGES ow ELEMENTARY TEACHEas.—A return of the ages of certified teachers now engaged in the elementary schools of England and Walea gives certtin• curious results. The total number of male teachers is 15.300, and of female teachers there are 21,511. Of 20 years of age there are 31 males and 72 females; of e 0 years there are 53 males and 21 female,; and from that age the excess of males over fe- males until 76 is reached is very remarkable. There are two males and one female 76 years of age, one of each sex 77 years old, one of each sex 78 years of age. The females be- tween 20 and 38 greatly outnumber the males, from 22 years of age to 25 they are more than double the number of males, but from 38 years the males show a preponderance (except I at the age of 43) until the 70's are reached. A CHESHIRE ESTATE UNTAXED —The guardians of the I Nantwich Union have received a letter from „the Local . Government Batrd stating they have caused to b)ir noted for ' their consideration the case of exemption from rating of the Beam Heath estate, Nantwich. By a local act of Parlia- ment the trustees of the estate are freed from paying any rates Gr taxes, and the income derived upon the property is distributed in the tows, each householder receiving a sove- reign annually. The guardians have called the attention of the hoard to the fact that all the charitable institutions in the United Kingdom are rated, and regard it as a glaring injustice that the Beam Heath estate is not required to con- tribute any money to the funds of the union. The board say there is no probability of the matter being dealt with in the present session of Parliament. BOATING ACCIDENTS.—A Little Curtabrae farmer, named Neil, was drowned on Saturday evening, together with hiaa son, by the capsizing of a boat in which they were returning , home from Millport, a village upon the island of Great Cunabrae in the Firth of Clyde. Five young men rowing on the Liffey at Dublin, on Sunday evening, were thrown into the water, and two were drowned. A young gentleman, named Gifford, on Sunday, rowed big brother and himself into Plymouth Sound. He then undressed and jumped into the sea. Whilst swimming about he was seized with cramp. The boat meanwhile drifted from him, and his brother was unable to render him any assistance. Two amateur fisher- men hearing his cries, however, pulled to the spot, an,' one, named Everett, jumped into the sea without divesting him- self of any clothing. The body of Mr. Gifford, however, soon disappeared. Everett was subsequently picked up by a man-of-war's boat, much exhausted. NEWSPAPER PRESS FUND—The annual festival was held on Saturday evening at Willis's Roams, London, Lord Hampden presiding. Cardinal Manning and General Gra- ham were among the speakers. The latter said that the presence of newspaper correspondents in the field might embarrass a general, but that difficulty might be overcome by mutual good feeling. He bore testimony to the services rendered in the last campaign by newspaper correspond- ents.—The Ch4rman spoke of the progress made, especially by the provincial press, and dilated on the functions and public benefit of the press. The press might exist without Parliament, but Parliament could scarcely exist without the press—that press which stood higher than in any other country in the world, justifying the pride felt in it by Englishmen.—Mr. Hyde Clarke' the treasurer, stated that the subscriptions amounted to close upon £l,ooo.—The musical arrangements, which were under the direction of Sir Julius Benedict, were highly attractive. Mr. Sims Reeves sang" Tom Bowling " and "The Bay of Biscay." The other vocalists were Mdlle. Reg,eiana, Miss Gertrude Gris- wold, Signor Novara, and Mr. Frederick King. LIBERAL VICTORY AT LINCOLN.—The polling at Lincoln on Saturday resulted in an easy victory for Mr. Ruston, the Liberal candidate, who received 3,234 votes as against 2,263 recorded for his Conservative opponent, Mr. Han. The Liberal victory is all the more gratifying seeing that the Censervatives, who, at the General Election, were disor- ganised had now a new organisation; they had started a Conservative working men's club; they had been harangued by Lord Cranbrook and Mr. Henry Chaplin' M.P.,some time ago, and three days before the election they had been cheered by the presence and speeches of Sir Richard Cross, M.P., and Mr. Edward Stanhope, M.P., to say nothing of Mr. Marriott, M.P. The Conservative candidate, Mr. Richard Hall, was very popular among all classes, especially the working class. Conservative sp-akers vehemently denounced the foreign policy of the Government; no abuse was spared. Quotations from Mr. Frederic Harrison, Mr. Laboochere, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, and other Liberals, were all invoked to defeat the Liberals. The election was settled by the simple question, "Gladstone or Salisbury?" THE SUSPECTED MURDER AT NEW BRIGHTON.—Mr. Mor- ris, who was arrested at Wallasey on the charge of poisoning his wife, has b)en released on bail. He says he is gtad that he will now have an opportunity of meeting the accusations which for some time past his late wife's relatives have uttered against him. Mr. Morris had been married twice Previously, and had a fortune of about £5,000, besides an income of £l5O per annum. In April last the magistrates of Wirral, by direction of the Home Office, held a private in- quiry, and decided that there was no foundation for the charges against Mr. Morrie.—On Wednesday Mr. Morris was before the Wallasey justices, and on an application by the prosecution he was again remanded for a week en bail. The witness Whittle, on whose testimony the charge mainly rests in the absence of a searching analysis of Mrs. Morris's body, came forward and stated that she had not in any de- gree withdrawn her previous statement—that she saw the prisoner put" something "into his wife's medicine, which she afterwards drank. Whittle appeared greatly anxious not to do anything "illegal," and said that if her previous depositions was of that nature she " would not stand by it." The prisoner's counsel intimated that if at the next hearing nenhime, more was brought against his client an application would be made for bi immediate discharge. The magistra- tes requested chat those having charge of the prosecution would ex nelite the inquiry as much as possible. EARL SPENCERAT .BELFAST. —The Lord Lieutenant of . . . .

accompanied by Countess Spencer, Arrived in Bel- fast on Tuesday evening, and was escorted by a large pro- cession to the Mayor's residence. There was but the faint- est exhibition of the ill-feeling towards his Excellency which has been so loudly proclaimed during the past week. The Orangemen of Belfast held a meeting on Monday night, at which a 't protest" was adopted, for presentation to his Excellency, against his policy of suppressing loyal ad encourar,'ing disloyal meetings. Loyd C. J. Hamilton. M.P., presided, and indulged in a great amount of vitupera- tive lamtuage directed to Mr. Gladstone and his " contempt; ible" Government. Lord Arthur Hill, M.P , said that in case peaceful protests against a "slavish submission of the authorities to arnarchists and revolutionists" had no effect, it would be the solemn duty of the loyalists to prepare for the inevitable outcome of that surrender —a repetition of what was done at Derry and the Boyne. Lord Spencer was very cordially received in Belfast on Wednesday. His Lordship unveiled a portrait of the Queen in the Town Hall, and afterwards laid the foundation stone of a public library.

NEWTON RACES. Judge, Handicapper, and Clerk of the Scales, Mr. Richard Johnaon ; Starter, Mr. R. I'Anson ; Clerks of the Course and Stakeholders, Messrs. Davrsoa and Johnson ; Secre- tary. Mr. J. E. Pardey. TUESDAY. -

The curtailment of the Newton Meeting to two days was the work of the Stewards of the Jockey Club, who, when they had to re-arrange the various gatherings of the year in order to prevent that "undue multiplication of meetings," which had been so, much complained of, had no enviable task. However, experience has proved to most clerks of the course that a two-days' meeting pays better than a three, and it is hoped this will be the experience of the Newton management, for the famous midway gathering between Manchester and Liverpool has a history that time will not impair in a historicil sense, although competition here, there, and everywhere might have done, had not the meeting been cut down. Newton is a very ancient place. At a little farm-house just bdow the railway arch which spans the Warrington road, Lancashire historians say one of the kings of Northumberland lived. The said Image is now being modernised, and is fast losing its old English aspect it once had. The early morning broke very gloomy, and for a long time rain threatened, but happily it held off and gave place to heat. The attendance was very good, but there was only one steward present, Mr. Lee', and he at once appointed Mr. R. Gladstone to act with him according to rule. All the entries went to the post for the All-aged Welter, for which Paparona was made favourite. She alone of the three placed preserved a straight course—probably owing to the better going in the centre of the track—and she won Cleverly by a neck from the Princess Alice colt, who evi- dently stays well. For the Copeland Welter the Cataconia mare made the pace so hot that she had everything in trouble, except Herald, but Herald always commanded, and won easily by six lengths, which distance separated the second and Cirrus. Londonderry, a powebfu/ short-legged colt, by Castlereagh out of Blue Ninny, started favourite for the Gol borne Park Stakes at 9 to 4, whilst a better style of colt by Pero Gomez out of Bonny May was rather neg- lected at 5 to 1. John Ostorne, who rode London- derry, had his horse weli in hand, and, bringing him up half way in the straight, be settled the others, and won in a canter by half a length. Only six starters put in an appearance for the Manor Cup, for which Newton, after his defeat of Corrneille in the Dee Stakes (and the latter's vic.ory over Lucerne at Ascot), was backed against the field, although he carried 11b. over-weight for Bowman's assistance; whilst Hesperian, who was ridden by W. Platt, put up 21b. over-weight. He nevertheless started second favourite, whilst Campanile was next in demand. The remainder were on offer at 100 to 8. A singular acci- dent was witnessed in this race. Dutch Roll and Campanile I set the pace, but they had only proceeded a few strides be- I fore Monacella struck into the heels of Blairgowrie and threw the jockey. Dunn, heavily. At first it was feared he was severely injured, but he was immediately examined I after being carried back to the stand. Luckily no bones were broken, and the little chap escaped with a severe shak- ing. Monacella, after she had got rid of her jockey, sadly hampered the rear lot, which were thrown all abroad, whilst Campanile dropped back last, behind Newton, five furlongs from home. As they reached the foot of the hill Monacella had headed Dutch Roll, who was attended by Blairgowrie, and when the riderless one had jumped the rails instead of going into the straight, the race asseLned a new phase. Blairgowrie was the first to give way, and long before they reached the distance Hesperian had headed Dutch Roil, and, taking up the running, he looked like coming in alone to the half-distance, where Newton began to creep I up, but he could never get on terms, and was beaten a length, which distance separated second and third. Juniper started favourite for the All-aged Sell. hag Plate, but she is Very moderate, and stopped to nothing at last; indeed, Sophonisba beat her in a canter, and was I bought in for 75 gns. Maqtla Boy made play at such a pace that he looked all over the winner of the Hunters' Flat Race until half way in the straight, when the hard ground I affected his dickey leg, and he was easily beaten by Gracie, who was bought in for 130 ens. Marsh boy pulled up very lame. The Makerfield Handicap brought out seven run- ners. Harebell IL started a great favourite, with Chameleon next in demand; Jane Shore and Earl Chatham were also freely backed, whilst 7 to 1 was laid against Sweet Sound, and as much as 20 to 1 was on offer against Review, although, as a matter of fact, his owner took 70 to 10, but a fair price to return would be 10 to 1, as very few book- makers laid their money. Fleta set the pace, but she was done with half way in the straight, when Harebell 11. took un the running, and looked to have the race in hand until Review rushed up so full of running that he soon settled the hopes of the Nottingham division of sportsmen, and won easily by half a length from the favourite, who was three lengths in front of Fleta, who had the same advantage over 1 Jane Shore, who was placed fourth. WEDNESDAY. Glorious weather favoured the concluding day of the Newton fixture, and although the Cup is not the i-nportant race it was in years gone by, it has its attraction for the local people, who made a better show than or. the opening afternoon, while the meeting was again well patronised by the professional element. The ground was still very hark but this did not affect the fields, and some interesting racing was witnessed, a start being made with the Grand Stand Plate, which proved the goad thing it looked for Export. Zig— aag compensated the Chilton people for his defeat on the previous day by taking the Lyme Park Stakes after a good race with the Manchester winner, Nightcap; and after Hedgehog had landed the Earlestown Plate, five came out forth. Newton Cup. Duncan, who declined his Ascot en— gagement, started favouite, and won by half a length from Billycock, but his performance was not considered suffi— ciently meritorious for any move to be made in his favour for the Northumberland Plate. Truce, alter showing a lot of temper at the post, landed the Juvenile Plate, and the Tocher filly took the St. Helens Welter.
