SWINDLERS AT THE RACES. It has become to be looked upon as a mere matter 01 fact that the races bring into Earlestown the " scum " of the two great cities, Manchester and Liverpool, who seek to ply their nefarious practices upon the unsuspecting and easily-duped individuals. This Tear has been no exception to its predecessors in that respect. Visifors to the common could not fail to notice the presence of the customary three- card tricksters and their gangs of " sweeteners,' or the dubious-looking scampish individuals apparently desirous of a friendly rub against others sides with a cunning glance at their pockets or watches. Then there were the usual ot- dlice ice gamblers e3g.rta,asanimni apgdobenbi persons isednt nishangset attendance,nyevrwee dai egkariietglnaeg.nn, ctttiahereyneoe dcfl eh common the large cowardlylmßabornin olte a' number elasnlwi e dr escape. l s el ibate. sey r os A' of: v;istcpeewi onraNi dni erw the races each day a special court was held at the Earlestown Police Station. and the guilty ones were brought up to re- ceive the punishment they so richly merited. On Tuesday, I before Robert Houghton, Esq , a dozen individuals were. charged with offences arising out of gaming. Henry Ton- i ham was charged with gaming with cards, and George I Brown, Isaac Hargreaves, and George Smith were charged I with aiding and abetting. A fine of 203 was imposed on each prisoner, with the exception of Smith, who was dis- charged. Patrick Donnelly and Richard Ford, for gaming with cards, were also fined 20s and costs. The following persons were each fined a like.amonnt for gaming with dice, Michael Bird, Joseph Lees, Margaret Robinson Saml. L Williams, James Sharpies, and James Robinson. Or: Wed- nosday, before George McCorquodale, Esq.., Robert Ent- wistle WAS fined 203 for gaining with cards; William Baines was fined a like amount for gaming with dice ; a like penalty was imposed on Thomas Rooney and Chas. Walker for gaining with " turning-tables ;" and Elizibeth Jones was also fined 20s for gaming with a "Billy fair play." Henry Wilson was brongnt up on a charge of attempting to pick r pockets, and he was fiend 20s and costs. STRIPPING A "WELSHER." An unusual incident, and one which created a lively in- terest, was witnessed on the race-course on Wednesday- Towards the close of the day's racing, one of the numerous "welshers "got hold of the money of several young men on the assumption that he was a bookmaker, and attempted to make a clean sweep by decatnping. Unfortunately for him, however, he WAS observed, and, the irate individuals. whom he had attempted to " fleece " quickly laid hold of bite. He was seizrd in the middle of theecourse. opposite the briek-bars, thrown to the ground, his pockets rifled, and what money there was therein thrown in the air. The would- be " welsher " was not even then allowed to escape, for the, angry crowd literally rote the man's clothes from his body, leaving him naked. The man ultimately got away from the crowd and succceeded in placing a few rags round his body, making himself it little more decent than when his captors had finished with him.

_PERIAL PARLIAMENT. ' HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took is seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four o'clock. Tan MANowas-run Slur CANAL BILL.—On the motion of the Earl of REDESDALE, the Manchester Ship Canal Bill was read a third time and passed. Eaypr, &c.—Lord CARLINGFORD (in the absence of Earl Granville) said a telegram had within the last hour been re- ceived by the Government stating that the fall of Berber was still open to great doubt. In reply to a question by Dord Salisbury, Lord KIMBERLEY said the communicatioas With France on the subject of the Conference were new 'closed, and the terms would forthwith be communicated ta the other Powers. On MondaN the Government hoped to be able to make a statement on the subject to Parliament. THE IRISH LAND ACT.—The Duke of ARGYLL called at- tention to the working and effect of the Irish Land Act, and Moved for various papers connected therewith. The noble flake, who spoke for over two hours, delivered a trenchant criticism on the land legislation of the Government, much aPPlauded from the Opposition benches. Lord CARLING- HORD prefaced his defence of the Government by the obser- vation that the Duke of Argyll had delivered a speech of great ability and eloquence without anv clear conception of the subject with which he dealt. After some remarks from the Marquis of Waterford, the Earl of Leitrim, the Lord Chancellor, Earl Fortescue, and Lord Derby, who spoke in the hearing of five peers, the motion was, with slight altera- tion agreed to, and at twenty-five minutes past eight their lordships adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes to four o'clock. MisceeLeereons.—Replying to a storm of questions, the ATTORNEY-GENERAL said assizes would continue to be held iS every county as before, and also in every place as before, With the exception of Kingston-on-Thames. Of 54 assize towns 40 would have only one judge; the remaining 14 Would continue to have two. An assize would be held at Birmingham twice a year —Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to lir. Cyril Flower, said the Government were by no means indisposed to entertain the subject of the purchase of a por- tion of the Blenheim pictures; but no offer had yet been made which they would have felt justified in accepting. —.Replying to Mr. Bourke, the PREMIER repeated the Statement as to the Conference made in the other House by Lord Kimberley.—Answering a supplementary question by Mr. Bourke, the PREMIER confirmed his declaration that the Whole of the proceedings in respect of the Conference would fall to the ground without the assent of Parliament He could not agree to submit the negotiations with the French Government to the HOU9O before they had been laid before the Powers—ln answer to a question by Sir M. H. Beach, Air. ASHLEY confirmed the newspaper reports of the defeat Of Usibepu by the Boers and Zulus.—Mr. Ruston, newly- elected for Lincoln, and Mr. Huntley aPearthy. who suc- ceeds Sir John Ennis in the representation of Athlone, were Introduced and took their seats, loudly cheered, the first by the Liberals, the second by the Parnellites. THE EntrcaTime ESTIMATES —The House then went into Committee of Supply, aud Mr. MONDELLA, in a lucid 111:keech explained the education votes. He pointed out that for the first time in the history of the Education Depart-1 bent the sum required for public education in England and Wales exceeded three millions sterling. The actual SUM allowed an increase of over £77,000, which chiefly arose from increases in the annual grants for day and evening scholars. The schools inspected were 18,540, showing an , increase of 251 over the preceding year. They afforded ac- 'commodation for 4,670,000 children, being an increase of 123,000 over last year. The scholars on the register num- bered 4.273,000, an increase of 84,009 over last year. The Scholars in average attendance were 3,127,000. being an in- crease of 112,000, figures which. Mr. Mundella observed, ShOWed steady progress all along the line. At the present time, exclusive of all private adventure schools or middle class schools, one in every six of the population was ,aPon the relic of the elementary schools, a far aigher number had ever been reached in English education. --Mr. STANLEY LEIGHTON moved an amendment to reduce the vote by the amount of increase in the charge foi in- aloectore, upon which he based a vehement protest against alleged over-pressure in schools. He was followed by Mr. 4. Buxton, Mr. Walter, Mr..J, G. Hubbard—who contended That religious education ought to be connected with all aehools receiving grants from the State, failing which he ..,_alated for an increased grant for voluntary echools—Mr. Welter James, and Lord Algernon Percy, who supported Mr. Leighton's observations on over-pressure in schools.— Illingworth proposing to give a new turn to the debate, ....the Chairman suggested that the amendment before the Committee should be disposed of. The House was cleared for a division, but this was not insisted upon, and the amendment was negatived.—Mr. Illingworth contended that over-pressure was greatly exaggerated, and with res. Peet to 'religious education, observed that the State leaving withdrawn from auv responsibility in regard to religion, the national educational system should cs confined to secular teaching, religious instruc- tion being dealt with in some other way.—After loins words from Lord Burghley and Mr. Spencer, who dif- fered on the circumstances tinder which a School Board was established at Northampton, Lord George Hamilton de- elated, amid cheers from Mr. Warton and Mr. Tomlinson, that the whole voluntary system was in peril." This lie Illustrated by a narrative of circumstances under which a tiehool Board was established in Willesden against, as be alleged, the wishes of the large Majority of the inhabitants, and contrary to the spirit of the Act and contrary to the 4,l,‘st as administered by Mr. Forster.—Mr. FORSTER pointed 'oli With examples, that in 1871. several cases occurred Where, as at Willesden, the school accommodation not being 111101Cient, a School Board was ordered by the Department, contrary to the wishes of the majority of the ratepayers. Re warned Churchmen not to strain the Act. If the mana- gers of voluntary schools tried to make Dissenters come to their schools, they would hasten legislation which they Would not like.—The debate was continued by Mr. G. Tal- cot and Mr. L. Stanley.—The vete was agreed to, and, the remaining orders disposed of, toe House adjourned at a ' quarter past two o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TVESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a (I/tarter-past four o'clock. ,„ Ildreceer..eamons.—The Earl of Sandwich and Viscount -lOrrington took the oath and their seats. Lord Dorches- ter bore testimony to the exaggerated nature Of the reports ,S.hotit the yeomanry riots at Lichfield. Lord Morley under. '°k that careful inquiry should be made into the matter. Just before the House rose the noble lord stated that he had !eceived a televam from the Inspector of Auxiliary Forces, la which he stated that the reports of riotous conduct among the Yeomanry were "absolutely without foundation.' , '4ll the motion ef Lord Redesdale a Bill dealing with pigeon Shooting was read a second time. Lord Sudeley moved bthe second reading of the I:Lyda-park-corner (New Streets) the object of which, he explained, was to enable angements to be made with the local authorities to take Charge of the maintenance of new streets in this locality, It alte.„. intended to refer the Bill to a Select Committee.—Lord f,owts moved the rejection of the Bill, a motion which had "le support of Lord Salisbury and other Conservative peers. a division the second reading was refused by 94 votes against 70 —The Earl of MOUNT-EDGCUMBE moved the rond reading of the Cornwall Sunday Closing Bill.—Lord UNWELL moved the rejoction of the measure, which was BaPlaorted by Lord Aberdare, the Bishop of Carlisle, the rehbishop of Canterbury, and the Earl of Kimberley.— esertheless, on a division it was rejected by 57 votes algainst 39.—One or two other Bills were advanced a stage, 1/44 at five minutes to eight their lordships adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair shortly after twe o'clock.

Egypt. : A SNUB FOR MR. A. BARTLETr.—Mr. AAR. r;tap-BairrtErr, under the guise of a question, adminis- led six interrogatories to the Under-Secretary for Foreign t'''asirs with respect to affairs inEgypt. As the Under-Sec- starY pointed out, three of the questions were matters of ?Pinion on which the member, for Eye must form his own 111(.121:mint. Answers to the other questions did not add mu- tt 1118 material to information already possessed by the pub- f s• This shorter catechism was supplemented by questions ro Sir Herbert Maxwell, Mr. J. Lowther (2), Lord Folke- 7ne (2), Sir W. Barttelot (2), Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett an ad- .uttional four, making ten to his credit. Replying to oue of :-.Grd, Folkestone's questions, Lord E. FITZMAURICE pleaded taat it was " impossible for him or anybody else under any circumstances to be expected to know what Hussein' Xlmlifa said to somebody else on April 23." Mr. Orladstone at length interposed, and protested against the practice of Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett. "Lie is," the Premier said, " constantly making grossly inaccurate statements which he coolly ascribes to me. I never used e words he has uttered." This referred to a statement by 1▪ 13e member for Eye that the Prime Minister had informed l'ise House that the fall of Berber would not affect the post- , "Ns at Khartoum. "I must say," the Premier continued, alllid loud cheers from the Liberals present, " that unless ~ttle hon. member changes his habit no attention ought to be ▪ Sid to him." Replying to Sir Henry Tyler, Mr. Glad- said it had been the duty of the Government to COO- Very carefully ail.questions relating to the probability sending an expedition southward in Egypt. Amongst others the question of the expediency of constructing a :I.lllway between Souakim and the Nile had been under con- .teleration. Further than that he did not think it would be 4er the public interest that he should make any statement. ta.TRE FRANCRISE BILL.—The House then resumed corn- • on the Franchise Bill.—Mr. HERRy FOWLER pro- a new clause providing that the Act shall come into 7• eration on the first day of January. 1585, which, as has Zteady been explained, has the practical effect that the 04!"IY-ereated electors would be able to exercise the Iran- i, Ise on the let of January, 1.886.—Mr. GLansroNa said .ITe Proposed clause would enable the present House to deal ,Ith redistribution, whilst it would not absolutely make the ration of the new franchise dependent upon the passing ta Redistribution Bill. On the part of the Government be ,eartily accepted the clause.—The matter, which has a1:4k6:1(1,Y :4k6:1(1,Y been twice discussed, was further considered by Mr. d• B tlfour, Mr. C. Lewis, Mr. Collins, and Mr. Rtikes.- 2rd REINDOLPH CHURCHILL expressed the opinion that the arantee- given by the Government that they would next , proceed with a Redistribution Bill Was of some and was one not to be lightly repudiated. It" ▪ asked what steps the Government would take la NW session proved too short for deal- • with redistribution; and whether it might not be pas- du to relieve the working hours of next year by issuing "lig the autumn recess a Boundary Commission.—Mr. TONE said the Government having giveFi a pledge to • e_ a redistribution scheme next year were bound to take toolahsidiary steps to carry it out.—Sir & NORTIIC3TB exception to the proposal about the Boundary Commis- • observing that the further they proceeded with the

Bill the more clear it became how inconvenient it was not to have contemporaneously introduced a redistribution scheme.—Mr. Tomlinson, atiempting to prolong the discus- Ellen, was met by loud cries for the division, which he re- sented by a motion to report progress, ultimately withdrawn. —Mr. C. Lewis having made a second speech, and after some words from Lord John Manners and Sir Robert Peel, the committee divided, the clause being carried by 258 votes against 130, a result hailed with loud cheers from the Ministerial side.—Progress was then reported, and the Re- port of Supply being agreed to, the sitting was suspended at ten minutes to seven. ORDER OD ButswEss.—On resuming at nine o'clock, Mr. STEYENSON moved the adoption of e new Standing Order to the effect that on Wednesdays, if the debate on the first order of the day, or any order that has been reached by two o'clock (not being a proceeding in Committee, nor oil the consideration of a Bill as amended, nor oid the consideration of Lords' amendments) be continued until five o'clock. Mr. Speaker shall put the question then under discussion ; and if the previous question, or a motion of adjourntnent, or an amendment to the main question sball have been moved, they shall be severally put, and afterwards the main ques- tion shall be put without further debate.—This was seconded by Mr. Haareerns.—Mr. Gieensroxe thought the matter was worth the trial, and agreed to its adoption as a resolution, though not as a Standing Order.—The motion was also op- posed from the Conservative side by Mr. Warton, Mr. Clark, Sir W. Barttelot, Mr. Chaplin, and Sir S. Northcote, finding a warm supporter in Lord R. Churchill.—At tweuty minutes to twelve Mr. PULESTON moved the adjournment, which on a division was carried by 115 votes against 92—a result greeted with prolonged cheering from the Conservative benches. The actual majority was made up by the votes of the Parnellites. Lord R. Churchill and Sir H. Wolff voted for the motion.—Mr. A. O'CONNOR brought forward his motion on the French case, and, the remaining orders dis- posed of, the House adjourned at fifty minutes past twe. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker entered the Housie at ten minutes past twelve o'clock, but there was not a quorum until one o'clock, at which hour the right hon, gentleman took the chair. CAURCLI PATRONAGE BILL.—Mr. LFATIIAM, in moving the second reading of this bill, WAS quite sure that the patronage abuses would long since have been swept away had it been generally known that the right to take care of other men's souls was a marketable one. This bill provided that the patron of a living should receive half the patronage value, the patronage thereupon passing to the Crown. It proposed that the change should be effected through the agency of Queen Anne's Bounty Board. Public opinion, Mr. Leathern said, demanded a bill like this, which would prevent' scandals such as that of purchasing of an advowson by an eminent jeckey, who gave £1,500 I for it, and of the Racecourse, Company which, denting to enlarge the racecourse by the addition of a portion of the glebe, found it necessary also to buy the advovvson. Mr. Rylands seconded themotion. Mr. Albert Grey moved AR amendment declaring that "this House, affirming the pin- ciple that Church patronage is a trust to be exercised for the benefit of the parishioners, is of opinion that no reform in the law affecting Church patronage will be efficient or satisfactory which does not enable the parishioners to veto the presentment to a benefice of any clergyman whom they i consider unsuitable. This was seconded by Mr. Brinton. Sir R. Cross, being in favour of the principle of the Bill, suggested that it should be referred to a Select Committee, a propesel he recommended to the House by offering to serve upon the Committee himself. After some words from Mr. Cropper, Sir William Harcourt said the system of selling the cure of souls was one of the greatest dangers of the Estab- lishment and could not be defended. He criticised some of the details of the measure, but agreed to the second reading, which he regarded as a declaration by the Houte of Com- mons that it condemned a practice that was injurious 'and ecandaleus.—Mr. TALBOT also agreed to the second reading, in the hope that the Bill would be referred to a Select Com- mittee —Mr. Illingworth and Mr. Stuart Wortley supported Bill.—Mr. L. STANLEY supported the amendment, regarding it as a necessary supplement to the Bill. —Mr. Hubbard and Mr. Cubitt would agree to the second reading.—Mr. Rideau]) (as Mr. Illinzworth had done) answered some charges brought against Nonconformist members of obstructing Bill designed to remedy griev- ances in the Church.—Mr. LABOUCABRE declared that he would neither vote for nor against the Bill. He was opoosed to all tinkering up of the Church of England. If his support was wanted they should bring in a Bill for the disestahlishment and disendowment of the church. Amid manifestations of interest en the Conserva- tive aide the hem. gentleman lightly sketched such a Bill, a principal feature in which was that he would leave to the church all moneys that had been left it within the last I twenty years. After some words from Mr. Tom Collins the I House divided on the amendment, which was rejected by 141 votes against 83, and the Bill was read a second time. I On the motion of Mr. Stanhope it was referred to a Select Committee, Mr. ALBERT GREY giving notice that he would ' move that it be an instruction to the Committee to intro- duce clauses in the Bill in the sense of his amendment. I Mr. Warton talked out the Yorkshire Sunday Closing Bill, and at five minutes to six the House adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tnuitsnay. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—SeveraI measures of secondary import- ance were advanced a stage in the House of Lords.—Lord STANLEY of ALDERLEY proposed to condemn the Education Deportment for " forcing " a School Board on the perish of Bothwell, Northampton, and insisting upon the 'creation of a new school in a Dorsetshire village.—Lord CARLINGFORD defended his department, which, he maintained, had done nothing out of the common or in any way oppostel to public Policy. The resolution was negatived.—Earl GRaNVILLE informed the House, in-replying to a question by Earl De La Warr, that there was much exaggeration in the reports of French designs on Morocco. He bad received solemn assur- ancee from the French Government that they hail no wish to annex, protect, or cause trouble in that country, witn which they were now in friendly negotiation regirding some States in the interior.—The House adjourned at a quarter to seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIiteRSDIY.

The Spe—asire-r-t;ok-the chair at four O'CIOCk. THE LICHFIELD DISTCRBANCES.—Lord HatammoN, in answer to a question about the Lichfield disturbances, said he was not fully satisfied that the statements made in the newspapers hal been sufficiently investigated, and he had directed that a further inquiry should be made into the matter. Tug DEFENCE OF EGYPT —ln reply to Mr. Bourke, Lord HARTINGTON said Her Majesty's Government were of opinion that the British forces now in Egypt, with those of the Egyptian Government, were sufficient for the defence of Upper Egypt against any danger that appeared likely at present to menace it. 11p to the present time the command and disposition of the Khedive's army had been entirely dis- tinct from that of the British forces in Egypt. Recently, however: to avoid confusion, instructions were given to make arrangementfl that the Khedive's Government should place the command of both services and the joint disposal of all the forces in Egypt in the hands of the general officer commanding the British forces. Sir E Wood would command the Egyptian ttoops.—ln answer to Sir- S. Northcote, Mr. GLADS roNE said he would make a short ex- planation on Monday with reference to the French nego- tiations in such a way that any member could mike any 1 observations on it.—S.me time was occupied by Mr. B art- lett's repudiation of certain charges of inaccuracy of state- ment made against him two or three evenings ago by the Prime Minister.—Mr. GLADSTO/sIE, in his reply, said the hon. gentleman's statements indicated a carlessness of habit which he hoped he would correct. THE FRANCHISE BILL—The House having gone into Committee on the Franchise Bill, Mr. Houtnswon.rx moved a new clause proposing to repeal the existing seven miles' limit of residence for " occupiers "in boroughs, and extend the limitation to 25 miles. This extension, be argued, was called for by the change of circumstances, since the seven miles limit was enacted in 1832, consequent on the growth of many boroughs; and the fact that their centres were being more and more devoted to business mar- posse, while those who carried on that business resided at greater distances from the towns. Mr. GLADSTONE strongly opposed the proposal, which, he said; was intended to ex- tend the principle of doable voting. The clause was re- jected by 137 votes to 38. The remaining proposed new clauses were disposed of, and the Chairman was ordered amid Ministerial cheers to report the bill as amended to the House. It was announced that the stage of report would be taken on Monday. The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill was then taken up, and, the remaining orders disposed of, the House ad- journed at five minutes to two.

"What a incomprehensible Mirandy's got to be sauce she went to thur 'cademy," remarked Mrs. Homespun to her husband. "Why, wot's the gal been doin' now?" asked Daniel. "Doin'!" exclaimed Mrs. Homespun •, " w'y, she said she must go to her room to disrobe, as she wished to retire early." "Disrobe and retire?" murmured Daniel; "wot's them, ma ?" "I dunno," replied ma • "but she didn't do nothin' o' the sort. She only undressed and went to bed. Did yer ever hear o' eich p'evarication?" Judg- ing from the groan that came from Daniel, it is safe to pre- sume that he never did.—American Paper. TuE PRESTON BANK FRaUDS —TULLY DISCITARGED.— Considerable surprise was caused at Preston on Thursday morning by a telegram front New York stating that Gerald Thomas Tully, in custody for forging papers and embezzling £15,000, had been discharged. Tully Was on Monday ex- trauited by the Commissioners. His lawyer then appealed, and the case came before the Appellate Court on Wednesday. The judges reversed the decision of the commis,doner, and discharged Tully, bolding that he WAS not extraditable, and taking as a precedent tha decision given by Lord Jostle. Cockburn in the Windsor case. This morning detective Brown wires that he alarts home to-day in the Baltic. Another cablegram says:—Tully has been re-arrested on a civil action to recover £15,000 from the prisoner. :Unless the prisoner finds bail for this sum he can by the law of the State be kept in custody for two years, taking a non-resident in New York. By this actima the bank hopes to recover the money Tully has with him. SHAM CHAWPAGNR.—The champaene districts of the Conti- nent, produce sorne 300.000,000 bottles annually. Onlv cc e- h .11 of this quantity is exported, anel yet England and Americs aloue are said to consume more than twice this vast production. From whence does the balance come? From the apple orchards on both sides the Atlantic Yes, it is these aphle orcbards that are responsible for most of the cheaper obampag, es Now OahniaCit tc CO. are offering an AMERICAN CIDER CTTAMPAWIE—the PURE turas of American apples—which they might easily pass off as a champagne at ten times the price: but they prefer to call a spade a spade! They are confident that everyone who tastes this most delicious and wholesome beverage, will, like Oliver Twist, ask for more.—idet.

EGYPT AND THE FALL OF BERBER—MESSAGE FROM THE MAHDI. CAIRO, SAMTIRDAY.—The fall of Berber is announced to- day by the Governor of Dongola, and it is stated that the False Prophet's Ameer is marching upon the town, The Governor, who some time ago disregarded the order sent to him to evacuate the town with the garrison, now himself purposes to take this step. Cam, MONDAY.—The Mudir of Dongola telegraphs to Nubar Pasha that a messenger from the Mandi has come to him with letters naming him Emir of Pongola, and exhort- ing him at once to join his standard if he,hopes for salva- tion at the last day. At the conclusion of a long religious and fanatical peroration comes the practical advice that the Mudir is to hold Dongola for the Mandi if he can, but if the Turks should prove too strong for him he had better leave and join the Matadi at El Obeid. The Mandi declares that he will make short work of a Turkish military expedi- tion to the Soudan should one be sent. The Mandi's Emir Shemaun is also making an active propaganda, and the other day he met Sheikh Jebran and invited the latter to join him. iMason Bey telegraphs from the far eastern Soudan that Gedaveef had fallen. He states that King John intends marching on Barka, and that he has three thousand Gallas round Adowa. The population of Assouan and the neightourhood appear to have been panic-stricken by the news of the fall of Berber, and are said to be leaving in considerable numbers. In consequence of this report Capt. Bedford has visited the town on an armed steamer, and his presence has had a re-assuring affect. Standard. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY.—Official contradictions are given to the report that Bessem Pasha .would shortly be despatched on a naission to the Soudan, and to the statement that the Ottoman Government had agreed in principle to send Turkish troops to the Soudan. THE DEFENCE OF LOWER EGYPT. CAIRO, THURSDAY.—The Egyptian cavalry has left Cairo for Aesouan, to which place it will be conveyed in flat-bot- tomed boats, towed by steamers, iestead of marching the distance. Admiral Hewitt telegraphs that he will sail for Mauritius on the 26th Inst. Captain Speedy will remain at Massowah Pending the ratification of the treaty concluded with the King of Abyssinia. Four dlficers and twelve men of the Royal Engineers are expected here in order to complete the strength of the com- pany now under orders for Suakim. THE ABYSSINIAN EXPEDITION. ADEN, MONDAY.—Admiral Hewitt has arrived here on his return from Abyssinia. CAIRO, MONDAY.—The 28th Company of Royal En- gineers has been ordered to Suakirn. A telegram from Mason Bey, Governor of Massowah, announces that Admiral Hewitt's mission retu nei there on the 12th met, and that King John has engaged to. secure the relief of the Kassala II garrison by way of the Gallabat district. According to official intelligence, the Gallas have assembled at Adowa ' with that object. THE PROPOSED EXPEDITION. A Woolwich correspondent says a stock of railway mate- rials in store at the Royal Arsenal, which is to be sent at an early date to the Red Sea for the purpose of constructing a military line from Suakim to Berber, has been inspected by Royal Engineers. A ship has been selected for its convey- ance, and is expected at Woolwich this week. Two small locomotives, purchased about two years since for a Govern- ment railway in Cyprus, will form part of the equipment, and orders for others have been given. They are adapted to the narrow-gauge tramway laid down at the Royal Ar- senal. The rails are to be laid to form a line only 18 inches I wide. The engines are 15 to 20-horse power, capable of I drawing about 40 tons. It is calculated the entire line can l be constructed in about three weeks. There is no activity In the Commissariat Department. The Press Association Chatham's correspondent says it is intended to immediately despatch a comfaany of Royal Engineers from Chatham for service in Egypt as a railway company. The eight company, under the command of Major Scott, has been selected, and is being made up to its full foreign service strength from the dep6t companies at Chatham. THE ANGLO-FRENCH AGREEMENT. A Paris correspondent of the DaiZy News telegraphs:— You may depend upon the following as an accurate state- ment of the principal points determined in the preliminary agreement between England and France with respect to Egypt, which is now being discussed by the other Great Powers, as distinguished from those which are left over for initiation in the Conference itself :—The English troops , will remain in Egypt until the lot of January, 1888, unless ' in the view of her Majesty's Ministers the establishment of i law and order makes it practicable to withdraw them at an earlier period. The occupation may be continued beyond the date just named if, in the opinion of the British Govern- ment, supported by one of the other Great Powers, the withdrawal of the forces is then inexpedient. The British occupation up to the Ist of January, 1888, is therefore at the discretion of the British Government, and after that date it will'practically remaia so, being limited only by a unanimous decision of the Powers against the prolonged oc- cupation. As this absolute unanimity against what may be the judgment of England is beyond human probability, the discretion of England is left substantially uncontrolled with respect to the duration of the military occupation. 2. The President of the Caisse de La Dette will always be an Eng- lishman, and he will, in the event of a tie, have a casting vote. The report circulated in some quarters that as Presi- dent of the Caisse he will have a seat in the Egyptian Council of. Ministers is without foundation. 3. The state- ment that as all moneys collected either for the debt or for administrative purposes will be paid into the Caisse, the members of the Caisse will thus practically decide upon all expenditure is incorrect. 4. The proposal that England should advance £8,000,000 to Egypt at 4 per cent, does not form any part of the agreement with France nor enter into the preliminary negotiations with Powers. The question is one which will be gserved for the Conference. 5. Any loan which England may make will rank before the Privileged Debt, on which, as well as on the Unified Debt, the interest will be reduced. This, however, is a matter for the Confer- ence. One concession of the utmost importance has been made by France, to which I think it prudent net to refer explicitly just now, but which will be found, when the time for disclosing it arrives, greatly to strengthen the case of the British Government, and to remove the objections enter- tained in many quarters to the prooosed arrangement as limiting England's freedom of action during the term of the British occupation of Egypt. [ understand that M. Ferry is by ne means anxious that England should guarantee the interest on the proposed loan of £8,000,000, on the ground that such a guarantee might be used by England as a plea for a prolonged occupation of Egypt. The rumour that Prince Bismarck is ill-inclined to Egypt because of her recent action in matters affecting German interests, and be- cause he views with distrust a cordial understsnding between England and France, is mere conjecture. It is in contradic- tion to the Prince's own statements. MARRIAGE OF A DAUGHTER OF THE PRINCESS ALICE. ST. PETERSBURG, SATURDAY.—Princess Elizabeth, of Hesse (daughter of Princess Alice), made her state entry in- to the Russian capital to-day. The Emperor and Empress left the Winter Palace at one o'clock, and drove to the Nicholas Railway Station to receive the hjide. ST. PETERSBURG, SUNDAY.—The marriage of the Grand Duke Sergius Alexandrovitch of Russia with Princess Eliza- beth of Hesse was solemnised here to-day, in the chapel of the Winter Palace, with extraordinary pomp, according to the rites of the Orthodox Church. and afterwards by a clergyman of the Lutheran Church. In the afternoon a State banquet was held. This evening a State ball will be given at the Palace, ou leaving which the Emperor and Em- press will accompany the newly-married couple in a magni- ficent State carriage, drawn by eight horses, attended by a mounted escort, to the Palace of the Grand Duke Sergiue, which is situated opposite the Anetchkoff Palace. The Duchess ot Edinburgh and Princess Victoria of Battenberg will join the bridal procession, which will be almost as splendid as the bride's state entry yesterday. By the express command of the Empress, out of consideration for the motherless condition of the bride, the whole ceremony has assumed proportions of unusual magnificence. THE SUEZ CANAL. PARIS, MONDAY.—The Technical Committee of the Suez Canal Company assembled to-day, and fixed the programme of its future meetings, at which the construction of a second canal or enlargement of the existing canal will be discuesed. The committee will sit daily after the 19th inst. FRENCH DIVORCE BILL. PARIS, THURSDAY.—The Senate to-day commenced the debate on the second reading of the Divorce Bill. Article 1, abrogating the law of 18113, by which divorce was abolished in France, was adopted by 158 votes to 115. In the Chamber of Deputies several resolutions relating to the colonial forces were agreed to. THE NISERO AFFAIR. Tau HAGUE,NONDAY.—In the Second Chamber to•day the Government introduced a bill authorising a credit ot one and a half million florins for the augmentation of the Dutch naval forces in Acheen, in order to enable the Government to act with more vigour against certain dependencies of that colony. Dr. ileernskerk, Minister of the Interior, in present- ing the bill, admitted that it was the duty of the Govern- ment to do their utmost to obtain the liberation of the crew of the Nisero, now held prisoners by the Rajah of TAnom, and to punish the guilty parties. The bill was ultimately agreed to by 45 votes to 10. BELGIUM AND THE VATICAN. ROTA; SATERDAY.—Th consequence et the result of the Belgian elections, the Vatican yesterday sent instructions to Monsignor Rinaldini at Brussels to open negotiations with the Ministry for the re-establishment of diplomatic relations between Belgium and the Holy See. GER VIANY. BERLIN, MONDAY.—The German Parliament to-day re- sumed the debate upon the Workmen's Accident Insurance Bill, and agreed to the first three paragraphs as proposed by the Select Committee, providing that the sum insured shall not exceed the amount of one year's wages. A motion in- troduced by Dr. Buhl, permitting chiinuey sweepers to participate in the advantage of the bill, was unanimously agreed to. The TageWatt announces the a womut has been arrested at Eiberlield with four boxes containing explosives in her possession, her intention being, it is aeserted, to cause In explosion at Wiesbaden. The journal adds that the Em- peror's visit to that place was abandoned in consrquence of the discovery.
SOUD&N.

SPAIN. THE SPANISH BLACK HAND SOCIETY. MADRID, SATURDAY.—Seven of the fifteen members of the Black Hand Society, wbo were recently sentenced to deatb. were executed to-day at Xeres. The sentence OR seven otners has been commuted to penal servitude for life. The last of the fifteen committed suicide in prim.

div.head: FIGHTING IN ZULULAND.
div.p: FIGHTING IN ZULULAND.

DIJELBA4f, SATURDAY.—The Boers mod the Usutus have attacked and completely defeated Usibequ, on whom they inflicted heavy loss, burning his kraals and capturing his cattle. Usibequ has arrived at Ekowe. THE UNITED STATES.—THE PRESIDENCY.—RAIL- WAY ACCIDENTS. _ _ . _

Nrivr YORK. SATURDAY.—A largely-attended meeting of Independents hostile to Mr. Blaine was held at Boston last evening, many prominent men being present. Resolutions were adopted opposing the nomination of Mr. Blaine, ex- pressing the hope that the Democrats would bring ,a proper man before the people, and appointing an executive com- mittee with instructions to call a Convention after the Democratic nomination has taken place. A collision has occurred to-day on the Camden and Atlantic Railway, New Jersey, between an ordinary and an excursion train. Eight of the railway officials were killed and many others re- ceived injuries. One of the railway telegraph operators is held responsible for the catastrophe. !WY Yortx, WEDNESDAY.—A conference of prominent Independent Republicans was held yesterday, with the view of arranging a system of formal opposition to the nomina- tion of Mr. Blaine for the presidency. • ',Taw YORK, TRIIRSDAY.—The Democratic State Conven- tion met yesterday, and elected delegates to the Chicago National Convention, the majority of whom favour the nomination of Mr. Cleveland for the presidency Of the Uni- ted States. No name was, however, put forward for the nomination at Chicago. DISSOLUTION OF THE BELGIAN SENATE..

----- - - --- BRUSSELS, WEDNESDLY.—A Royal decree is officially published this morning dissolving the Senate and fixing the new elections for the Bth prox. The Belgian Chambers are summoned to meet on July 22nd. THE ELECTIONS IN BULGARIA. .

WEDNESDAY.—Accordirg to information received here up•to yesterday evening the elections to the Bulgarian National Assembly have resulted in the return of 45 Liberals, 11 Conservatives, 20 Radicals, 22 Mussulmans, and 50 other candidates not yet classed. M. Zankoff, the Premier, has been elected in six districts, and M. Karaveloff, the Ridical leader, bias been returned for Sofia. The election could nz,t be held at Vratzs, Widdin, and in two ether districts owing to riots accompanied ti 7 conflicts between the hostile political parties. At Vratza the disturbances assumed a serious character. One man was killed and several injured.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The Bradford Infirmary is to be extended at a cost of £12,000 Relief works are to be commenced in Sydney to find work for the unemployed. After a nine hours' service on Sunday the Glasgow police arrested 16 persons who were drisking in a shebeen. A cotton mill, near Hebden-bridge, was destroyed by fire on Saturday, and damage was done estimated at £12,000. Sir John Lubbock's Shop Hours Bill, which it is expected I will be read a second time on June 25, needs to be well I supported by petitions. About 4,00(r operatives are out on strike at Bradford. At ' , the Police Court, on Monday, two men were each fined 20s I and costs for intimidation. Extradition has been granted in the case of Tully, late manager of the Preston Bank, who absconded some months ago, and was recently apprehended in New York. He will , at once be brought to England. Bench alarm was created amongst the passengers en a , Furness Railway train on Monday evening by the engine and tender running off the line near Sandside. No one was hurt, but traffic was delayed and great damage done to the , permanent way. In the Grand Committee on Law on Tuesday, the Muni- , cipal Elections (Corrupt Practices) Bill was ordered, as amended, to be reported to the House. A maximum scale Of expenses to be allowed was inserted in the bill after mach discussion. Tax HEALTH EXHIBITION.—H is estimated that nearly 50,000 persona visited the International Health Exhibition in London on Saturday. This gives a total of over 576,000 up to the present time--a number far exceeding those who attended the Fisheries Exhibition during the corresponding period. Tun TORY CAMP—The Daily News is informed that the truce between the parties in the Council of the National Union of Conservative Associations is more ap- parent than real. In the course of a few weeks a deter- mined effort will be made to oust Lord Randolph Churchill from the chairmanship. Pceonn OF hisccrs.—A remarkable occurrence has taken place in Rhondda Valley, acres of the mountain sides and Lops being carpeted with the bodies of icsects rather larger than, but resembling caterpillars. The inhabitants are re- moving them by burning. Specimens have been sent to .University College. London, for examinatton. LEAP FROM AN EXPRESS —On Saturday. a boy, about 11 years of age, named Halliwell, jumped from a Southport train which was passing through Ainsdale Station at the rate of 40 miles an hour, but he escaped with a shock and some trifling bruises. He had taken a ticket to Ainsdale, and, finding that the train was not stopping, he determined to jump out. COUNTY COURT WORK.—The number of plaints entered in the County Courts of England and Wales during 1833 was 991,002 not exceeding £2O, 11,263 above £2O and not exceeding £5O, and 683 by agreement above £5O. The total was lower than in any year since 1876, and the total of actions determined without a jury (610.009) was the lowest since 1877. LONDON TECHNICAL SCHOOL.—The additional amount of money—some £3o,ooo—required for the completion of the Technical College at Soqth Kensington, for which the prince of Wales made an appeal through the newspapers a short time ago, is now guaranteed, and all necessary arrangements for opening the college will probably be carried out in time for an inaugural winter session. Fentrian OF A CANAL EMBANKMENT.—A high embank- ment of the Dearne and Dove Canal, between Lewelin Bridge, Worstborough, and Swaithe Colliery, near Barnsley, buret on Sunday. Fully 20 yards of the embankment, 20 feet deep, collapsed, draining the canal for about five miles. Considerable damage was done to the Manchester and Shef- field Mineral Railway. Worstborougb Sewerage Farm and works along the valley also suffered from the outburst. BisnoP FRILSER AND WEALTHY CHURCHMEN.-011 Satur- day the Bishop of Manchester, in a sermon on the re- opening of St. Bride's Church, Brooks's Bar, Manchester, referred to the want of liberality towards Church purposes on the part of wealthy Church people in this diocese. There were, he said, many noble types of individual and family munificence, but there were rich men who had "learned the art of buttoning up their pockets to perfection." KILLED WHILE PIGEON FLYING.— A man named John William Christian has died at the Ashton under-Ljoaa In- firmary from the effects of pistol shot wound. Deceaeed and two other men went out on a Sunday morning, about a fortnight ago to fly pigeons. Oae of his companions had a revolver to frighten the birds, and he was complaining that he could not fire it, when it went off, the bullet lodging in Christian's thigh, whence it could not be extracted. Tux SALVATION ARMY.—On Saturday the foundation stone was laid of the new building in Lisson-street, Edgware- road, adjoining the Metropolitan Railway Station, London, and the building to be erected will accommodate in the upper and lower rooms an aggregate of 3,800 persons. " General " Booth stated that the total cost would be about £3500, of which a large amount had been promised, whilst several handsome donations were handed in during the pro-‘ ceedings. Ilia laying of the stone was witnessed by a very large concourse of members of the "Army," the female sol- diers formiug the majority. FATAL CARRIAGE ACCIDENT.—An inquest was held at Berkeley, Gloucestershire, on Monday. on the bodies of Mrs. Palairet, wife of Captain Palairet, J.P.. and Miss Minnie Gilbert Smith, a visitor from London, who were killed by being thrown from their carriage on S4urday. The ladies had been on a visit to Sir George Jenkinson, ot Eastwood Park, and when returning to Berkeley the horse took fright, and, running op a bank, the ladies were thrown upon the road. Mrs. Palairet sustained dislocation of the neck, and Miss Smith a fracture of the skull. The former lady lin- gered until the arrival of her husband. A formal verdict was returned. Moe. GLADSTONE ON AMERICA AND DYNAMITE.—In re- plying to inquiries made by a gentleman connected with the American press, a letter, from which the following is an ex- tract, ban been received from Mr. Gladstone's secretary He (Mr. Gladstone) fears that there is no probability that, at his age and with his engagements in this country, he will be able to visit the United States. With regard to the tone af the American press on the dynamite question, Mr. Glad- stone must excuse himself from expressing an opinion which could net serve public interests. He maY, however, 83V that he has the fullest confidence is the friendly sentiments generally of the American people towards this country." THE OFFICIAL HECEIVER.—A very interesting case has been heard in the Supreme Court before I.srds Justices Bag- play, Cotton, and Lindley.—Mr. Registrar Murray some time ago refused to sanction a scheme of arrangement drawn up by the creditors of Messrs. C. and G Clark, bookbinders, by which the debtors' bankruptcy petition should be dis- charged when a committee of three creditors entrusted with the carrying on of the insolvent businees should so decide. No accusation was brought. against the good faith of the creditors or the correct conduct of the debtors. The point to which the Registrar took exception was simply this: After a petition in bankruptcy has been filed the creditors and debtors should not be allowed to make an arrangement by which the discharge of the bankrupt should depend upon the approval of a committee of the creditors without the inter- vention of the Court. The three judges who heard the ap- peal agreed that inch power could not be delegated, and that after a petition had once been filed the approval of the Court must be had and obtained before the debtor is dis- charged. In fact, the Official Receiver is absolutely master of the situation once a petition has been filed.—Pall Mall Gazette.

_ MARRIED WOMEN AND THEIR PROPERTY: IMPORTANT CASE AT ST. HELENS—Before Mr. filinkhorn and Alder- man Cock, at the St. Helens Town Hall os Friday, a married woman named Mary Gritnshavr was charged with stealing .£6 55., one shawl, Ova jackets, two dresses, two pairs of stockings, and one gold wedding-ring, the property of William Grimshaw, her husband—Mr. swift (who appeared for the prosecutor) said this was a case of considerable pecu- liarity. The parties were in the unfortunate position of hnsbantrand wife. Prosecutor was a widower with two children, and defendant a widow also with two children, on to the 14th February last, when they were mar- ri4d,, and she went to live with him at Keswick Cottages, near to Denton' Green-lane. As was usual on such occasions, prosecutor gave his wife a wedding-ring. In a box in prosecutor's bedroom there was the wearing ap- parel named in the charge, which had belonged to his late wife, and in the dressing table drawer prosecutor kept his money in a brass box, which bad a complicated lock, and could only be opened by some one acquainted with it. On' the sth June defendant appeared to have made up her mind to leave her husband, and defendant called Sarah Grim- shaw, a daughter of the prosecutor's, to her bedroom and fished her for Sc, which she knew her husband had given her to pay an account with. On unlocking tbe drawer the de- fendant rediarked that that had saved the drawer. Tile girl went downstairs again, and a little while afterwards heard a noise in her father's bedroom. She went up, and found the defendant with a hammer in her hand. The box was broken open and the apparel spread out upon the bed. Defendant then broke open the dressing table, took out the money-box, laid it upon the floor. and as she could not open it she broke it open with "the hammer, took out eight sovereigns, and threw them aside, saying that was what she would leave for for him, and sbe then put six sovereigns into her own pocket. After the wedding the defendant pawned the ring, and on prosecator redeeming it he kept it in this drawer. Defendant took the ring and put it on her finger, and then, patting on a Paisley shawl, and making the appaawl into a bundle. she went out, saying to her stepdaughter, "Farewell for ever." A day or two afterwards she sent for her own two children, and prosecu- tor learning th it she was at Gerard's-bridge he took out a warrant for her apprehension.—After the evidence had been given the prisoner pleaded guilty to stealing vs, and the other charges, relating to the wedding-ring and apparel, were withdrawn.—Mr. Thnmas, for the defendant, submitted that although techically such an offence might have been com- mitted, the Act never contemplated such a proceeding by a harsh and creel husband against an inoffensive wife. De- fendant bad been taken from her work by the prosecutor and treated like a dog iii his house, and while his children slept in beds her children bad to sleep on straw. She could en- dure it no longer, and only teak sufficient money to keep her until she found emp:,;vment again—The Magistrates, after hearing Seree,nt Gilligan say he had known defen- dant nine years ta-nii knew nothing wrong against her until she began courting the pima enter, said there were strong mitigating circumstances in the case hut the Act compelled them to send rietsi.d int to prison. They, boweyer, thought )ustice would be met by seven daye without hard labour.

SATURDAY, JUNE 21, 1884.

THE Ward Meetings of the Conservative party which havb been held in Warrington during the past few months have been organised, as we have been ostentatiously told, for the especial benefit of the working-man ; ' but the working-man does not seem to have taken to them very kindly, for the attendance has become "flue by degrees and beautifully less." At the last meeting. which was held in North-East Ward on Monday evening, there was a judicious delay of a quarter of an hour in the commencement of proceedings, for at the hour fixed for the meeting there were less than a hundred persons present. It would seem that the working-man is begin- ning to find Sir GILBERT GREENALL Out ; that he is not to be taken in by empty ex- pressions of regard which are belied by open threats of intimidation, aild by direct votes against his interests in the House of Com- mons. There was a cry raised at the meet- ing that the Conservative candidate had been unfairly attacked and misrepresented; but if that had been so we may be quite sure that, under the circumstances, Sir GILBERT would have been well supported—that there would, in fact, have been a crowded meeting. It is really paying too great a compliment to our influence to suggest that we have written Sir GILBERT down. He alone is to blame if he does not stand well with the electors of War. rington, for he has vc,ted himself down in the past, and has talked himself down in the present. It is amusing to note how the various orators at the rnerting on Monday night attempted his defence, and, oratori- cally speaking, "perished in the attempt." Mr. T. V. TAYLOR appears to have come specially primed for the occasion, but he made nothing of it. He sought to grapple with the "The Three F's ; " but he is amongst the light weights. and they overpowered him With regard to the first of the F'4—" Flood" —he seems, after the manner of Conservative speakers, to have missed the point; and requires to be told that working-men who have any self-respect utterly resent the attempt to intimidate one of their class be- cause he dares to speak his mind. They are not to be mocked with meaningless talk about regard for the working-man, when at the very same time it is sought to crush one of their number between the heavy barrels of Wilderspool'ale and what was deemed to be the nether-millstone of the London and North - Western Railway Company. Sir GILBERT for once showed some discretion (or was it forgetfulness?) in saying nothing about " Flood " on Monday night, but he did manage to deliver himself on the question of Fishing—" the miserable question of fish- ing," as one speaker described it, uncon- sciously coming down rather heavily on " the odd old fellow," whose speeches, never by I any accident political. are. above all things, piscatorial., Sir GILBERT sticks to it that there is no fishir,g because they fished and took all the fish ;"' but then he informs us he is no fisherman, and the fishermen tell another tale. rhey regard it as a wonderful coincidence that the prohibition followed upon his failure to win .Warrington at the last Parliamentary election, and as "wonderful and yet again

Mr. I. S. LEADA.m, who, along with Mr. S. RIGBY, has been chosen by the Liberal , party to do battle with the Conservatives in Mid-Cheshire at the next General Election, has opened the campaign by delivering ad- dresses at Altrincharn, Lymm, and Sandbaen• Mr. RIGBY, as already announced, is com- mitted to engagements which will prevent his addressing the electors this year, unless there should, unexpectedly, be a dissolution of Parliament ; but meantime he may safely leave the platform to his skilful colleague. His speeches are admirable, and, as they .are likely to be widely read, they will serve the Liberal cause far beyond the area of Mid Cheshire. Mr. LBADAM shows himself thoroughly master of the topics he deals with, and he has a way of driving the nail , home and clinching it which makes him a formidable opponent. He has, for instance, made Mr. Bitooxs look so ludicrous with his , plea of being "a moderate Conservative that he will not, in all probability, go out of , his way again to seek to curry favour in that fashion. Mr. LEADAM'S appeal to the , history of Conservative Administrations is well-timed, for it puts it beyond- .. doubt that they have been so bad in the past that there is no trusting them in the future. - The farmers of Cheshire who feel the need of wider knowledge in relation to agriculture, will do well to "read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest" Mr. LEADAM's revelations as to the money squandered by the "city companies created for the express - purpose of giving technical education to the workmen of Great Britain." "Nearly the entire site," he said, "of the city of London belonged to these city guilds, and their an- nual revenue exceeded one million 'sterling. In whose hands was this money? Was it Ifl the hands of the persons for whom it was in- tended—tailors, cordwainers, grocers, salters, &c.? They would not find men of this class in these companies. The money was in the hands of Conservative lawyers, in the hands , of Conservative stock-joblsers„ was in the - hands of members of Conservative aristocratic , houses. There was money enough in these „ companies to found ten universities for the purpose of encouraging agricultural and manufacturing industry." The "moderate Conservative" would of course leave these iniquities untouched, but Mr. LEADAII is in earnest in demanding that abuses shall be swept away. His estimate of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL as the new light of the TorY party shows that he has careiully weighed his • lordship up, and found him wanting. He may well call him the will-o-the- wisp of the Conservative party, seeing that he proves ' himself to be " evetything by starts, and nothing long." He pointed 0u... Lord RAN- " DOLPH'S inconsistencies on the Franchise Bill, and on the Egyptian question. With regard to the latter, it is well that Mr. LEADAIsA ex - prised the absurdity of tit:, suggestion to bring back ARABI Pasha from Ceylon, for his lord- ship, utterly forgetting the " patriotic" ARABI and his efforts to get rid of foreign control, coolly proposed no later than Wed- nesday last that thi: country should annef, Egypt. Is this "moderate Conservatism, or is it downright robbery, or does one thing in this case involve the other ? Mr. LEADAM is engaged in a good work in laying bare the hollowness, not to say immorality of the policy of such men as Lord RANDoLpfr CHURCHILL, who would "wade througn slaughter" abroad in order to pri.vent Reform at home. We have had enough of the rule of aristoczatic farnilie: in thi, country ; must have in the future " men of m ,rit andi mind," and to this cid the people, who soon have power in their own hand:. must see to it that the EGitR.TONS give 1_ lace to the LEADAms as their rep,esentatives in tne Com- mons House of Parliament.

POACHERS AT HALTON.—At thq Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. James Handley, John Sheltoe, Alfred Hinton, and William Rawlinson. young men, were summoned to answer a charge of trespassing on land at Halton in the occupation of William Baker, in search of game without authority. Each defendant pleaded guilty. P.S.Loundes proved finding the defendants en A clover field between Halton and Reck Savage at half-past four o'clock on the morning of the Bth June. Accompanying them was a black and white greyhound and IL I nrcher dog. Shelton who had been twice previously convicted, was fined 40s and costs 10ead, or in defeultla month's hard labour; blenton was fictei lOs and costs lOs Bd, or 14 days hard labour; and Rawlin- son, who hot been previously convicted, was fined £1 and costa 10s Si, or 2b days hard lab mr. . SITOCLING FATALITY AT WIDNES.—About one o'clock on Thursday afternoon a cart laden with coal was, poising be- hin 1 West-street, in charge of a boy named Patrick Morrie, 14 years of age, when it came in contact with the yard wall of a House occupied by Mr. Henry Wilkinson. The force of the collision WAS MO great that the greater part of the wall, which was built of brick*, .surmounted with coping 'atones, area demolished, the debris falline inte the yard: At the time Mr. Wilkinson's two children and the child of a neigh- bour were playing in the yard, and the mass of brickwork fell noon the youngest, a boy aged two years and nine menthe, injuring.; his bead, face, and tweast in a fearful manner. Dr. Richards was immediately called in, and after examining the boy he aavised his removal to the Liverpool Infirmary, and Mr. Wilkinson therefore took his son to tbat institution, but he died shortly after admission. Strange to say, the deceased's elder brother escaped with a few slight scratches, and the neighbour's child withodt injury what- ever. The cart belonged to Messrs. Oates and Davies. coal merchants, Whines. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BlLL.—This Bill, on Monday, passed its third reading without opposition in the Houee of Lords. A meeting of members of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce the same day adopted unanimously a petition ' to the Home of Commons asking that the Bill should be re- jected, as the Canal might he productive of great injury to the navigation and condition of the Mersey. It is said that Mr. W. B. Forster will be chairman of the House of [ Commons' C:onmittee on the Bill. Before the Select Com- mittee it will be 'opposed as strenuously as it was in the Lords. It will 'be remembered that last year, whilst it passed the Commons, it was thrown out in the Lords. Havidg this Session being passed in the Lords, the opponents of the measure are hopeful that the reversal of Orem- stances mac he complete. The London Correspondent of the llianeheste,r Guardian says :—" The Ship Canal Bill, having been read a first time in the House of Commons on • Monday, has now fairly started on its final course. What , its fate there will be can at present be only matter of con- jecture, but the experience of last year favours the belief that the Bill will be sanctioned. In that case its difficulties in regard to Parliament w,ll be ended, and this gigantic scheme will pass into the hands of the engineers; but against this anticipation must be placed the fact that, as I undeistand, all the principal and the stronzest opponents of the project, undeterrel by the decision of the Duke ef Richmond's Committee, are resolved to again contest the I Bill. They are doing this in face of the fact that the Howie efllhill Was least likely le._ lliiiBtitri Or 'Alm ho I Lie ~) ill; Yale arra fetnieg it lasi year.— tt is probable that the Bill will reach the Select Committee of the House of Commons within a fortnight from this time." MAkaLtetn AT FARNwonrw.—There were considerable re- joicings at Farnworth on Thurtelay morning an the occa- sion of the marriage of Mr. G J. Neil, of Rose Lea, Fern- worth, to Miss Elizabeth Houghton, szcond danglyer of Mr. Williera lieughton, of Prospect Rouse, Crow Wood, near FarnWorth. Plage Were dying from mmy prominent points in the township, the Parish Church bells were sending forth a merry peal, and near the residence of the bride's father a triumphal arch had been erected by Mr. Houghton's ten entry, who made generally merry.Ouring the day. The bride received numerous presents. , THE NATIONAL TEMPERANCE CONGRESS.--Fine weather favoured the opening proceedings on Saturday afternoon of , the National Temperance Congress at Liverpool. A gala was held in Kensington Fields, which was attended by between 3,000 and 4.000 children, representing the juvenile , societies of every section of the temperance movement in the city. Mr. W. Crosfleld, ,J.P-. (local chairman), and Mr. 'J. R. Macdonald (the local secretary of the congress), the , Hen. R. Hobson anq J.-Hirst, and Messrs. Edward &nes. , B. M'aranahan, T. Crodeld, W. J. Sutcliffe, J. Filltpatrick, , J. B. Collings, &c., were present, and took part in the gala. 1 On Sunday morning and evening, sermons bearing ' on the subject of temperance were preached in upwards of 100 of the places of wershq) 'of . all denominations in Liverpool and neighbourhood. The The sittings of the Congress was formally inaugurated on Monday evening in the Rotunda Lecture Hall, when the, opening address was delivered by the president, the Right Rev. the Lord Bishop of Exeter (Rev. Dr. Temple). There ' WAS a good attendance, and amongst those on the platform were the Yen. Archdeacon Hardsley, the Revs J. 13urbidge, S. Pearson, C. Garrett. it. B. Baron, F. G. Armour, and Post- sues; Drs. Townson, Marsh. Moore, and Howie; Messrs. W. Croseneld, A. Belfour, Clarke Aspinall, Dr. Richardson (London) Mr. J. Whittaker (Scarboro'), Mr. W. J. Andrews (Leeds). Mr. W. Livesev (Preston), Col. Young (London), and Mr. W. I. Palmer (Reading). The Bishop of Exeter's address was a powerful appeal in favour of total abstinence. 'The bishop does not wish to coerce onyone into such a prac- tice by the brute force of the law, and takes courage from the results of steadyappeals to the understandingothich have had great effect upon the medical profession, insurance cons- penile, and general opinion. What he calls the sympathy of numbers is a matter on which he lays great stress. His lordship even goes so far as to say that if all the charity 1 that now finds an outlet in the many forms of altnegiving in this country were to cease, and the givers were to join the ranks of the temperance reformers, the help to the poor and the blessing to the nation would be greater than from all the money they now bestow. On Tuesday Dr. Richardson's address on "The scientific basis of the temperance reformation" presented the medical view in favour of temperance in its strongest form. He aseurned that if only he could prove that alcohol is not necessary and that it differs from othsr unnecessary things in being also an evil thing, he would have proved the scien- tific basis of the temperance movement. He accordingly set himself to demonstrate these two propositions, and mein- tainee that for warmth, strength, activity, and felicity, animal life has abundant resources without using alcohol, and that when alcohol is used it produces a prejudicial effect, whether upon man or the lower animals. Papers were also read by Dr. llPMurtry, of Belfast, on "The Wise physician's attitude towards alcohol," and by Mr. A. Gor- don Miller, of Edinburgh, on "The results of intemperance from a surgical point of view." Mr. Miller's experience has convinced him that the great majority of accident cases that are treated at hospitals result from the use of drink, that the closing of public-houses on Sunday in Scotland has a decided eff.ct in reducing the number of cases, and that still further benefit would result from earlier closing on Saturday nights. At Wednesday's sitting the social and educational aspects of temperance were considered. Professor Calderwood, of Edinburgh, presided and delivered an address in which he showed fleet temperance reform bore upon the common businesa of life and contributed towards upholding the dignity and promoting the true happiness of men. The temperance movement bad still to encounter a dead weight of prejudice which it should be the aim of its advocates to overcome. The Rev. Dr. Mecfadyen, of Liverpool, read a paper upon the social aspectaeof temperance. A discussion followed in which Dr. W. B.ltichardson and other gentle- men took part. In the evening Dr. Richardson addressed a large meeting of working-men. Meetings in furtherance of temperance were also held in connection with the Congress at Birkenhead and Bootle. At the morning sitting, on Thursday, temperance economics and statistics were dealt with, the principal speakers being Sir Win. Collins, of Glas- gow, and Mr. Wm. Hoyle, of rottingion. In the afternoon a conference on temperance work in relation to children took place. At night a crowded public meeting was held in Hengler's Circue. Cardinal Manning presided, and spoke at considerable length on the evils resulting from the drink traffic. Amongst the list of temperance friends ievited by the Mayor and Meyorese of Liverpool to meet the Right Rev. the Lord Bishop of Exeter, rat the 'NWT' Hall on Tuesday last, we notice the names of the Rev Thomas Hip- po!) and Mrs. Rippori, Mr. and Mrs Itoheee Crenett, Mieeee Garnett. Mr. Councillor Dexon, and 31r. Wm. Roberts, hon. sec. Warrington Temperanie Union.

CORPUS CHRISTI PROCFSeION AT DITTON. 'The ennuil celebration of the feast of Corpus Christi took place at the College of the Sacietv of Jesus at Ditton on Sunday afternoon. As usual, the gorgeous Catholic ceremonial brought together a large concourse of people, and it was computed that nearly 4,020 persons were present In the Church of St. Michael and the grounds of the col- lege during the afternoon. An hour before the time an- nounced for the commencement of the service people took their seats in the sacred edifice, whose beauties of architec- ture and rich decoration ware furthe: enhanced by the tasteful disposition of bright flowers and choice plants upon the various altars Rnd the handsome paintings of the sta- tions of .the Cross which embellish the walls of the build- ing. By half-past three the building was crowded to its ' utmost limits, and the service then commenced by the Ger- man choir singing with the exquisite harmony for which they have mum famed in the suarounding neighbourhood, the music of the "Veal Spiritus Sanctus.' The Rev. Father Bares, of St. Francis' Church, Liverpoolenafterwards preached a sermon bearing upon the ceremony of the day. At the conclusion of the discourse, the priests, habited in rich vestments, emerged from the Sac- risto. followed by the choir and students, attired le surplices, and groupemdeatnhwemaleelveisit(t,bilefod t before e efihieh.,a, l latane I the acovlites having hi lld Lisa 0011106 154112 44, perfume !neduse. The choir 4tll-glfteir the se ul etAadri7hl2olt';ia "o Father tionvia, sang Haller'e hymn and Ett's anthem of " Pangue Lingua"; and this concluded the procession walked down the centre aisle and through the gates to the right, and into Ithe ground of the college'. At the Lead was borne the ban- ner of the Holy Family, and was followed by the young girls of the school tastefully dressed in white, bearing ban- ners and flowers. Then came the young unmarried women of the congregation, who bore in their midst an image of the Virgin wreathed with green leaves. Following were the male members of the congregation wearing red and blue scarves and sashes, upon which the holy cross was conspicu- ous, many of them bearing bright coloured banners illustra- ted with various ecclesiastical devices; and then came 16 members of the Brigade of St. Xaciers' Liverpool, adorned, with regalia, and bearing banners aloft. The Ditton braes band, the college cho r, the students, and 24 priests fol- lowed. The sound of bells and the fragrance of incense warned the spectators of the apprditch of the Sacred Host, which was borne beneath a canopy of white and gold by the Rev. Father Weidenmann, the rector of -the college. On one aide walked the deacon, the Bev, Father Pllll f, and on the other the Rev. Father Joehring, sub-deaceo, while preceding the host were 12 girls of tender age wearing long veils and blue sashes.who scattered flowers in the path. Following were at least 1,500 persons. Dur- ing the procession through the garden the band played sacred music, and the choir chanted hymns and psalms. A stoppage was made at the college entrance, where an altar, beautifully decorated with flowers and choice plants, had been erected, and here the Rev. Father Weidenmann per- formed the ceremony of the benediction, after which the procession reformed and returned to the church. Accom- panying the procession were the Rev. Father Warners, theologian at the Vatican Council, and author of several theological and controversial works; the Rev. The annual meeting of the Improtannent Commissioners for the purpose of electing .a chairetsn for the ensuing year was held in the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. W. H. Linaker took the chair, pro tens, and there were present Meters. Meadowcroft, J. Norman. P. 11-isc.e, F. Fairhurst, J. Williams Dobson, J. Pritchard, and W. Brooks, secretary. Mr. Norman rose to nominate a gentleman to occupy the position of chairman, who he was sure :they would all agree with him, that if be were elected, he would be the right man in the right place. 113 meant Mr. Robert Shaw. Mr. Shaw had daring the past year worked very hard, especially on the committees; and his labours in cmnection with the Ship Canal and other projects had borne fruit. Mr. Williams seconded the motion. He thought they could not make a bet ter selection if they were going to have a change. Mr. Briscoe had great pleasure in supporting the motion, which on being put to the meeting, was culled unanimously. In the absence of the newly appointed chairman, Mr. Briscoe now took the chair, and Mr. Norman said he had great pleasure in moving that the best thanks of the Board be accorded to Mr. Meadoweroft, the retiring Chairman, for the manner In which he had conducted the business of the Board during the past year. Since be (Mr. Morgan), had been a member of the Board, he did not think they had had a man in the chair who had conducted the business better than Mr. Mea- dowcroft had done. Ile had been, he might say, "all things to all men." He had not stifled discussion, but he had done everything that be possibly could do to make matters comfortable all ronnd. He had asked Mr. Meadow- croft to take the chair for one year, but he could not see his way to do so. He was :sure many members would have been glad to have seen him occupying the posi tion again. He trusted Mr. MeadoncrOft would long con- tinue a resident in Runcorn and a member of that Board' for a more useful gentleman they could not have.—Mr Fair' burst seconded the proposition. During the abort time he bad been a commissioner he had felt it to be a pleasure to ' sit at the Board with Mr. Meadowcroft in the chair, for he believed that gentleman had conducted the business satis- factorily to them all. He was very sorry indeed that he was not occupying the same position during the next year, bat be supposed that the dnties in connection with his own work increased; and he (Mr. Fairhurst) had often been sur- prieed that he could devote so much time to the tiublic ser- vice.—Mr. Dobson supported the motion, observing that Mr. Meadowcroft had maintained the honour and dignity of the Board, and by the tact and ability he bad displayed, and the gentlemanly and impartial spirit he had manifested, he had won the estlem of the whole Board.—The motion was carried with acclamation.—Mr. Meadowcroit, in reply, sriirl the kind and cordial way in which they bad shown their appreciation of his services during the past twelve months was really almost too much for him to reply to. He did not, however, tab e any credit to himself for the satisfactory way in which the business bad been done. He thought the credit belonged to the members. When they were good enough to elect him as chairman he intimated that ! it was necessary in order to deal in a satisfactory ! manner with the duties which devolved upon them that he should have their confidence and support, and he was pleased to say that he had had that in a most thorough and complete degree. He thought the result had been that the duties bad been more agreeably, and certainly he could say without fear of contradiction not less efficiently, discharged, and they had also dissipated some of those apprehensions which existed twelve months ago. (Hear, hear.) He could conscientiously say he had endearoured to do to the utmost of his power what his position required of him, and they also had done th dr part. They had not certainly harrassed any industries, or neglected any public duty, and he thought if they continued in the same way their duties would be more agreeable to them all. He believed the gentleman they bad elected that day would realise the expectations they had formed of him, and be did trust that they should continue in the future as they had during the pas twelve months. The only measure the Govern- ment had utssed was the Bankruptcy hill, and the only thing in connection with that measure was that they had been able to give a large number of Radical lawyers and election ,agents respectable and very profitable pokitions. (Applause.) When the Liberals went into office Ireland was contented. They did away with the Peace Preservation Act, saying force was no remedy, and immediately gave Ireland two of the most cruel Coercive Bills. The Conservatives were accused of having no policy, but it would be better to have ,no policy at all than adopt the policy of the Liberals. (Ap plaase.)—The Rev. George Bond seconded the resolu- tion'l and it was unanimously carried.--,-In replying, the Cha rman said mos.t of them vould recollect that two years ago he was pretty-well hauled over the coals because he mentioned the subject of Fair Trade. Now, he was pleased to see the Franshise Bill brought in because it was a ner- feet Certainty that the result of this bill would be that Fair Trade wn ald ha properly considered and forced upon Parlia- ment. They had had soinethicg like IP years bad trade in the country, and there was no likelihood of it getting bet- ter. And why? Becalm other. countries had learned how to supply their own wants. They also sent the produce of t eir own lands and the labour of their hands into this country free of deny; and what England sent to them was heavily taxed. Was that fair? ("No.") Would they sit down and allow themselves to bat thrown out of work simply for the cry "You must not interfere with Free Trade." Would it serve them to ha told that any amount of bread stuff could come into this country free if they had not the money wherewith to buy the bre.d, even if the loaf was better than our own? If they made up their minds to have Fair Trade they would get it. He concluded by expressing the opinion that it was perfectly tight that the franchise should be extended, but at the Paine time redistribution ehould be atteuded to.-- l'he proceedings then terminated.
