div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

A Diart..ThrosT LOIMMR.—At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Saturday, Hannah Harkins, a middle-aged woman, who occupied a furnished room at -Bradley's lodging-house, Liverpool-street, was charged with stealing a blanket and other articles, value 19s, the property of her landlord. Pri- soner pleaded guilty, and having been convicted seven times, was sent to prison for one month. Simons a SIATILT WITH A BRICK Cmpritn.4--Before Mr. H. Baxter (Mayor) and Dr. 'fwyford, at the Town Hall, on Monday forenoon, Mary Buckley, of Bccleston, was charged with unlawfully wounding a young man named Peter Ker- nan, on Saturday night.—Superintsndent Johnson stated that the orisonor was charged with unlawfully wounding Kernan by striking him on the head with a "brick chip- per," injuring him severely.—Peter Kernan, the prosecutor, whose head was "plastered," deposed that he was a labourer, and lived in Gordan-street. On Saturday night lie was standing in High-street, when some bother took plaos be- tween one of his brothers and some other men. He inter- fered on his brother's behalf, and immediately afterwards the prisoner came down an entry and violently struck him on the head, severely cutting it and causing him to lose a large quantity of blood.---Uwo other.witnesaes stated that the woman struck the prosecutor on the head with an iron bar, "somethinglike a poker, with a sharp end on it." Ker- nan was rendered nearly insenetble.—The defendant, who denied the charge, was fined 163 and costs, or in default seven days' imprisonment. ,
ALLEGED CORPORATE FRAUDS - £7OO DEFAL.

div.head: CATIONS.
div.p: CATIONS.

For some weeks rumours have been pretty widely circu- lated throughout the borough that a strict investigation of the b)oks and accounts of one of the departments of the St. Helen's Corporation was being made, and the matter has been brought still more prominently before the.ipublic by reports that defalcations and frauds amounting to a large sum have been discovered. We are enabled to state as a fact, that a close and searching examination of the books is being made, but it is being conducted with the greatest pos- sible secrecy for well-known reasons. It has, however, leaked out that the irregularities which have been bresght to light represent a sum of about £700; and we understand that the investigation is far from having been completed. The officials are extremely reticent about the affair, but pending the completion of the examination of the books, any definite statement upon the matter would be prema- ture. One rumour is to the effect that part of the system of fraud was in over stating the supply of paving acts— more being entered and paid for by the Corporation than was received. There is naturally considerable excitement in the town in the matter.

• PAVING COMMITTEE—ALLEGED IRREGD- I LAIHTIF.S. • Seine-discussion took place on the subject of the alleged irregularities of the late borough surveyor Mr. mart), at the monthly meeting of the Paving Committee, on Wednesday. , The Cnairman (Alderman Johnson) in answer to questions by several memb.Ta as to the credibility of these rumours said he thought that whatever might be the case that com- mittee had not neglected its duty. Whatever might come to his ears he should always say that that committee had never done anything to bring disgrace upon themselvee, and that the public could say nothing against them if anything were to coins out.—Mr. Walker asked if any charges had come out.-41r. Belsher thought it was vite time that mat- ter was cleared up and brought before the Council. He didn't think that matters of that kind ought to be dealt with in a hole and corner way. If there was anythiag wrong they were entitled to know. He was as much entitled to know as any chairman of committee or any officer of the Corporation and if there WAS any ecandal it ought ts come out —The Chairman asked what scandal he was referring to and Mr. Belsher replied that he was referring to a public scandal which was the talk of the town. He supposed there was some inquiry being made.—The Chairman said there was.—Mr. Belsher : Then I say that as a member of the Council I am entitled to know what it is about.— The Chairman : You must appeal to the proper authorities. —Mr. Hanson: Is it • true that Mr. Hart received In some irregular way, pe•quisites equal to hts nominal salary.—The Chairman: If 1 may state my own opinion, I should certainly say it was not.—Mr. Hanson : I just wanted to know; I don't want to say anything more.—fhe Chair- man: I don't know anything more than Tott do with re- spect to his receiving perquisites or anything else —Mr. Walker asked if there was going to be any system adopted to check these sort of things —The Chairman said he hoped I so. He could only say it was no fault of that committee, but he wasafraid that some materials sent there had not been checked as they ought to have been. That, however, I was not the fault of the committee. They gave instructions to their servants, and they ought to be .c arried out; it could not be expected that any member of that committee c ould go after their officials every hour of the day to see that they did their duty.—Mr. Walker said he should like to k.,ow what sort of check there was going to be.—Mr. Belsher hoped that someone would he in a position to put that matt•a square at the next Council meeting. He trusted that in consequence of the investigation that was taking place, ' there would he a reprt to the Council at the next meeting as to the state of that affair.—The Chairman said that all he could say was that, he supposed, on the instigation of the Mayor, he, as a chairman of one of the committees, was called to a meeting at which certaitt statements were made to them, and it was considered advisable, from these statements, to pursue a certain course which he was not at lib.trty to make public. That course was being pursued. and he supposed there would be a report.—Mr. Walker said he should like to know where the chairmen of the committees got authority to keep anything from the committees. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman eaid that if he was to tell them everything he heard, and he was to impose malt} them the same conditions as were imons-d upon him, he had no doubt at all they would acknowledge that it Wee Most proper, having in•riew the ends of justice, that these thirge should not ha made public.—air. mcKech- nie thought thst as an investigation was • going on the men- here of that committee ought to have an opportunitir of givingan opinion.—The Chairman then said that if that diSCLISSiOn WtS to go on farther ho would have to ark tlyt reporters to retire.—The reporters then, in accordance with the request of the chairman, retired from the roct72.

This annual athletic festival, which is one of the most important in the North of England, was commenced last evening, in what is known as the "show field," Farnworth. The total number of entries for the two days approachea

- - 500, an increase upon last year, but some disappointment ; was expressed at the fact that George, of the Mosely Bar- riers, would not this year put in an appearance. This oinis- , sion of a favourite was somewhat compensated for by the , entry of Snooks, George's great opponent for the amateur championship, who will compete in severel races to-day. Last evening the events were confined to competitors resi- ding in the district, and although the entries were very nu- merous, the contestants did not number in very great force. Uelike last year, when the weather resembled December rather than June, and rain descended On torrents, the at- mosphere, although dull, wee warm là genial, and this, combined with the prospect of excellent sport which was fully realised brought together a large assemblage, no loss than 3,000 persons circling the enclosure whilst upon the grand stand there was quite a bevy of fair ladies, and a number of the local gentry. The committee had made their arrangements with their usual-care and discre- tion, and everything 'passed off. irr a pleiuiant and harmo- nious style. The president of the club is Mr. F. THE SHARP HORSE TRANSACTION BY A RUNCORN MAN. ,

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Henry Watkin, a. respectable looking Man, who resides at Halton, was brought up on remand charged witk feloniously stealing a horse, the property of John Wood, cab proprietor, of 14, Ludwig-ro id, Antield, Liverpool, on the 24th May. Mr. Hitchen appeared for the defence. The facts of the case were given in last Saturday's Examiner. The prosecutor said on Saturday the 24th Mey, he was standing in Char- , lrytte-stregtjAyeTiiol, when the prisoner was brought to him 'by iyi6 tivse &tilers. The p.tiOnef inqgffed if ff'„; ;tome Iwas for sale, and he replied tho: IL; viaatt a) for it. To test the speed of the horse, witness drove the prisoner and the two dealers to a public-house in Lime-street, where they bad a drink at the prisoner's expense. The prisonet offered £l7 for the animal, and then, at his request, they all went to Fletcher's Restaurant in Whitechapel and had dinner, for which he paid. Afterwards the prisoner agreed to take the horse to Runcorn, and it was booked at the railwax station. Witness asked for the purchase money, but the prisoner said he had not the money with him, but be would go down to the restaurant and see if a gentleman who owed him some money had come. He was unable to find the gentleman, and witness deckled to accompany him to Run- corn for the money. Here the horse was put up at Tuckey's stable, and together the prisoner and witness went to Halton. Witness was placed in the parlour at the , prisoner's house and left alone for half an hour, when the prisoner returned ap I said his eldest son had gene to Frod- ' steam to pay some accounts and had taken the cheque book, and that he would send the money on Monday morning. Witness decided, however, to take the horse back to Liver- pool, but when lie reached Tuckey's stable be was informed that the prisoner's son had fetched the animal an hour pre- viously. As be did not receive a cheque on Monday morn. ing, he riga* Went to Halton, but he could not find the prisoner until night, when he caught him going down a field. The prisoner said the horse was at Acton Bridge and asked a it- nesafor a sovereign for try ing to sell it. Witness said he would get the animal without paying, and on the Wednesday after several futile attempts to get the money or the horse, he took oat a warrant for the prisoner's apprehension. He obtained the horse on the following Friday at Mr. Booth's farm, Acton. On the 7th inst. the prisoner came to him in Charlotte-street, Liverpool, and asked him it he was satis- fied with the £5 his brother had given him for his expepses. He replied that he was, and prisoner said he was glad it was all over, that he was only having a lark, and that it was £2O out of his pecket,—Cross•examined by Mr. Hit- then: The prisoner treated 'him like a gentleman at Hal- ton, and they had a cauple of soles for tea. He did not take the 1.0. U. to Mr. Robertson, because it was BO vague that he thought the prisoner was making fun of him. When he saw Watkin at Halton on Monday night he told him that the farmer he had taken the horse to would not buy it, , and that he had left it at Acton Bridge.—Jaiines Tuckey tie- posed that the horse was left at his stable, and removed by the prisoner's son. By Mr. Hitchen : When the horse was brought to the stables Wood said that it was Watkin's horse.—Charles Watkins, son of the pri- I saner, said on Saturday night the 24th May, his father told him that he had bought a horse, which was then at Toe- key's stable, and that he must go down and fetch it. His father did not tell him which way to bring the horse. but he took it through Rock Savage, having to call at Mr. Bar- ton's. On Monday, he took the bores to Acton Bridge and put it in a field belonging to Mr. Booth. On the Friday he delivered the horse over to P.S. MeMichael.—By the Bench: He had been to Fredshare on the Saturday, but did not take his father's cheque book.—Edwin Field, of the Norton Arms, lial'on, deposed to the prisoner's son placing the horse in his stable at ten minutes to eleven on Saturday night.—P.S. McMicheel proved receiving the hon.() from the prisoner's son, and PS. Walley deposed to apprehending the prisoner in Mr. Hitchen's office on Tuesday the 10% inst. He made no reply to the charge.—Mr. Hitcher% con- tended that a proper sale had taken place, and that the pri- soner was virtually charged with stealing his own hors,; but Wood, instead of suing for the payment by a civil pro- cess, had taken the present action, expecting to get his money quicker.—Mr. Brundrit said the Bench considered there was a prima facie case for a jury, and. Mr. Hitchen, having called A. Chew, booking clerk at the station, and Isaac Walls, a porter, the prisoner was formally committed to Kuutsford Quarter Sessions for trial.—Mr. Hirchen ap- plied for the prisoner to be liberated on bail.—Superinten- dent Leah objnted, but the Bench consented to take bail in ' the prisoner's own recognizance of £lOO, and two sureties 1 of £5O each.

div.head: CONSERVATISM AT WIDNES,
div.p: CONSERVATISM AT WIDNES,

- On Monday evening a meeting W 8 held in the Widnes Volunteer Hall under the auspices of the South-West Lan- cashire Conservative Registration Association. The room was about half filled, but it was very early apparent after the proceedings commenced that there was a good sprinkling of Liberals amongst the audience, references to Mr. Glad- stone, the Franchise Bill, and Free Trade evoking expres- sions of approval and cheers. Major Cross, president of the local Conservative Assofiation, presided, and with him on the platform were the Revs. G. Bond. M.A. (vicar of Fern- worth), J. Wright Williams (vicar of Widnes), Messrs. T. B. Royder, J.P., Edward Banner, JP., W. J. Stew,art, and J. Williams (of Liverpool), R,. Lewis, P. Briscoe, W. Treacy. J. MatthAs, H, White, T. Carlile, F. Neil, A. Jordan, R. Kidd, T. A. Bullough, Jos. White, T. H. Annett, S. Patin, T. Shorrocks, J. Foley, and R. Whiteside (secretary).—The Chairman said he was very pleased to meet them all again. Though not new dwelling amongst them he still felt the greatest interest in everything that took placein Widnes. At the same time he thought there were many able young men to carry on the good work in Widnes, and if they could appoint a successor to him—(" no, no")—the sooner they did the better, because the work would very soon require a i person to be on the spot to attend to it, his opinion being that a dissolution of Parliament would not long be delayed. (Applause.) Be then introduced Mr. J. Williams, of Liver- pool, to deliver his lecture on " What is a Liberal?" The lecturer said what was called modern Liberalism was in reality nothing more than a spurious imitation, and after a i reference to finance, the franchise bill, free trade, the Egyptian question, the Transvaal, and Afghanistan, he con- cluded by claiming that the Conservatives formed the truly kLiberal partv.—The Rev. G. Bond moved a vote of thanks to the lecturer, and in doing so instituted a coinparisoa be- tween the late Lord Beaconsfield and Mr. Gladstone. It used to be complained that Lord Beaconsfield was a minis- ter of sensations and surprises. Way, he did something, but the present man had done nothing but mischief. Len] Beaconsfield's surprises were strokes of genius arid foresight. Re saw what was coming, and he tcok steps beforehand to prevent disasters, but this man was all behind the cows tail they had hoard of. (Applause.) When the thing could not be prevented he came tact the tail. Referring to Gordon, the retz. gentleman said he believed there was not a man in the room but would rise up and turn the preQent ministry out of the place if they deserted Gordon. (Ap- plause) He was worth the whole lot of them. (Applause.) —Mr. T. B Boyden seconded the motion,_ which was c _ _ . . . . - '

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, TAURSDAT.

' . There is in political circles just now a pause of profound expectancy. On Monday Mr. Gladstone is to lift the veil and dispose of all rumours by. disclosing the real settle- ment with France. Upon this the Conservatives with great presence of mind nye already resolved to move a vote of Censure, and they look to wavering Liberals to help them to carry it, and su turn out the Ministry. The gravity of the crisis is not underrated by Liberals, including members .o] the Ministry; but the apprehension that weighed down die party last week, more particularly on Monday in last week, is considerably lightened. The result of the Lincoln election for one thing his raised the spiiits of the Liberals, testifying as it does at a critical time to the staunch loyalty of the country to Mr. Gladstone and his policy. Again the gross falsifications put forward by enemies of the Government, purporting to be the terms of the settlement with France. have had an effect quite contrary to that in- tended. At first they depressed the Liberals, but upon proof of the absolute baselessness of the most monstrous of them a reaction followed. People have come to think that, how- ever unacceptable the settlement may be, it cannot be so bad as it has been painted. They ar... something in the condi- tion of a man who has been threatened that he shall be flog- ged with a cat o' nine tails and when the time for carrying out the sentence arrives finds that he is only to be thrashed with a birch rod. That is not, of course, what tbe friends of the bondholders planned to brine about, but nevertheless remains.

In the meanwEile butiness is getting forward in the Commons. It is true that the Conservatives have suddenly returned to their old practie3s and have re-commenoed to obbtruct the Franchise Bal. That it is well.known is with

Ithe dis.incr and specific obj Act of throwing it over till the debate has taken place on /policy in Egypt. They feel if the Government are to go out and appeal to the country they bad better not have in their hands the completed Fran- chise Bill. The coming debate on the third vote of Cen- sure wsuld, however, be the dying struggle of the party. When they have had another good beating they would ad- mit to themselves that they have done enough for one ses- sion, and business would go forward at a steady rate. There is a good deal yeeto be done, much more than can be ac- complished. The Merchant Shipping Bill, though it stands on the Order Book, is practically gone. It is generally be- lieved that another great measure, the London Government 11, is safe,. a passage in a private letter just written by Mr. Gladstone to Mr. Firth confirming that view. Nevertheless, I happen to know that this bill is also marked for destruc- tion though the official announcement of the fact would pro- bably not be made for another lortnight. From one point et view it is a pity that speeches made at the House dinners of the National Liberal Club are not reported for the Press. I have recently attended two, and have been much struck with the high quality of the oratory. At the first dinner Mr. Chamberlain presided, and made tke beat speech I ever heard him deliver. Last night Mr. John Morley as in the chair, the other speakers being Mr. Henry Fowler and Mr. Illingworth. Mr. John Morley is a man , whom no journalist con name without recognition of the great honour ha does his profession by beloniag to it. It is with the &cutest pleasure I note the indications frequently given, and from divers quarters of the strong hold Mr. Mor- ley has upon the public mind. This has just been testified to is two distinct ways. One was at the poll of the northern miners, when Mr. Morley stood at the head of the list among the men they desired to have address them; and again in reelect of this dinner at the National Liberal Club when, at the secretary informed me, there were more applications for seats than there had been on any former occasion since the serietoof dinners were instituted.

It is the same in the Hansa of Com Mons, where, howeva late the hour may be, or however tedious a discussion may have grown, the ris:ng of John Morley is a signal for that profound silence and close attention which form the highest tribute to personal character. What was noticeaole in Mr. John Morley's speaking last night WAS the entire absence of that nervousness which .has militated against his perfect success as a speaker in the House. He spoke without notes and without hesitation, every sentence being, from a literary point of view, perfectly framed, and pregnant with thought. He will, in time, come to this manner in the House—is, in- deed, rapidly approtching it compared with his earliest effort It was a bold undertaking for a Prince in the Israel of Literature to stlp into the arena of practical politics and public life. The experiment has been made in many other cases with conspicuous absence of success. John Mill is a name that immediately comes to tbe mind when John Merley is thought of, and everybody ktows what kind of a business John Stuart Mill made of it. Mr. Morley has evidently and with a full sense of the difficulty of the strugg • made up his mind to win, and with ever' essay I. am in- creasingly convinced that be will do it. There cat be no question as to the success a Mr. Irving Bishop in the bank note trick essayed last night, or rather this morning, for it WAS one o'clock before the crowning feat was accomplished. There was a large and distinguished , aadience, including many members of Parliament and some ladies. As Mr. Labouchere would not promise to put in an appearance. Bishop had invited Mr. Bradlaugh to preside on the ground that be was a friend of Mr. Labonchere, and not likely to he taken in. But Mr. Bradlaugh has enough on I ' his hands just now, and did not appear, though the audi- ' coca were kept waiting a quarter of an hour for him. Then Mr. Edward Stanhope, the coming Leader of the Conserva- tive Party according to some authorities, was elected to the chair, and a committee formed of well kno.en gentlemen ahove suspicion of collusion. The place was very hot and crowded, and the people were on the whole in_a hostile tern- ' per. In particular one full-faced person, the only man with -an unknown name on the committee, was constantly and inconsequentially interposing. At brief intervals he was to ite seen waving his hat overthe crowd and exclaiming "As one of the committee—." He never got any further than that, being howled down by the company Or snubbed by Mr. , Stanhope. All these things made' it very hard for Bishop I to work. It was half-past eleven when I arrived, and I I understood that one attempt with a bank note tried with Sir Healy Holland as a subject had failed, which made the audience more sceptical than ever, and caused the full-faced man to wave his:hat more frequently, and observe "As one ' a the committee—" with fewer pauses.

Taking Mr. McLagan, M.P., first, bolding his right band 4 in his left, Mr. Bishop, being blindfolded, drew figures on a black board. These turned out to be 33425. Sir Henry Holland held the note in a sealed envelope. It had been put there by Mr. Stanhope, and Mr. McLagar] who, going out of the room, had in a remote portion of the corridor secretly ascertained the number. Being appealed to Sir H. Holland said th it this numbsr was wrong, at which there was some groaning, and the fat-faced man violently waved his hat and again alluded to the fact -that he was "one of the commlitee." M. Bishop now proposed, by way of re- creation,-to try another experiment. He took Mr. Healy and proposed that if he would locate in some part of his body an imaginary pain he would tell him where it was'. Mr. Healy, after bis manner, showrd signs of obstruction, but was at length induced to offer himself to be experimen- ted upen. He first wrote down in shorthand " tba tor) of my tight ear," and made me the repository of the secret. Mr. Bishop took him in charge and manipulated him, ' finally declaring that the supposed pain was at the tip of his left elbow. This, of course, was wrong, and the fat- faced man triumphantly waved his hat. lam bound to say that, closely watching the experiment, I noticed that Mr. Bishop mane several quick passes towards tpe top of the right side of Mr. Healy's face, and as qnickly returned to the neighbourhood of his left elbow as if he had be.en checked. I have little doubt, if the truth were known, that Mr. Healy had determined that the pain should be found on the opposite side from that where he bad located it, and that his wilfpiness checked the operation wken Mr. Bishop had got on the rigkt scent.

After this Sir Henry Holland was tried with a bank note, \ and in a very few minutes the right figures were written down, 33,245. Mr. McLagan then explained that het had actually been thinking of the fignres 33.425, having inik• vertantly transposed two of them. It is impossible to itaagine any more perfect test than this. If according to Mc. Labouchere there was a confederate in the bctiness who had made hirn-ielf acquainted with the number et the bank note, Mr. roshop would of course have writter it right the first time. But what he wrote was the figures and their 'sequence which were musing through the mind of Mr. McLagan—that is to say, he read his thoughts. This inad- vertence of Mr. McLagan's must for ever settle the question of collusion. After this event the fat-faced man put on his bat and went home; and indeed it was time for everyone to go, for it was half-plot one in the morning. • After reading "The Chaplain of the Fleet," I ventured to expeess tke opinion that Mr. Beeant is the greatest living novelist. Reading "Dorothy Foreter " cotrfirms that opinion. This is more than a novel. ft is living picture of times past away a hundred and seventy' years ago. We have the laces tho people, the mode of thoughts, and the manner of i speech. Without exception. all the characters in the book I are real men and woolen. not painted dolls, or painfully jerking marionettes. Mr. Besant is one Of the few novelists, who, writing eory in autobiographical form or dead, t form can .n ,k the scory-tellsr personally interestiv. How difficult this is we knew from the failure of Dickens in "David Cutperfled," and Thackeray in" Pendennis." In these hooks the least interesting person is the nominal hero. " Ilirothy Foster " is a charming English girl who talks i little of herself, but whom we seem to know and I thoroughly onderstind why Lord Derwentwater should have fallen in love with tor.

The Embankmest is growing into one of the finest streets in Europe. Toe trees planted some years :Igo have now taken firm root, and their greenery mikes a goodly show. I am glad to hear that we shall presently hiO3 removed the unsightly sk-let,in of the Nat 0041 Opera House, whose smoke-grimed ribs and ugly hoarding have long been an eye- I sore. The wreck is to he eold for building materials, and it

is to be hoped will shortly ne carted away. There is not much to show, but an immense amount of money has been sack in this abortive enterprise. .1 understand that there are livemillion bricks on the ground, besides a whole forest of timber. The failure of the original projector to carry out this noble project of a National Opera House has inflicted , considerable loss on the Metropolitan Board of Works, who are the ground-rent landlords, and who have all these years been out of pocket. It is curious to nate that of the £272 collected at West- minster Abbey on Hospital Sunday, whilst seven ,recktess people each put in a fourpenny piece, not less than £6 12a 9d was taken in threepenny bits. What s curious mind it must be that deliberately seeks out a threepenny bit to put in a collection box. Three honest pennies seem infinitely preferable. But the poattlarity of the threepenny bit as a token of charity is undying. Ina country town, •I know an old lady who keeps the greengrocery shop once remarked that she always knows when there has been a missionary sermon and collection at the church, because the parson 'Pays his weekly bill in threepenny bits. I did net disturb her faith by asking what was the parson doing with the threepenny bits dedicated by the charitable to the heathen.

div.head: DREADFUL .BOAT ACCIDENT OFF FRO DSEIAM. FOUR MEN DROWNED.
div.p: DREADFUL .BOAT ACCIDENT OFF FRO DSEIAM. FOUR MEN DROWNED.

A boat accident of a shocking description occurred in the Mersey opposite Frodsham Marsh on Sunday evening, four men being drowned and two narrowly escaping with their lives. About three o'clock on Sandier afternoon a small cock-boat, which had been " decked " and had a mast fixed, arrived at Weston Point, and seven men landed. It was evident that they were "fresh in drink," and they were re- fttsed admittance to Clark's Weaver Hotel, hut subsequently they obtained entrance to a beerhouse, where they had some liquor. They remained there until shortly after five o'cicck, when they left, and six of them entered the boat at the end of Weston Point Pier. The seventh refused to go on hoard, and asked for 31 to pay his fare over Runcorn Bridge. His friends subscribed thet amount, and he departed. One or ' two of the pen in the boat then commenced larking, and as they did not seem able to manage a boat, and there was a fresh breeze blowing, several people on the river wall wetcjied them sail towards the Frodshatn side of the river. When below the Lightship the boat was seen to capsize, and the occupants were soon struggling in the water. Aequickly as possibly, John Fulton, mate of the steamship Ashurst, and William Ryan, the second engineer, and James Cowley, captain of the fiat Lily, of Northwich, obtained a boat from the schooner Corymbus, of Middlesborough, which was lying off the docks, and pulled towards the scene of the accident. le consequence of the tide being two hours on the ebb, they got along with difficulty, and it was not until an hour Later that they reached the capsized craft. Before the arrival of Fulton and his companioue, Wm. Worrell, keeper of tjee lightship on the Marsh, saw the up- set and jumped into the water. He was successful in get- ting hold of Woods by the left hand. He looked to the safety of Loftus, but could see nothing of the other four men. In his dangerous work Joe was assisted by a yeang man named Wm. Bleas-, of the fishing smack" Mignonette,' belonging to a Mr. Poole, of lVidues. Woods on getting ashore made off across the banks toward Hale, evidently sue- feting from great excitement, hut he was fetched back by Worrell and told to render some assistance. He got iota the boat with Worrell and Blease and on reachieg the spot where the boat had capsized he again got out of the boat and ran away. Loftus wag taken on board the lightship, where he revived, and then a search was made for the four missing men. Two of the bodice were recovered at half-past nine and another at eleven, when the secrets was given up, as it was stated by Woods and Loftus that theta were ertiy five of them in the boat. On Monday morning, however, it was reported to the lightship keeper that there was another man, Barber, missing, and the body was recovered by Wor- rall at six o'clock the same morning. Information of the accident was conveyed t 3 Sergeant Johnson at Fredshaue about two miles away, and the three bodies were taken in a cart to the Queen's Head. The names of the deceased are John Woodward, of Dudgeon, near Hale, labourer, widower, leaviug ten children ; Cornelius Sweeney, St. Helens, bricklayer, single; Bernard McDermott, St. Helens. labourer for Mr. Harrison. bender, single; John Barber, Dudgeon, near Hale, married, and leaves a widow and seven children. The names of the survivors are James Woole and Bryan Loftus, both of Hale, and unmarried. The inquest on the bodies was held at Frodsham, to Tuesday evening, by Dr. Churtoo, the Coroner for West-Cheshire. It appeared that the deceased and three other men met together accident- ally near the Hale Lighthouse, on the Lancashire side of the river, and as a boat belonging to one of them (Barber) was lying close to, it was agreed to take a short sail to Weston Point, on the Cheshire side of the Mereey, a dis- tance of two miles. At Weston they had a member of " drinks " together at a public house called the VYaterman'e Arms, and one man, living at Runcorn, left the rarty and went borne on foot. By five o'clock there was a stiff breeze over the river, and at that hour, the tide being on the ebb, the men started for home. The evidence as to their condi- tion was rather cmflicting, but they were more or less under the influence of drink. They had scarcely got half a mile from the Cheshire shore when a !sudden gust of wind caught the sail with such violence as to break the mast. Just at , this moment one of the men, named Bryant Lortite, lest his hat, and while he and his companions were endeavouring to recover it, the boat ;alphas:a throwing Sweeeney, M‘Dermott, and Wocdwood into the river, while Barber, Loftus, and a man named James Wood, clung to the boat, which immediately righted, though fiiled with water. Sweeney, M'Dermott, and Woodward were at once drowned, and Barber soon became exhausted, and, releasing his hold on his boat, also sank. The 'nester of the Frodsbam Lie lit- ship saw the affair, aniwith all possible speed rowed to the spot and rescued Wools end Loftne. All the bodies were recovered by the mister of the nein:hip (William Worrell) and ether men. The verdict was "Accidentally drowned." hhedeoufbsueenloeonrfegolzoef Woodward and Barber took place at Hale, on Wednesday afternoon.
