div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JUNE 21. 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JUNE 21. 1884.

throats of the unfortnuate crew, and he thought they would find, if they should meet Mr. Brooks to render him assis- tance at the poll, that when he gave hie votes in the House of Commons they would be as diametrically opposed to everything that they (the Liberals) understood as Liberal principles, whether moderate Or firm, as the most complete Tory could wish. (Applause.) He warned them to be aware of such pi micel craft in politics as Mr. Brooks. Candidates of beth political partieswere,so to speak,in the position of set- vents seeking a equation. If a person sought a situation, whose antecedents were antagonistic to what the employer desired, and said that he had changed his ways and would be different in the future, the employer would naturally pre- fer to take one with good cenduct in the pact rather thau the penitent one. Mr. nooks and Conservative candidates who came before them in the garb of moderate men, were in the position of penitents who, having a long list of pre- vious convictions against them, asked to be taken on trial in the place of men of comparatively unblemished character. The bad character of the Conservative party in the past must never to lost sightof by an English constituency when it was invited to lend its support to the Conservative party in the future. (Apptause.) They ought never to forget that the Conservative early which Mr. Brooks represented, whether be called himself moderate or not—the party for which Mr. Brooks with faithful discipline would vote in the House of Commons—was the party which, 80 far as they were concerned, they knew had suppressed while it bad the pow•r the right of Englishmen to meet and discuss poll • tient questions, and the party which, session after session, resisted the claim of Englishmen to read a cheap newspaper —(shame)—a party which was opposed to free- dom of religious opinion and which put penalties upon dissenters—(applause)—penalties which would have forbidden some of the !nest esteemed and honoured citizens from getting those municipal offices which in Manchester and other large towns they so worthily adorned. It was the party which was opposed to the education of the people for fear, he supposed, the people should find out what hum- bug the Conservative party was, the party which was in favour of the slave trade and resisted the efforts towards emancipation of Wilberforce and others, which endeavoured to tax the bread of the people, which did so tax it, and which brought half starved workmen up and punished them for their dissatisfaction with cruel penal laws. Not one of the charges in that indictment against the Conservative party could to coneradicted by Mr. Brooks. It was only a few years since the electors had an opportunity of seeing how a Conservative administration acted when it was in • power. and it had been revealed that so far irom the Con- • servatives having really turned their backs upon those prin- • ciples that they represented so hang, they had, not in Eng- land so much as in foreign comitries, once more put those ' odious principles into force. If they read their Conserva- tive papers they might see how in these moderate days the , Conservative party were foremost in the good work of edu- cation ! How anxious the Conservatives were that the , masses should be really intelligent, and how confident they were that if knowledge was diffused amongst the people a I Liberal Government would never again be admitted to take a share in the administration ef national affairs? (Laughter.) At , Altrincearn he inentioged the last effort of a Conservative . Government to supprel, free political debate when, in 1867, ' such Government threatened a massacre because the artisans ;of the towns were demanding a right to vote. Had they forgotten what happened only some nine years ago in India r during the administration of the late Conservative Govern- , ment ? Then the Conservative Government passed an Act which deprived the Indians of their vernacular papers and • put the editors of those papers in gaol, because they pro- . testei against a war in Afghanistan, which they foresaw would make them poorer than they were. Nine years ago a the Conservatives were what they were two or three genera- -1 tions ago, and the principles that Mr. Brooks called moder- t ate were those which Liberals were accustomed to call r odious. (Applause.) They heard "Peace with honour" a still spoken of in every Conservative speech. (Laughter.) 1 He would tell them what peace with honour meant for some of the unhappy inhabitants of Eastern Europe who were , replaced by Lard Beaconneeld, against the protect of Mr. i Gladstone, under the ferocious tyranny of the Turk. Lord ' Beaconsfield determined, in his love for Turkey, that Mace- I donee should be restored to the rule of Turkey, and the cen- t sequence of that act he would give in the wordtof Mr. a Forster. Two years after such restoration, according to Mr. Forster, " Macedonia was in a terrible condition, and was . over-run with brieands, who terrorised the country; there was no law, no order, no security for life property, or and things were getting worse and worse by sheer rottenness." a That was an example of what the Conservatives • held up to admiration as the result of peace with honour. They might depend upon it that the Conser- vative attitude towards their own subjects and to foreigners was not changed, and the plague would break out again on an early opportunity if once the Administration were in • power. There was one House of the Legislature which was an excellent exponent of Mr. Brooks, for of course it would a be heresy to say that the Lords were ever immoderate. (Laughter.) But the attitude of the Lords towards measures . which were submitted to them by Liberal Governments reminded him very much of the story if the doctor who was asked his opinion as to the way in which cucumbers should be taken. The doctor said, "You must peel it, slice , it, add some pepper, sonic salt, and some vinegar, and then— throw it out of the window." (Laughter.) That was pre- cisely the line that the Lords were accustomed to take to- wards Liberal measures, and when he recalled one or two that had been treated in that way they would see that there was very little satisfaction to be got by a progressive nation out of a hat Mr. Brooks called moderate Conservatism. The House of Lords opposed the Irish Land Act. The Agricul- . tural Holdings Act was so treated by the Conservatives and the House of Lords that a great deal of its effect was destroyed. They threw out the bill for Local Government ' in Scotland and the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, and in fact if one read the catalogue of the bills that the Lords had thrown out and amended. one fel t inclined, in tal king about Mr. Brooke, to say like Lord Clive when he plundered India, "He was astonished at his own moderation." Taking the ques- tion of education, the speaker said that since the present Government came into power a Royal Commission had been issued for the purpose of enquiring into the system of technical education in England, and discovering and repair- ing the deficiencies. The Commissioners pointed out in their report, that in nearly all the English institutions for imparting technical education, there was a want of adequate funds, tf professors, and of museums and laboratories. The report also described the city and guilds of London Insti- tute 'for technical education, and said that subscriptions towards the maintainence of that organisation were inade- quate. He must confess that the subscriptions of the liveried companies of the city of London towards the institute for the better education of workmen, reminded him of the con- scientious burglar, who sent back the electro-plated spoons, and kept the silver ones. (Applause). These city compa- nies were created for the express purpose of giving techni- cal instruction to the working men of Great Britain. The great majority of them at the present time discharged no functions or duties for the good of the community of any kind, and there was a general system of jobbing away their great wealth. The members who had the administra- tion of these close corporations divided the property amongst themselyee, and he had been informed, that it was no uncommon thing for aldermen—he was net specifying any person in particular—to belong to two or three city compa- nies in order that their share of the spoil should be greater. Nearly there entire site of the city of London belonged to these companies, whose availabfe revenue exceeded one mil- lion sterling a year. and who let out property in the city at very much less than. it would fetch in the open mar- kets. This money was designed for tailors, cordwainers, salters, ; but in whese hands was it ? It was in the hands of Conservative lawyers, of Conservative stock jobbers, and of Conservative aristocratic houses. There was money enough in the city companies to found ten uni- versities for the purpose of eneourageng agriculture and the ' manufacturing industries. During the last Conservative Administration an inquiry into these companies was demanded, but was defeated by 96 moderate Conservative votes. (Lanehter.) Since that day there had been other people to' cleal with, and an inquiry bad been set on foot, the result of which, he hoped, would be that we should see funds originally intended for promoting technical instruction no longer grossly diverted from the purpose for which they were created. Then there woe connected with this question the great siabject of London. Advantages were enjoyed under locae administrations in Manchester. Warrington, and elsewhere bathe provinces, which were not possessed by the • people of tendon, and there was great need for the reform of the Government of the Metropolie. ihe Corporation of London had large revenues, and' to give an idea of bow the money was empeneed in some instances he would mention that the sewed £27,000 was spent upon. a banquet given to the Prince of Wales. Be was in ferour of showing hospitality to the Prince of Wales, but hhought that was more than, was necessary. Some of he items were astonishing. There was £V3O for men te cards and £5OO paid in gratnitios to the city officials, who all drew pretty lanee stipende Is it was. This was another point on which the moderaee Conservatives and the Liberals were at difict lime. The Liberals said that this money should not ne 'jobbed away. at the expense of the ratepayers, and the Con- servatives had Riven notice through Mr. Fowler, the present Lord Mayor of London, that the London Government Bill was to he fought line by line. He would give them a epee cimen of what was called Conservative reform, because they were assured by Mr. Broke and his friends that they were not opposed to reform, and that any moderate, or rational, or well-considered reform would always have their support. There was a bill which professed to be a reform Bill before the House of Commons this sessions_ It was backed, amongst other things, by that very reforming name—because he 0088 art advanced conservative—of Lord Randolph Churchill—(loud laughter)—and it was a reform tO which he wished to call public attention, and particularly the at. tendon of those interested in agriculture. Ass Fellow of the Collene of Oxford he (Mr. Lotdam) had had a share in the administration of seine considerable estates. No farmor would contradict him when he slid that college landlords were amongst the most generous in England. No tenant under a College of Oxford or Cambr,dge was asked whether be voted Whig or Tory, or ran any risk of being turned out of his holding without compensation, or with icadequate compensetion, if he voted against the wish 01 the land- lord. A tenant might be of any religious persnaoion, and enjoyed a practical security of tenure. Those colleges were national in4titutes, and since the Liberal Government had , abolished tents, had become the property of every man • Churchman .1r Nonconformist. After tests mere abolished Mr. Baring offered £lOO,OOO to Brazenose College on con- eition that it would elect a certain number of Fellows who should be members of the Church of England, but the Rift was rejected, as it was believed that the condition attached in it would practically have been an evasion of the law. Lord Randolph Churchill was of opinion, be supposed, that the Universities at Oxford and Cambridge would bear a little blood letting. lie (the speaker) believed that great

div.head: REPRESENTATION OF MIDCHESHIRE. LIBERAL MEETING AT ALTRINCHAM.
div.p: THE REPRESENTATION OF MID- CHESHIRE. LIBERAL MEETING AT ALTRINCHAM.

• A meeting of Liberal electors and non-electors of Mid- Cheshire was held on Saturday evening at the British Schools, Altrincham, mainly to hear an address from Mr. L S. Leadham, who fias recently been adopted as one of the liheral candidates for the division. The other liberal caniidate, Mr. Thomas Rigby, will not address political meetings during the present year, unless there should be a dissolution of Parliament. Mr. Leadatn, who on Saturday evening made his first public appearance in the constitu- ' encv, had an enthusiastic reception, and spoke with marked effect for over an hour. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. W. Latham, president of the Mid-Cheshire Liberal Asso- ciation, and there were- on the platform the Revs. A. Mac- kennel, Joe. Johnson, J. E. ()gems, C. D. Rutland, and F. Wainwright, (Se. John's, Altrincham), Sir Joseph Lee, Messrs. Claud J. Morris, W. Milne, N. Clegg, Abraham Haworth, Jesse Haworth, R. Verdin, T. W. hillick, H. T. Gaddure, Geo. Hooke, C. Broadbent, E. L. Ashworth, C. E. Smarmier, H. G. Menthe, Professor T. D. Hall, G. Bowen, A. Fletcher, F. A. Roberts, A. E. Paterson, and others. The following polling distrivs were represented at the meeting: Altrincham, Nhrthwieh, Sale, Knutsford, Lymrn, Thelwall, Sandbach, Winsford, and Grappenhall. The CHAIRMAN, who was greeted with cheers, thanked the Liberal electors for their unwearied kindness to him during the time he was their candidate. He was certain there was a Liberal majority in Mid-Cheshire. It was pro- posed that night to pass a resolution about the Reform Bill, of the passing, of which this year he (the chairman) had good hopes. When the bill was passed he thought Mid- Cheshire was safe for two Liberal members. If the dissolu- tion came before the bill was passed, he called upon the electors to do their best to return the Liberal candidates, in order that the voice of the people, and not the voice of a clique, might be heard in the councils of England. (Cheers.) • Mr. LRADAX, who was received with loud cheers, ac- knowledged the great honour conferred upon him by the Liberal electors of Mid-Cheshire through their representa- tive assembly commonly called the CAUCUS, and expressed his sense of the great services which his predecessor, Mr. Latham, had rendered to the constituency. (Cheers.) One excellent result of the caucus was the greater harmony which pervaded the Liberal party. Was the Conservative ,party united? WAS there any particel3r principle upon which the Conservative party was agreed? Lord Salisbury made a speech the other day, in which he advocated the per- petual extension of the empire. It was a very serious matter when the extension of the empire meant increased taxation, the paralysis of domestic legislation, and last of all—and this must certainly came if they adopted the maxims of Lord Salisbury—universal conscription. (Hear, hear.) 1 After referring to Lord Randolph Churchill, Mr. Leaden] went on to speak of obstruction in the House of Commons, and expressed his surprise at seeing that Mr. Warburton in his recent speech at Sandbach stated that Mr. Gladstone knew that there was no such thing as Commons obstruction. Mr. Warburton also said that the Midlothian dream of peace, retrenchment, and reform was nearly over. He (Mr. Leadam) should have occasion elsewhere no doubt to say something about the Midlothian dream of retrenchment; they would hear something that night about the Midlothian dream of reform, . and the Midlothian dream of peace. Passing on to speak of the Fiknchise Bill, Mr. Leadam remarked that the line taken by Lord Salisbury was that which the Conserva- tives had always adopted, that legislation was not reqmired, and he reminded his hearers that Sir Richard Cross had

moved an amendment the object of which was to exclude county lodgers from the franchise. Conservatism had shown itself in the debates on the Reform Bill to be what it hid always been. 'intrust of the people tempered by fear was the sign of Conservatism. If, since 1832, when the Liberals obtained the ascendency in this country, there had been greater harmony among classes, a truer loyalty to the Constitution, contentment where there was once anarchy, prosperity where there was once starvation, he begged them to reflect that these results were the outcome of a series of Liberal measnres—(cheers); and he trusted they would show their appreciation of the value of these measures and of what might be expected from the same party in the future by continuing to support. that Government to which their presence at that meeting testified their adhesion. (Cheers.) Mr. Rommtv VSIMIN, representing the Northwich polling district, moved a resolution expressing the confidence of the meeting in Mr. Leadam as a candidate for the representa- tion of Mid-Cheshire, and pledging the meeting to use every legitimate means to return him to Parliament. He was sure th At the caucus had selected the proper person to represent Mid-Cheshire. The CHAIRMAN remarked that in the district of North- wich.there would be a larger increase in the number of vo- ters under the Reform Bill than in any other district of the

Mr. Wm. LONG, representing the Grappmhall district, se• onded the resolution. He was afraid his district was the most Tory of the division, but, under such a Franchise Bill as they hoped to get, even Grappenhall would give a better account of itself than it had hitherto done. (Hear, hear.) Mr. FRED. PLATT (Altrincham), asked if Mr. Leadam was in favour of the disestablishment and disendowment of the Church of England. Mr. LEADAM replied that he accepted the principle that the State which had created the Establishment and endowed it had the right to disestablish and to disendow it. When the majority of the people; of the country expressed a de- sire for disestablishment and disendowment these measures should be carried out. At this moment, however, he did not regard the question as one of the foremost questions of the day. It might, perhaps, be called a secondary ques- tion.
The resolution was carried unanimously, and with cheers. Mr. CLMJD J. MORRIS moved the following resolution : _

That the electors and non-electors here assembled eXDress their warm approval of the measure now before Parliament, whereby the right to vote for representativls its Parlismert will be conferred upon a large number of persons hitherto de- barred from the eats cis, of this privitege, and trust thst the Government will not be prevented by the factious opposition in either House from passing the hilt this session. And that a copy of this resolution be sent to Dlr. Gtadstone and the mem- bers for this division of the county. _

He remarked that the Reform Bill represented the wish of the Liberal party to do justice to many thousands of their fellow-countrymen. (Hear, hear.) They all believed that the hill was a just measure, and that the Government and the'Liberal members supporting them were doing right in pushing it forward. (Cheers). r. L. ASHWORTH (linutsford polling district) seconded the motion. The resqlution was adopted.

Mr. T. W. KILIICE having taken the chair, Mr. GEORGE HOOKE moved a resolution thanking Mr. Latham for his services in the chair that night, and " for his unwearied exertions on behalf of the Liberal party at all times and in all places."
Mr. C. E. Swa'ming seconded the molien, and Mr. Laniaar having briefly acknowledged the vote the meeting, which had been throeghoat of an enthusiastic character, terminate.

div.head: MEETING AT LYMM. SPEECH BY MB. LEADAM.
div.p: MEETING AT LYMM. SPEECH BY MB. LEADAM.

On Mondny evening a well attended meeting was held at the Mission Hall, Lymm, in response to an invitation iesued by the general committee of the Grappenhall and Lynam districts of the Mid-Cheshire polling divieicia, to bar An address by Mr. I. S. Lead'am' M.A., one of the can- didates for the division in the Liberal interests. Mr. Long ' presided, and amongst those also present were Councillor Broadbent, and Messrs. T. Bendel], Dan Boyd, R. McKay, J. A. Swanwick, J. Hudson, Welfor6, G. N. Watson, Brewt— nall, Cartwright. Dells, It.e. The CHAIRMAN said that it was always a pleasure to him te come amongst the Liberals of Lynam, from the rather more Tory district of Gropenhall. He had that night sr very agreeable duty to perform in introducing Mr. Leadam to the meeting. When that gentleman was amongst them twelve menthe ago he produced a very pleasant impression. , which he was rinitesurewould be strengthened by what would be heard from him that night. Mr. Leadarn came fresh to • the work to a constituency which, he hoped, wo in some . measure prepared ter the acceptance of the thorough I Liberal principles in which they bad been educated by their friend Mr. Latham. (Anplauee.) lie thought they would all agree that the committee had done well in obtain- ing a candidate of Mr. Leadam's ability to represent them in the House of, Commons, (Cbeers,) What he wished expressly to impress upon the meeting was not only that they should evince an enthatiasm ia meetings ef that kind, but that they should also leave such meetings with the de- termination to endeavour to propogste the principles of Liberalism. It was well that they should look forward to the time when elections would be more pure, and when each man would be able to lend himself to the work of returning to Parliament the man of hie choice. _

- Mr. LEADAIA who was received with. cheers, said that the chairman had reminded them that upon the last occasion be (Mr. Leadam) was present in fuvmm was upon the occasion of the candidature of their friend Mr. Latham, and he (the speaker) then delivered an address in which he cogfined himself chief* to agricultural topics, because he had for years past investigated to the best of his ability the pro- blems which had been before the public in connection with the land question. (Hear, hear.) In doing so he had had the good fortune to make- the acquaintance, and, he believetl, the friendship, of many farmers is various parts of Beg- ' land, but not hitherto in, Cheshire. He hoped, however, that from the period of his candidature he might form the determined opinion as d thatt to • e acquaintante of the geatlemen distieguished in the agricul. e rural world of Cheshire. The reoeon why he fancied that the Liberal electors of Mid-Chesbirteyu w n wereceyre t oof be e irtu was at:no ()cat desirable wfas x. because onauscetshoe were, as the app-ndage of a great family. As it was a very good thing in delivering an address to take a text, he pro- posed to take one from a speech given by Mr. Brooks the other day. Mr. Brooks said that "he would ask moderate men of the Liberal party to remember how much nearer the Conservative piny bad drawn to the moderate Liberal party." Now, all that he could say was that if Mr. Breolas turned his back upon the ancient principles of Conservatism, if Mr. Brooks really felt himself drawn nearer to the Liberal party, he would meet Mr. Brooks half-way and would invite him to take a place upon his election committee. (Laughter and applause.) He had a grea, idea of men sticking to their principles and not attempting to gain hostile votes by professing to be half disposed towards principles that were entirely antagonistic with theirewn. They would all have raid how pirate craft had by making signals of distress lured on to destruction vessels that came to their aid, and had cut the unhappy

as were the resources of these Universities they were in- adequate for the work of the nation, Lord H. Churchill proposed that the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge and the colleges should be compelled to sell all their leaded property, and put their money into console, in which event the land would be forced upon a glutted market, and the reduced income which the money, if invested in consols would yield, would materially itnpair the value of the uni- versities as educational institutions. The land thrown upon the market would pass into the hands of great owners, and swell possessions alteady too great. What was the attitude, Mr. Leadam asked, of their moderate friends towards the Franchise question. Why, they said that it was a super- fluous luxury that mid-Cheshire could do without, and he had no doubt that were it not for the Liberal rnovonent they would leave the franchise and redistribution to solve themselves in the milennium. There was another subject of interest, and that was the Merchant Shipping Bill of Mr. Chamberlain. Lord Salisbury said that that bill vrae "mon- strous fantastic," and a Conservative member proposed that it should be read that day in six months, which meant never it all. Why was this? It was not that Conserva- tives, as individuals, were less humane than Liberals. The reason was to be sought elsewhere. Just as a false religion might obscure tree religion so a false principle might as it were take the place of and obscure humanity. The Conser- vatives had a golden calf that they worshipped. Their gol- den calf was class interests. Their worship of class in- terests compelled them in the hope of catchier" the votes of what they called the harassed classes, to suoport every abuse which Liberals endeavoured to expose. (Hear, hear.) The Liberals lost votes by this exposure of abuses. But they lost these votes because they considered national in- terests first and class interests second. (Loud cheer). Councillor C. BROADBICNT proposed "that this meeting desires to thank Mr. Leadam for his address, and cordially pledges itself to do its best to secure his return, together with that of Mr. Rigby, at the next Mid-Cheshire election." He was sure that the favourable impression made by Mr. Leadam at Lamm twelve mouths ago had now been rt- flowed, if not increased. He was sure they were most fortu- nate in their candidate. Mr. Leadam, though not a land- owner in Cheshire, understood the land question, which would come prominently before the country when the Fran- chise question was disposed of. Mr. Leadam had a thorough knowledge of Liberal topics ant of the land ques- tion. Mr. Rigby had that knowledge but he had also a practical connection with the county, so that with two such candidates he thought that they would give a good account of themselves and their party at the next election. (Ap- plause).

Mr. 'DAN BOYD seconded the resolution, which was sup- norted by Mr. Brewtnall (Thelwall), Mr. Welford, and Mr. Evans, and carried by acclamation. A vote of thanks to the Chairman proposed by Mr. HOLT and seconded by Mr. CAMERON, brought the proceedings to a close.

MEETING AT SANDEACH. A meeting of "the present and Incite electors" of the Sandbach district of the Mid-Cheshire division was held on Tuesday evening in the Providence Schools, Sandbich, for the purpose of supporting the Government in its•efforts tO pass the Franchtke Bill. Mr. G. W. Efatham presided, and he was supported on the platform by Mr. Leadam, Mr. W. Shirley-Shirley, Mr. R. Bygott, Mr. E. Eardley, and others. There was a large attendance—Mr. R. Bygott moved, and Mr. E. Eardley seconded, a resolution in favour of the Franchise Bill.—Mr. Leadam, who was very cordially re- ceceived, spoke in support of the resolution. He remarked that Mr. Brooks, one of the Conservative candidates, had recently approached that part of the constituency in sheep's clothing, and had informed them that he was so very nearly a Liberal that it was most diflicult to distinguish him front a moderate Liberal. The Conservative party had always posed as the friend of all rational and necessary reform, but when the present Liberal Government introduced measures of reform they were never assisted by the Conservative party. (Hear, hear.) The Conservatives professed to be the farmers' friends, and were very much surprised at the action taken by the farmers in 1880. The Conservative party had lived upon the farmers for a very long time, and very naturally they were considerably astonished at what they thought the ingratitude of the farmers. The Liberals, in order to repay the farmers, had tried to pass several bills pealing with agricultural matters, and in every case they were opposed by the Conservatives.—The resolution was also supported by the Rev. W. Mellor and carried unani- mausly.—A vote of thanks was ;afterwards accorded to the Chairman, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

A VIOLENT FEMALE—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Ellen Deans, of Earlestown, was „summoned for assaulting Eliza Mulbern. and also for damaging a washing- tub and other articles to the amount of 121.—The evidence was of a somewhat contradictory character, but the Bench consideied the case proved, and imposed a fine of 5s and costs, and ordered the defendant to pay 101 as damage. ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE.—At the Newton Petty See- eons, on Saturday, Patrick Dowd was charged under a war- rant with assaulting P.C. Ellis Ratcliffe in Hiet-street, Gol- borne, on the 31st ult.—P.C. Ratcliffe stated that the pri- soner was drunk and creating a disturbance, and as he, (witness) was locking another man op the prisoner rushed e him (witness) and struck him with a stick saying he would make him let his prisoner go.—The Bench commit- ted the prisoner for one month. ANTI-VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN : ANOTHER SUM. MONS.—Before H. Houghton and A C. McCorquodale, Esqs. at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, John Preecott, of Legh-street, Earlestown, was summoned to show cause why ,an order should not be made upon him to have his child vaccinited as required by the law.—The Clerk (Mr. White) stated that the cise had been adjourned since the last court day. It was necessary in that case that the magistrate who signed the summons should hear it, and cons,quentiv the case would again have to be adjourned until Mr. Gillespie (who had signed the summons) could appear—After some conversation Mr. Cooper, the vaccination officer for the Newton district, stated that he would withdraw the summons and cause a fresh one to be issued.—Tbe Clerk (to the de- fendant): Do you still object to have the child vaccinated ? —Defendant; I have a sufficient reason sir. lam prepared to state my reasons, but if the case is to be adjourned or dis- missed I would rather postpone them—The Clerk: I thought it would save you th 3 trouble of coming here again. —The Chairman stated that unless the defendant would pro- mise to have the child vaccinated nothing further need be said about the matter then.—The defendant: I reserve my defence.

_ CREW. TREATMENT OF HORSES AT NEWTON FAIR.— Several cases of cruel treatment of horses, arising out of the horse fair at Newton, en the 17th May, were heard at the Petty Sessions, held at tile Town Hall on Saturday, before R. Houghton and A. C. McCorquodale. Esqs. Samuel Cun- liffe was charged .with cruelly ill-treating a mare by work- ing it in an unfit state; and Alice Finney was summoned as the owner of the mare for causing It to be worked in an unfit state.—lnspector Campbell, of the Royal Society for the Prevention cf Cruelty to Animals, deposed that on the date named he saw the defendant Cunliffe in charge of a mare, which was excessively lame o a both fore feet,and was in a very weak and emaciated condition. He also found a wound on its back, which was bleeding, the blood running down the flanks. The mare WAS in a wretched state and was totally unfit for work.—Mrs. Finney was fined 2s 6,1 and costs, and the defendant Cnntiffe was ordered to pay the costs.--John Meadows was summoned for cruelly working a horse in an unfit state, and Inspector Campbell stated hat the case Was a very bad one.—The Bench im- posed a fine of 103 and costs.--Michael Lyons, for cruelly beating a mare with a thick stick on the 17th ult was fined 5s and costs.

_ ALLEGED TRESPASS IN SEARCH OP GAIRIL—At the New- ton Town Hall, on Saturday, John Goulden and Thomas Bassett, two young men, were summoned for treso teeing in search of game on land at Havdock, in the occupation of Mr. Edwardson.—Mr. Moore, of 'Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, represented the defendants.—lt was stated that the defendants were seen on the land in question by a gamekeeper named Watkins, who went towards them after bearing shots proceeding from the direction where the meta were. Goulden had a gun in his possession, and the two men on seeing the gamekeeper ran away. Watkins, however, parsued and succeeded in cap- turing him. He gave his name as John Jones. and said he resided at 17, Newton Common, but both the name and ad- dress were ascertained to be false. Watkins afterwards met Beseett in the Street and charged him with trespassing on the land along with Goulden.—For the defence Mr. Swift maintained that the keeper had made a mistake with regard to the man Bassett, and stated that that defendant was the wrong person summoned. He subsequently called Gouldeu, who severe that Bassett was not the man who was with him in the field. He added that he had only purchased the gun on the evening previous to the date named, and he simply went into the field, away from any houses, in order to see if it would shoot straight. He denied that he was trespassing in pursuit of game.—The Bench dismissed the case against Baneett, and fired Goulden 5s and coets. SINGULAR THEFT OF A COAT AT BunTONwcom—Before R. Houghton and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqs., at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Michael Burke was charged with stealing a black clath coat, value LE 153, the property of Martin Graham.—Superintendent Jackson stated that ore the Bth inst. the prisoner and the prosecutor were drinking , together in a public-house at Burtonwood, and they after- wards retired from the beer-house into the lane. They took a la of drink with them which they drank, and they after- wards fought, pulling off their coats. After the fight the prisoner picked up the prosecutor's coat, and went away with it. He was afterwards apprehended at the railway. station, Barlestown, and he then had the coat in his posses- sion. The prosecutor now refused to appear, so he (Sept. Jackson) had to ask that the Bench would dismiss the case. —The Clerk: I have read the depositions and I think there is a considerable doubt in the ease.—The prisoner was dis- charged. Rees SUNDAV.—The Sunday immediately preceding the annual races at Newton Common has always hem one of unusual interest to many persons. Up to a year or two a4O " Race-Sunday" was a scandal to the eatire neighbour- hood,and the trading and traffic carried on abeut the Com- mon was an "eye-sore "to all the peace-loving inhabitants of tbe town. A determined opposition to its continuance was made with the result that the authorities suporessed the trading, and the con=equent evils have almsst entirely dis- appeared. On Sunday, the beautifully fine weather drew some thousands of persons from the outlying districts of St. Helens. Warrington, Golhorne, Leigh, &0., and the vicinity of the race-course presented an animeted appear- ance. A number of police officers, however, were present te preeerve order, and everything passed off quietly, the majority of the persons contenting themselyesewith watkine round the "course," or resting themselves on the graesy slopes of Use Common.

SUCCESS OF ANEwrow ATHLETE.— At the 15th annual meeting in connection with the Southport Athletic Society, on Saturday afternoon, at Southport, S. Rimmer, of Newton, ran second in the final heat of the open half-mile Hat race. He had 6:5 yards start. J. A. Whit'orl, of the Liverpool gymnasium (60 yards), was first, and J. Ackwood, of Man- chester (70 yards), was third. A MIDNIGHT Fr.arrma AT NENTON.—Before 11. Hough- ton and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqs , at the Newton Petty Session •?' on Saturday, Andrew Martin, of Earlestown, was summoned for removing goods from a dwelling-house in order to avoid a distraint for rent.—The evidence was to the effect that the defendant occupied a house of which Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton, was the owner, and on the night of the 15th ult. he unlawfully removed his goods while £lO 63 was owing for rent. The value of the goods removed was £5, and the Bench made an order for the payment of double that amount.

NEWTON VOLUNTEERS AT LIVERPOOL.—Oa Saturday the Newton-le-Willows Company (G) of the 19th L.R.V. (Press Gaards), proceeded to Liverpool in order to take part in an inspection of the regiment in baton Park, by Colonel Thack- well, commanding the 8:h and 40th regimental districts. The various evolutions and drills were excellently gone through in the presence of a large concourse of spectators. The commanding officer (Colonel Whitney) afterwards spoke in encouraging terms to the members of the corps. There was a total of 521 of all ranks on parade. A Row IN Caow LANE.—At a special court held at Earlestown police station on Wednesday evening, before Geo. McCorquodale, Esq., William Hell, of Newton Com- mon, was charged with assaulting P. S. Longworth on the previous day; and Bernard Manuion, of Plank-lane, was charged with assaulting P. C. McGregor. The evidence showed that a disturbance took place in Crow-lane among some persons who had been to the noes, and the officers , attempted to suppress it. In doing so they were assaulted by the prisoners. Each prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months. THE UNITED SITNDAY SCHOOL TRIP TO WINDERMERE. —We learn with regret that the promoters of the United Sunday school cheep trip from Eerlestown to Windermere on race-Wednesday, have to put up with a serious loss as a result of the venture. The fare for the return journey was only 3s 6J, and the trip left Earlestown at 6.0 in the morn- ing, returning from Windermere at 7-25 p m, and from Ken- del, Carnforth, and Lancaster at later times. About 150 only, or one half of the guaranteed number, went by the ex- cursion; but those who did go thoroughly enjoyed their ders outing. The beautiful lake and the attractive scenery by which it is surrounded, were seen at their best, and all have expreseed themselves highly delighted with their visit to the lake district.

div.head: STABBING Al,vitn., T BURTONWOOD.
div.p: THE STABBING Al,vitn., T BURTONWOOD.

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before R. Houghton and A. C. McCorquodale, Esq., William Mur- ray, of Bold, was again charged on remand with cutting and wounding Martin Ford, with intent to c:o him grievous bodily harm, on the sth May.—Mr. Swift appeared for the defendant.—Superintendent Jackson stated that on the date named the two men were drinking in the Elm Tree beerhouse, at Burtonwood, and in consequence of tkem quarrelling the landlady ordered them out. The two men went out by the back door, and eventually Murray went towards his own home for the purpose of going home. The prosecutor followed him, and renewed the quarrel on the way. Some words took place, and it ended in Murray striking the prosecutor on the inside of the right thigh, the wound penetrating to the bone, and, he believed, ripping the flesh for some considerable distance. When the prisoner was apprehended no knife was found upon him, except a small penknife, which he scarcely thought would inflict such injuries as the prosecutor had received. Shortly before the prosecutor left the beerhouse he purchased a knife , similar to the one produced, and when apprehended and charged with the offence he said •• Well, I was obliged to do something; he should not have followed me." He had since made a statement to Sergeant Cemmins to the effect that he had a knife in his band when the prosecutor rushed at him, and in making a kick he was aceiilentally struck on the thigh with the knife—the prosecutor and other witnesses were then called, and gave evidence in support of the facts previously published.—For the defence, 51r. Swift maintained that it was Ford's own fault that he was in- jured, as lie followed Murray, who was on his way home. Murray had hitherto borne it good character, and he did not think he had any intention of stabbing the prosecutor, or that it was premeditated, as be was on his way home and Ford followed him.—The Bench committed the prisoner for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sesssions, and ad- mitted him to bail, himself in £5O, and two sureties of £25 each.

div.head: EARLESTOWN CHURCH SCANDAL.
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH SCANDAL.

The scene presented in the Church of St. John the Bap- test, Earlestown, at the services on Sunday was of a singular character. The second dismissal of the organist (Mr. el. J. Darman) created considerable excitement throughout the parish, and the announcement that he and the entire choir, whose voluntary services have been highly appreciated by the parishioners, had finally decided to give up their con- nection with the church tended to still further increase the general uncertainty which existed as to the course of events. Sunday forenoon's service was very thinly attended— there being barely twenty adult persons present. The Vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) bad again secured the assistance of Mr. Pemberton, deputy-organist of St. Augustine's Church, Liverpool, in order to have the service decently con- ducted, and Mr. Pemberton presided at the instrument which has been such a bone of contention for some months past. The old organist aud the old choir carried out their expressed intention of absenting themselves from the church and, as a consequence, the chancel presented a peculiarly deserted appearance. To do duty as a choir, however, six girls occupied the front seat of the choir stalls; but it need scarcely be said that their services in that re- spect were much below what the congregation of St. John's have been accustomed to. The curate (the Rev. H. E Smith), was again absent through illness, but the lessons for the day were read by a Mr. Henehaw, who on other oc- casions has given timely help to the vicar. The services were far less hearty than they have hitherto usually been, but such could only naturally ho expected after the dis- creditable scenes that have recently been witnessed. The vicar preached, but as he entered the pulpit several persons left be church. The evening service was of the same char- acter as that of the forenoon,Mr. Henshew again reading the lessons and the vicar giving the sermon. Mr. Pemberton presided at the organ. The offertories were taken both morning and evening, but it might 62 said as to the liber- ality of the congregation that it was conspicuous by its absence.
EARLESTOWN ASSOCIATiv.,I FOOTBALL CLUB.
ANNUAL. MEETING: .PRESENTATION GE .MEDALS.

I The annual meeting of the members of the Earlestown Assecittion Football Club was held at the Sunbeam lon, Wargraye, eon Saturday evening, when a very pleasant gathering was held. About 3() persons sat down to an excel. lent tea, the cost of which was generously defrayed by Mr. and Mrs. R. Morrie, of the " Snob-sin." At the subs, guent proceedings the chair was occupied by Mr. Peter Hastie, who was supported by Messrs. D. Davies, W. W. ()wen, J. Muecroft, C. Kelly, and other members of the committee and officers of the club —rho Chairman alluded to the progress of the club during the past seasoa, complimenting the players of the first team especially upon the bold bid . they made for the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup. He expressed the hope that the club would continue to prosper in future seasons, and pointed out the necessity there was for the members to be united and act harmoniously together. (Applause.)—Mr. Jamea Daxbury (secretary) was then called upon to read the report. After a few intro- ducting remarks, the report proceeded:—"l think I can safely say that the past season has been the most sacceesful for Earlestown Association football, and more particularly for the Earlestown Association Club. since the introduction of football in this dietrict. At the commencement of the season our club did badly in its matches, but finished the season in a very creditable manner. From a comparatively obscure position in the background of Association football, the Earlestown Club has nobly and honourably fought its way to the front. Out of the first ten matches we played— which included our defeat by Turton in the second round of the Lancashire Challenge Cup Competition—we were four times defeated, three games were drawn, and three were victories for our team. IQ those ten matches we scored 22 goals, whilst our opponents scored 25. against us. Since that time, however, a remarkable change came over our team—everyone appeared no improve , and work more consistently together, and the result was a series of brilliant successes. Our defeat by Tarton spurred us on to further efforts, and of the remaining /fa matches no less than 15 were well-earned victories, one was a draw, land the remaining three were defeats—the latter being ad- ministered by Liverpool Stanley, at Liverpool, and Evertort (twice), at Liverpool. In these 19, matches, we ran up a total of 57 goals, while our opponents only scored 23 goals. Out of the total of 29)matches which we played we won la, lost seven, and four were draws. We scored '79 goals and our opponents notched 43. In the competition for the Liver- pool and District Association Challenge Cup, we played five matches and scored 15 goals to only three by cur opponents. This I look upon as an unprecedented record, when it is cor.- sidered that we met such cluba as Bootle (last vear's winners of the cup), Liverpool Stanley, and Evert )fl ; and even our opponents have acknowledged that we can now honestly ' and fairly claim lobe placed on a level with the best clubs in the district. Our club has been honoured by the salec- I tin of two of its members to play in the Association matches against North Wales; amt each of our players has been presented with silver medals as the tanners-up for the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup. With regard to our second team, I ant sorry I have not been able to compile details of its doings, but I think the players deserve a word of praise for their exertions during the season. 1 regret that I cannot report as favourably with regard to our finances as I can upon other matters connected the club. Speaking roughly, I may may that our receipts have amounted to about £4O, which has all been expended, and there is still a little owing. Considering that nearly £9 has been expended from the funds of the club in railway fares for the players, I think it is not too much to expect that the members should pay up their contributions promptly, in order that the club's liabilities. may be met. What have we to de in the future? Have wo. to rest on our Present laurels and allow others to pass us in. the fight for victory and supremacy, or shall we still con- tinue in the path of progress and strive to attain the highest position it is possible for a club to attain ? Let us renew our exertions in the coming season, let us put forth alt the strength, energy, and determination we possibly condo, and not be downhearted at any temporary deceat or difficalty that may beset our path. But above all, let us be united, for without unity it is useless to hope for victory. (Ap- planse.)—Mr. Dexbury was complimented by the meeting uron his excellent report, and the taunters decided to adopt it.

A very pleasing ceremony was then pi rformed and thae. was the presentation to the players of the urst team the handsome silver medals, each enclosed in a separate case, which had been presented to the club by the Liverpool and District Football association as a mark of the honour at- tained by the Earlestown team in being the runners-up for the Association Challenge Cup. la the final tie of the com- petition for that trophy, as cur readers will be aware, Earlestown was only defeated after a most exciting and fast came, by one goal to none; their victors being Everton. The presentation was made by Mr. thistle, who complimented each of the players as they came forward to receive their medals, The fol- towing are the names of these who received the medals :-- Thomas Champion (goal); Robert Green (captain) and Frederick Emmett (backs); James Whalley, JAMB Dux' bury and Richard Bowker (half-backs); William Rich and Jmnes Ellison (right wing); Alfred William Dagnall (centre); James Sims and Joseph Cameron (left wing). As the recipients stepped forward they were very heartily ap- plauded. The election of officers. was afterwards proceeded with. *Mr. Duxbury was unanimously re-appointed hon. . secretary; Mr. David Davies was elected assistant secretary' and treasurer; and the following non-players were elected as a committee, there being 17' candidates- for the nine vacant seats :—Mesers. J. Muscrof), J. Dutton, P. Bastiee R. Morris (all re-elected), W. W. Owen, W. Moses, H. Dig- ital!, W. Blair, and J. Allen (new members), It was also decided to re-appoint Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., president: and several gentlemen were suggested as vice-presidents. A' - motion was passed that the secretary, treasurer, captain, and . vice-captain of the Ist team and captain of the 2nd teal , should also act on the committee, but no player to hase.A. voice in the selection of teams, For the post of captain Mr. James Whalley received a large majority of votes, ate Mr. Alfred W. Da4nall was re-elected vice-ceptain. Mr. K. Green (late captain) refused to again serve in that position. Hearty votes of thanks to the various officers of the club were accorded; and after the health of the host and hostess (Mr. and Mrs. Morris) had been. enthusiastically drunk, the meeting concluded. The rest of the evening was spent in a convivial manner.

RACE WEEK HOLIDAYS AND FESTIVITIES. The annual Newton races have again come and gone, and Earlestown, Newton, and the surrounding district is Win. beginning to assume Its normal aspect and appearance. The race-week is essentially the people's holiday in the district; for contrary to the custom observed elsewhere Whitson" tide is not looked upon as a holiday-time, or as a:festival of the calendar calling for special observances in this district- By common consent the race-week is regarded as the week of the year in which all classes of the community, Young and old, rich and poor, enjoy their holiday; give them- selves up to pleasure; return home to parents and relations; or visit friends at a distance, as the case may be. To all thus , inclined this week, the weather has been eminently favour' able, not a shower of rain having fallen on any day to mar the pleasant and enjoyable proceedings which have been going on on every hand. The Vulcan iron foundry has been stopped all week; the hands employed at the Viadact waggon works of the L. and N.-W. RailwaV company were stopped on Tuesday, and those employed at the works of Messrs. 'l'. and T. Vicars, were also stoPPedl , on Tuesday. The influx of numberless thousands of per' sons into the town on Tuesday when the races commenced gave it a very animated and busy appearance, but on the following day—the "Cup day "—there was a still further increase in the number of persons in Earlestown and New- ton. In fact it is stated that within recent years there have not been so many visitors to the races on any one day au there was on Wednesday. On both days many of the placed of business were closed. Many of the schools held their annual treats on Tuesday, while on Wednesday there was the united Sunday school trip to Windermere. Particular* of the various gatherings are appended i EaRLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY Scwoor„.—About 30G scholars attended the animal treat in connection with the Wes" leyan Sunday School, Cross-lane, Earlestown, on TuesdaY afternoon. On being formed in processional order, and headed by the splendid silk banner bearing the words "Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School," they proceeded along Bridge • street and Earle-street, to the residence of Mr. Hugh Parr, leader of the chapel choir and Sunday school librarian, where one of their recent anniversary hymns were sung. At the house of Mr. J. W. Emmett the scholars were drawn up in the grounds, and after another hymn had been sung three hearty cheers for Mr. and Mrs. Emmett were given. The procession was then re-formed and the scholars marched to Bradley Hall Farm, Buttonwood, where Mr. Kilshall kindly allowed them the use of a field. Here gaines and amuse- ments were carried on during the afternoon. Tea, milk, buns, currant bread, dm., were provided for the younger persons, while an excellent tea, at a small, charge, was sup- plied to the elder scholars, friends, and members of the con- gregation. Nuts and oranges were afterwards distributed. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCIICOL—The annual treat to the scholars of the Crow-lane Congregational Sunday school was a very successful gathering. They marched from the schoolroom, headed by the Lowton Tem- perance Brass Band, and proceeded to a field off Mill-lane, where the afternoon was very enjoyably spent. The usual refreshments were served out in the course of the afternoon. EARLBSTOWN GOSPEL Missroar.—The-annual treat to theo scholars of this mission took place on Tuesday afternoon. They assembled at the Co-operative Hall, and a procession of 160 children and 40 adults was formed. Headed by the large banner of the mission, they proceeded to a field at Buttonwood. owned by Mr. Reyes. and which had been generously placed at the disposal of the committee. The juveniles and children were conveyed in two hurries. Everyone thoroughly enjoyed themselves; and refreshments in the shape of tea, bread and butter, seed and currant breads, were supplied. Both on entering and leaving the field hymns were sung at Mr. byes' house. EARLESTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOL—Upwards of 200 scholars assembled at the school, in Legh-streec, early on Tuesday afternoon, when the annual field day was held.: Headed by the large school banner, they marched along the streets towards Buttonwood, where they entered a field, kindly lent by Mr. Fairclongh. On the way two hymns were sung at the residence of Mr. J. %V. Emmett. The after- noon was spent in footballing, racing, cricketing, and ether innocent games. The amusements were agreeably inter- rupted by the distribution of tea, milk, currant breed, nutu* oranges, etc. The return journey was commenced about eight o'clock, and on leaving the field Mr. Fairclough was- heartily thanked for kindly lending them the field. BAPTIST Surmay SCHOOL —The annual treat took place on Tuesday afternoon, when about 300 scholars assembled: at the schoolroom, and afterwards marched to a field in Crew-lane, which had been kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Cawley. In the course of the afternoon the jovenilea were regaled with milk, buns, dr.c.. and a capital tea was pro- vided for the parents and elder scholars, The usualgames were h artily indulged in until dusk, when cheers were given for Mr. Cawley. The scholars marched back to the schoolroom, where they were dismissed after singing and prayer.

. . VULCAN WESLMYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL —On Tuesday afternbon the scholars attending the Vulcan Sunday School marched from the eccoolroom to a field near Red Beak, lent by Mr. Williams, and bn the route sang hymns- at various places in the " and at the residences of Mr. Wright, Mr. Botch', and Mr. Williams. Milk, bans, nuts and oranges were distribut:d to the scholars and friends, all of whom spent the afternoon in a very, pleasant manner. On arriving back at the school short addresses were given by Mr. Cordiugly, Mr. Marti!), and Mr. Wright, and each of the scholars was presented with a package con- taining nuts, sweets, and an orange. VITRIOL SQUARE SCHOOL —The scholars of this school were regaled with their annual treat on Tuesday. afternoon. A large number were present, and after marching to a field lent by the Sankey Sugar Works Company, they onjoyed themselves in various games, dancing, drc. The band of the Warringtsn Workhouse was in attendance, and discoursed a selection of lively airs. During the afternoon the usual refreshments were served to those present.
The annual meeting of WO Lancashire and Cheshire branch of the British Medical Association was held in the Town Hall, Chester, on Wednesday, under, the presidency of Dr. .Waters.

MURDER IN AMERICA BY A WARRINGTON MAN. , The "Lawrence American" newspaper contains a long !account of a brutal tragedy which has been perpetrated in the city of Lawrence by a man named Thomas Lowe, who was born in Warrington in the year 1851. The murder is described art a "horrible, unprovoked, and most brutal one, the victim being the ten-year-old daughter of a respectaole and hardworking citizen, the brute who perpetrated the fiendish crime being a besotted, drunken, worthless wretch, who bas made North Andover his home for years, and too often made the city the scene of his bacchanalian car- ousals." The scene of the murder is on Rachwood-street, near Maine, in a neat, new, two-and-a-half story dwelling, recently built and occupied in part by Mr. Timothy Sul- livan, foreman of a section of the Boston and Maine railroed, who is the grief-stricken father of the victim. She was named Ellen, and her features were of a delicate and hand- some caste, and when lit up by a pair of biight blue eyes, with her wealth of light curly hair, she was the picture of Youthful beauty, On her neck were seen the marks effected by the murderer's hands, and there were several contusions and abrasions about the face. The medical evidence showed that the girl had been strangled to death. The deceased and a sister and brother were the only three in the house (the mother having gone ta attend a .funeral) at the time the murder was committed. The sister of the dead child, who,al- though only seven years old, Is unusually intelligent for her age, in reply to questions put to her by a medical gentle- man, says that " Tom " came into the house, but that De did not speak. He commenced to choke the deceased, and struck her several times. One of the blows felled her. Her reco- lection goes no further in the terrible deed, for when she regained.her senses her sister was lying on the floor, and " Tom " had gone. On her neck were deep indentations, which showed that he intended to strangle her. Her fAre- head bears the iniprint of the marks similar to that which a boot heel would cause; the left eye was completely closed, and the right orb partially, where the fellow dealt her ter- rible blows. When the affair was first reported, fears were entertained that a nameless crime had also been committed, but the medical examination dispelled this belief. Lowe made his firet appearance in North Andover about .15 years ago, and his manner of life has been in keeping with his bringing up "to the shadow of the gallows." Born in Warrington, England, in 1851, of English parents' he has been a "hard character" from his early youth. He has been in various parts of the world, and was a fireman on the 'ocean steamers for some years. His calling, howeve't, was a puddler in a rolling mill. He has left Nortla Andover several times, remaining only a year or two and returning to work at the Davis anti Farber Machine Co.'s works, where he was employed in various capacities, principally as a "helper" in the tlacksmith'ilehop. For some months he was employed by the Russell Paper Company. He has been arrested several times for drunkenness There are no relatives of the mur- derer in the country. He had been drinking, it is said, several days previous to the murder. The terrible tragedy has created a profound sensation, not only in the city but throughout the State, and thousands have visited the scene of the tragedy. Lowe, who is 33 years of age, and unmar- ried, has Mace his arrest been completely broken down. lie has been committed for trial before the Superior Court, to be held in October next.

WALKING DAY AT WARRINGTON. Walking Day, which may fittingly be termed the great Juvenile festival of this neighbourhood, was again celebra- ted yesterday; and as usual brought with it a brief respite 'from labour to the busy denizens of the workshop and fec- i tory, as well as to the shopkeeper and his assistants. The • popularity of this holiday notwithstanding that some seem •-to think it is held an. an iaopportune time of the year, ap- pears to be iii no way on the waue. As far as appearances went it was as widely observed yesterday as in any previous . year. No doubt the favourableness of the weather, the warmth of which was tempered by gentle breezes, contributed largely to the very numerous turn-out of the children and . their elders. At an early hour the streets began to put on a very festive appearance, owing to the suspension across • them of various-coloured flags and banners, and the ever- , increasing concourse of persons evidently bent on catching • early teeins to various pleasure resorts. Later on large numbers of the •• little folks " began to two Out and make their way to the various Sunday schools they attended, and were there formed into procession. Snortly after nine o'clock the procession of sceolars began to move front the several Sunday schools in accordance with the arrangements previously made. The scholars attending th 3 church schools, besides those from the Blue Coat and Union, and several schools of the dissenters beg-en to con- verge upon the Park and there arranged themselves in proper crder in front of the Town Hall. tech of the schools carried a large banner and. numerous smaller flags, upon which were scriptural and other suitable mottoes. loose, it may be easily imagined, tended to give the densely crowded streets a still more animated sad picturesque ap- pearance. The Salvation Army contingent Was another of those who assembled in front of the Town Hall. The leaders of the Army in the town having very thoughtfully sent oat a free invitation to the peer unprovided-for children, it is needless to say that their quota of juveniles was of forinideble proportions. As they passed along the streets. headei by their band playing characteristic tunes, they were the cause of a good deal of curiosity and interest, chiefly owing to the large number ot red-jerseyed "officers" and soberly-attired sisters who , were present. The greater numter of the Noncon- formist schools proceeded direct, after passing along some of the principal streets, to the places which had been fixed upon as the scene of their day's enjoyment; as did also the Catholic schools. Tae latter were preceded by the League Hall baud, the picturesque green uniform of which was very favourably commented upon. Tee Catholic schools may also perhaps be said to have carried oil the palm for the number, richness, and beauty of their banners and flags. The schools which gathered in the Park began to leave there suortly after ten o'clock in the following order, viz. :—Blue Coat, Union, Parish Churcb, St. John's, Crossley-street, Parr-street, St. Paul's, St. Berne- base St. Anne's, Sc. Peter's Mission, Holy Trinity, Bank Quay Church school, St. James', Emmanuel Free Church sehoil., teghotreet Primitives, Latchford Primitives, Salve- Lien Army. This procession passed along Parker-street, Wilson Patten-street, Bridge-se, Buttermarket-st., Church- at. The Church sceolars then went to the Parish Church, in which a short service was held. The officiating clergy- men were the Rey. Canon Dodd (Stretton), the Rev. W. Quekett, and the Rev. R. W. P. Montgomery. A short and suitable sermon was preached to the children by the Rev. Canon Dodd from the text "Honour all men; love the brothe, hood; fear God; hononr the king." At the conclusion of the sermon the children filed out of the church, and then went to their several destination. It is pleteing to know that, as far as we have heard, no accidents of any description have occurred, but that, on the contrary, every thing has passed off in connection with this great annual gathering of children in the most satisfactory way. In addition to toe various school treats, a variety entertain- ment was given by Mr. Martin Brown in the field adjoining St. James's Church, Letcuford, and was largely attended. ORANGISII AT WARRINGTOIC—The earl Of Smarms&lll lode of Orangemen held its monthly meeting in the 'Mile Lion Inn. Market-plane, Warrington, on Monday evening, Brother James Jolley. WM., presiding. There was a large number of members present. A report, which was con- sidered satisfactory, was read by the secretary, after which the following resolution was adopted:—" That the members of the above lodge desire to express in the strongest terms their deep and heartfelt sympathy with their Ulster brethren under the treatment they are receiving at the hands open unpopular and unconstitutional Government, which, by its recent conduct, proves moat conclusively that it intends to foster rebellicn, and prefers to ploteet rebel meelines, to the hurt, hindrance, and annoyance of those who are loyal to the throne and constitution of these realms; and in view of these throgs, we asanre our brethren of our utmost support, pecuniary •ense, but by every other lawful ,n:et onlyans, n a hiinl may 119 deemed necessary to sustain them in their efforts to prevent the invasion of their province by .-he ein was brought to a eloa:!, by the sing- negolfs.t" TheNh m National Anthem.

"WHO'S AFRAID?"

.. ___ _. ..........__ . Sir,—Snme Church of England parsons have a happy 1 knack of finding mare's nests, and our beloved orother, the It..v. E. C. E. Carleton, is one of them. His letter in your " Neutral " contemporary of last Saturday proves my case to the hilt, and his logical conclusion, as conveyed to the last few lines, is exceedingly rich. "If we repel these ill- minded assaults with the necessary vigour, it will be under- stood with whom the beginning of the struggle originated." me italics are mine, but the reasoning isn't! - . . . __ .

It has long been a favourite sneer with Churchmen at one particular Nonconformist minister in our town that he is a 'political parson ;" but if ever he had a political mantle, it has fallen on the Rev. Mr. Carleton. and I fear

it has clouded his brighter faculties. He is nothing—abso- lEttely nothing—if not political; and therefore will be certain to appreciate what occurred in the House of Comment last night. He will see "the beginning of the end " there ; for when Parliament, by a good majority, decides against the more glaring acts of the State Canrch, it will not be very long before minor ones get rooted out also. The re- presentatives of the people will carry out the principles of the Liberation Society' awl the "Purchase of Souls," "Church Tithes," and all the other oppressive grievancee wilt be swept away, 19 they ought to be, for ever. . .

odd times, put on their spectacles and scratched their wigs and were rather puzzled. They got over the difficulty by knocking one Act on the head and trying to make common sense of the other! Reforms to be improvements ought to be carefully carried out. Considering the loss of tine and confusion which must arise from the bullying and badger- ing of question and resolution mongers and windy men, I am rather surprised that our statutes do not contain a greater number of mistakes and inconsistencies. Now, as to the use that is to be made of this doctrine, as they say in Scotland. Clearly this is a very serious matter which requires a remedy. I feel sure that these honourable gentlemen do not intend to act as spies in the interest of the enemies of the United K ngdom. nor are their discussions intended to give intelligence or notice to the latter. Such a thing would be very like high treason, very properly made a capital offence. Such things would not be permitted even IPolemically or for the sake of discussing important questions.

- Some years ago much time was lost in inquiries as to whether the standing orders had been complied with in ap- plications for private railway, canal, or other Acts. To ob- viate this a legal examiner was appointed, to whom these matters are referred, as we have lately seen in the case of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. Could not such an officer, to be called " the question answerer," be appointed, whose duty it should he to answer qfteations, and to whom those members requiring answers might be referred ? Both pouting parties consider that the much-needed reform of our laws of real property is not far distant, but that in carrying out such reforms the Ten Commandments must not be lost sight of, as Mr. John Bright very well ob- served. No doubt it is as great a sin to wrong a landlord as it is to wrong any other class of her Majesty's subjects. In the changes which are at hand ths new land laws must be based upon mutual justice and equity, without which they will not bind men's consciences. It is not, I believe, in. tended to do wrong to any one, or to deprive ass' man of his properly. The changes will mainly relate to the tenure or way in which landed estates are to be held, sold, let, or transferred by their owners. Lord Cairns' Conveyancing Acts are considered to be (except in one or two particulars) merely nominal reforms, which have, as [am told by a corn- palest London authority, increased the cost of buying and selling and conveying estates considerably. A few re- marks on life estates and building leases another d am. air, vom olwlient servant, 17th June, 1834.
When I find clergyineit-thder'iding tithes,l always wonder if the renowned Hosea Biglow had them in his mind, when he wrote:—

" Oh, yes : I firmly du believe In humbug generally. Zer its a thing that L perceive To hsv a solid rally ; This heth my faithful sheplorrd been, In pastures sweet heth led me. An' this 'II keep the people greets To feed ez they her fed me.", Yours, truly,
June 19th, 1884.
CERBERUS.
MR. JOSEPH HOIVES AND MR. BOTTOMLEY. - THE LIBERAL V. THE TORY WORKING-MAN.

Sir,—lt will he within the recollection of your realer. that I have on two °cessions lecture! in your town under the auspices of the Liberal Association. the result has been that the Warrington Liberal Association has challenged the Conservative Association to put forward a representative man to meet me in debate, but the Conservatives for reasons best known to themselves have declined the challenge. THE LOYALTY OF ORNGEifE7. Sir,—lt is most interesting to notice the almost super- human eff ins now being in Me Dv our rosy friends to gain the confidence of the people. Means the most despicable ere being resorted to. Lard S tlisbury, trying to humbug the Weeleyans at Plymouth, descends to the use of lan- guage he knows full well would not be endorsed by his co- religionist% and I see the London Guardian, with due re- spect for c insistency, upbraids him for his "newly-found tolerance " towards th ae "schismatic." But what cares this valiant defender of Church and State, if by this means he can manage to win one more supporter to the already moribund Establishment? No wonder that the smaller fry of the 'fury party should resort to all and every insane to bring into disrepute the Gladetone Government, when they have such a noble example set before them. And for what is all this truckling with truth and honesty? Simply to gain place and position—neither more nor less than this. Now, I have no Wujection to the rory party making itself 'strong, surrounding itself by all the good measures and good inten- tions possible; but I also expect to know something of their policy. To abuse everything, and to, as Lord " Random " says, "oppose everything" for the mere sake of opposition is not good enough. Since the Liberals gained power, through the country taking the advice of Lord Beaconsdeld, and electing " men of light and leading," a society called Orangemen has, with a large amount of persistency, insisted upon pushing itself upm the public notice, and, what is most remarkable, these fanatics wish to pure as Loyalists. I fancy if they only kne v a little more of the history attached to the word, they would discard it, or else throw in their lot with the dra, mitardi, or disloyal prtion ?f. 1;45 Jriqh. popUlitiOn. lo I 1837 the Osatlgetnetl plotted to put Hide the Queen', accession to the throne in favour of the Duke of Cum. beldam], then Grand Master of the Orangemen of the empire, and this chiefly by the help of the Irish. A select committee on Orange Lodges of that date reports the Duke as having 2:39,000 men under his command, mostly armed, and all Irishmen; its Great Britain and the Colonies 140,000 men; that "your office is permanent and uncontrolled, your authority is discretionary, illimitable, and absolute." 'rfaese men were bound together by religious ceremony and sanction almost equal to an oath. The re- port goes on to say, "The object of this institution is to resist the spirit of reform, and to preserve those institutions best adapted to the gratifications of the interestsand feelings of its supporters." Of course I am aware, so far as War- rington is concerned, at least, that there are working-men who with most consummate stupidity have allowed them- selves to become members of Orange lodges. When they look keenly into the above quotation, and study what I fur- ther state, they will surely see for what vile purpose they are being used by those whose interest it is to keep them under their heel: The report goes on to say the effect of this in- stitution is "to keep up an exclusive association in civil and military society, exciting one portion of the people against the other ; to increase the rancour and animosity too often unfortunately existing between persons of differ- ent religious persuasions—to make the Protestant the enemy of the C atholic, aid the Catholic the enemy of the Protest- ant—by processions on particular days, attended with the insignia of the society, to excite to breaches of the peace anti to bloodshed, to raise up other secret societies among the Cttholics in their own defence and protection against the insults of the Orangemen. to interrupt the coarse of justice, to interfere with time discipline of the army." The committee points out the imperious necessity of suppressing the Orange lodges, and calls upon the HOMO to say whether the "law othcere of the Crown should not be directed to prosecute the grand officers of an these Orange lodges without delay." I hopel have proved my charge as to the Orangemen—in their more youthful days—beicg dis- loyal; and what is of far more imoortance to the well-being of society, they were, anti are to this day, the chief promo- ters of all the misery and religious animosity that exists in Ireland.

Sir,—The statement made by "Wiiliam Pugh, of 83, Nicholson-street, Warrington," in his letter to "R. A. Mor- ritt, Esq.," of Barnard Castle, ta the effect that Mr. flowes, when in Warrington. disclaimed all knowledge of the chal- lenge wade at Barnard Castle, is neither more nor less than a complete fabrication. I was present at both of Mr. Howe's lectures, and no mention of Barnard Castle either directly or indirectly, or of any challenge either there or elsewhere, except our own, was referred to by any person whatever. So much, then, for Mr. William Pugh's veracity. Permit me also to say that the Warrington Liberal Association will be only too pleased to "pit" Mr. Howes against any mini the Conservatives like to bring, either Mr. Bottomley or a better man, to discuss in public the question of ! Liberalism v. Toryism.—l am, sir. your obedient servant, HENRY ROBERTS, Sec. Warington Liberal Association.

CONCERTS AT THELWALL.—The annual concerts in con- nection with All Saints' church, took place in the schoolroom on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, the object in view be- ing the raising of funds for the choir excursion. On Tues- day the concert was very well attended and the various members of the choir rendered their songs in a very pleas- ing manner. Fear zlees were sung during the evening in , a manner which reflected great credit on the choir and the ; choirmaster, Mr. Evans. who had evidently trained his pupils well. Time song" Alice where art thou" by Mr Roe- beck, was well received, and Miss C Ellison gave "When Dasies Pied " in her usual good style. "I be quartette "Three 1 doughty men," by members of the choir, was encored, and the entertainment of Mr George [Julius (Manchester), caricaturist and mimic, took the audience by storm. Mr Tay- lor was encored for his song, "The beatswain's story." "The old brigade," snag by the Rev T P Williamson, and " Our Jack's come home toe:lay," by Mr P Ditchtield, were also encored. Songs were also given by Mrs Williamson, Miss I Edith Wrigh,, and Messrs Breortnall, Thumain, and Rey- nolds. The concert given on Wednesday evening was of a enperior character, and was sustained by the following ladies ' and gentlemen :—Mrs Williarneon, Miss Edith Wright, Mr Edward Reynolds, Mr Thurnam, Mr Frank Reynolds, Mr 1 Allen Avison, of Elalle's band, and principal 'cello of De Jong's band; Mr Oliver Gaggs, of the Manchester concerts: Mr John Marsden, of Manchester, accompanist, Rev T Pym Williamson, and the choir. The programme was of a I varied and claasical description. Several glees were given by the cbeir, and were well received; " Saftly fall the Shades of Evening," being encored. Miss Ellison repeated " When Daisies Pied," and Miss Edith Wright was very successful in her song, " Mrs Williamson sang, "When all was Young," with taste and feeling, and Mr Thurnam gave "May Dew " in very good style. A so'. and Sestette from " Patience " was well received, and Me E Reynolds sang The Raft" in effective style. A song from " Princes! Iris," by Miss Wright wss much appre- ciated. A principal and most enjoyable feature of this latter concert, were the contributions of Mr 0 Gaggs, Mr Allen Avison, ant Mr. Marsden. The room was nicely arranged with ferns and flowers, chinese lanterns. kc, and blocks of ice were placed in the windows to cool the atmos- phere. The concerts on both evenings were eminently successful.

ACCIDENT TO MONA'S ISLE .STEIMER —There was great excitement in Liverpool last night when it was found that the Mona's Isle was many hours overdue from the Isle-of- Man. It appears that the Mona's Isle, which is far-famed as the quickest and most richly-appointed of the Isle-of- Man fleet of boats, left Liverpool punctually at one o'clock on Thursday afternoon, and made a fine passage for about half the journey, when one of the piston-rods snapped and caused the cylinder to break. Steam was imme- diately shut off, band the anchor dropped, and in this condition the Mona's Isle remained until about midnight, when the King Orr" hove in, sight, and, coming alongside, lay by for a couple of hours, and then took her in tow. Tll3 numerous passengers on beard the Mona's Isle were thus sixteen hours in making the journey from Liverpool to Douglas, being landed at Liverpool after four o'clock in the morning.
