REFORM OF TITE HOUSE OF LORDIL—Lord ROSESERY moved the appointment of a Select Committee to consider the best means of promoting the efficiency of the 1101.1811. Considering the intellectual resources of the Chamber, it might do much better work. He suggested a joint Commit- tee of Lords and Commons to sit on bills of secondary im- portance, and a wider range of professional, commercial, and colonial representation in the House itself.—Earl GRAN- VILLE thought no practical good could follow the appoint- ment of a Select Committee, except on such specific ques- tions as private bill legislation and life peerages.—The Marquis of SALISBURY agreed that the appointment of a Committee on the abstract question would be a mistake.— Earl DERRY, on behalf of tee Government, promised sup- port if a specific subject of reference were inserted in the motien.—Lord ROSEBERY agreed to insert life peerages as I an amendment —The House divided :—For the amendment, I 45; against. 85 —The House then divided on the substan- tive motion :—For, 33; against, 77.—The motion was there- fore lost.
The House shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The House met at four &clock.

div.p: A TORY'S VIEW OF "LIBERALISM."

Sir,—ln your last issue Mr. H. Whitham, for reasons best known to himself, takes me to task for writing in defence of Sir Gilbert Green all who, from my point of view, has been abus,.d and slandered. If he has done a good thing for the town " More is meant than meets the eye." If he possesses anything and does not freely give the best of it to Radicals, he is still wrong, and then after all their clamour, if he pro- mises to consider their wants, and if he finds it possible and lawful to grant them 'a privilege in his perfume' property,. he is threatened with punishment for bribery. Why in the name of common sense should Sir Gilbert do anything at all for such men? Where are their Crosfields, Broadbants, Monks, Rylands, and other worthies of their way of think- ing? I presume Sir Gilbert did not make the land or the fishpond; no doubt he bought it with money honestly and lawfully earns-1. Your Crosfields and Rvlands have either land or money honestly earned no doubt, yet, at least seme of it ia wrung out of the sweatof the brow of Mr H Whithana and others. Let Mr. Whitham and the people who think like him look to this and see that their pets don't build large houses and increase their estates out of the blood and bones of Mr. Whitham'e "-ekes," and let Sir Gilbert and his work- ing-men alone. Sir Gilbert's men are satisfactorily paid and don't need to strike. They are paid and assisted in sick- ness, and pensioned for life when incapable of work, and should they unfortunately die leaving a widow she is pro- vided with a house and subsistence for life. But here cones a "bran new " grievance, Sir Gilbert does nothing for the working-men of Warrington according to men of ‘4 H. W.'s" stamp. yet here we have him complaining that Sir Gilbert actually employs Warrington men Co do his work, and he calls it a burden upon the town, because these men so em- ployed reside in Warrington and spend their earnings there. I had always thought money brought into the town from outside was much gain to the trade of the town, hut it ap- pears "H. W." knows- better. He then talks about endear- ing people to the land, and thinks if the people of- Walton had a vote they would he as happy as the cottazers of Town Hill, Warrington. Perhaps they would; we shall see when they get the vote! Oh ! but he has no political spite: he only cares for prin- ciples. I suppose that is why he goes 30 far as to write what he maeht to have known was untrue. He says, speaking of the fishing, that Sir Gilbert never intended the people of Warrington to have one particle of pleasure out o that sacred neighbourhood. Is it not a fact that Sir Gilbert did actually for some dine allow the people of Warrington, who chose, to fish in that sacred neighbourhood? At last Mr. Whitham•rambles into pelitice and defends Mr. Chamberlain's lubberly Merchant Shipping Bill. Whether it is a good or a bad bill I don't pretend to know. but at all events, the changes and alterations made in it since its original draft show that its author is only a 'peen- tine in such matters. He then brings um Egypt, the Soudan, and the happy state of Ireland. Well, in my opinion, Egypt signifies bungle, the Soudan blunder and bloodshed, and Ire- land plunder and coercion. In conclusion I would advise him and his abusive Radical friends to have the Common decency to attack principles and not persons. Political life and morale in Warrington would he better for it. But if" Mr. W." wants to write about poli- tics. and if he must argue with some one, let him as one of the caucus, before which Mr. W. Crosfield has promised to bow; rioiticdty explain what this thing is they call Liberalism. Let him bbtturi it and inform us whet alterations he requires I to be made in the British constitution, that it will be made so perfect that even be will become a Conservative, and then if not convinced that he is right,.! m y argue the matter with him. At preeent-Whigism, Ll6eral ism, and Radicalism are to me like the three thimbles and pea trick: now you see it and now you elon't."—Yoursobediently, FAIR PLAY.

Since Blackstone's Commentaries were first pnb• fished in 1165, tlse veriest stickler fur the maxim "Stare I enper antiquas via!" will allow that most of the legal alterations made- are imnrovernents. Now-a-dars noipick- ling tubs are foand in Newgate yard for human heads, to he displayed on Temple Bar. ha Dodsley's Landon and its environs, 17614 there is a print of Temple Bar with three lofty poles surmounted by heads. Happily this state of things has passed away. The late 'Meter of the Rolls in his evidence before a com- mittee of the House called attention to the ctreless way in which statistics are constructed. by which learned judges are seriously embarrassed in the administration of justice. Lymm was all astir on Wednesday, in canseqnence of the marriage of Miss Bedell, daugnter of the Rev. James Be- dell, tbe esteemed Congregatioaal minister. The bridegroom was Mr Richard liarris.Boyd. son of Mr Robert Boyd, Glas- gow, and member of the engineering firm of J and T Boyd of that city. The Congregational Church had been beauti- fully decorated for the occasion by scholars and friends, the pulpit in particular being bright with evergreens and flowers. Three archways Of evergreens and flowers had also been erected, one at the entrance of the residence of the bride's father (Foots-crag), another across the canal bridge, and the third at the gates of the church. The interesting ceremony WAS performed by the Hey A MacKennel], B A, of Bowdon, assisted by the Rev Win Boyd, LLD, brother of the bride- groom, the church being crowded during the proceedings. The bride was charmingly attired in a cream satin with brocaded front, and trimmed with lace, and was adorned with orange blossom. Her sister, Miss Annie Bedell, acted as brides- maid, attended by four little boys in sailor coeturne as pages. The best men were Mr J Robson and Mr Clement Boyd. After the nuptial knot had been tied, the invited guests, about 60 in number, partook of the wedding breakfest in a large pavilion which had been erected on the lawn at Mr Bedetl's residence. The happy couple subsequently drove to Warrington en route to " bonnie Scotian i." At five o'clock the echolars, to the number of 200, at the invitation of their pastor, partook of tea in the schoolroom, afterwards making merry in outdoor games until nightfall. The Lytton Temperance Band paraded the village in the evening and played several tunes in front of the residence of Mr D Boyd (brother of the bridegroom) who has for some years lived at Lyinm. Amongst the presents were silver salver front the teachers and elder scholars of the Sunday school ; silver and crystal and butter cooler from Miss Bedell's Sunday scholars; and a dining-room timepiece from the employees at Shettlestone iron works. STALING CABBAGES AN ASSAULTING THE POLICE.—A young in in named liohert Newton wee charged at the War- rington County Sessions, on Wednesday, with having, on the 14th inst., stolen seven cabbages, value 61, the Property of John C aldwell, and also with assaulting P.C. Whitting,- ham —The constable stated that on Saturday night he was on the road leading from Orford Green to Orford Hull, when he saw the prisoner t +king cabbages from a field close by. Prisoner said his cousin gave him permission to take them, and on witness ask'ng hUn for the name of his cousin be allow down the caribaoss, crock at witness, and attempted it) run away. The two then had a severe struggle.—The Bench fined prisoner 101 and costs, or 14 days, in respect to each charge.

BERATIIM.—Last week the name 0 Mr. E. Badley, War- rington, was erroneously given as havinz Na.. 3 bar let to him at Newton rases; it should have been Mr. Weary, of Manchester. BICYCLE ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.—An unfortunate accident occurred to a Mr. Bodle whilst out on his bicycle on Wednesday evening. When passing along near Bold- street he was endeavouring to keep clear of a child which was in the roadway but unluckily upset his machine. He fell With such foree that one of his wrists was broken, some of the bone-splinters being driven through the flesh. lie at once went to the sargery of Dr; 6. Smith, who dressed and attended to his injuries. CAUGHT IN glue ACT. —At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, Michael Feeney, a young man, was charged with stealing a suit of clothes value 30s, the property of Michael McGann, a farm labourer employed at the farm of Mr. Skel- lon, Great Sankey, on the let inst. It appeared that on the date named the prosecutor was in the stable, when he heard a noise in the room above, in which he slept. On going thither he found the prisoner in the room with the suit of clothes under his arm. The clothes had been stolen from a box in the room, which had been burst open. The prose- cutor asked him what be was doing there and he replied I was only looking at them" (meaning the clothes). Prose. cater seized him, however, and took him to the Penketh police station, where he handed him over to P.C. Slingsby. —He was committed to prison for a month. ATTEMPTED RESCUE BY FEMALES--A young man named Patrick lcurke, a forge-hand, living at 22, Gee-at., was on Friday charged at the Warrington Police-court with having been drunk and disorderly; with assaulting P.O 's Hennessy and Hollingworth, and with assaulting John Featherstone whilst assisting the police. It seemed that on the previous night prisoner had been making a dieturb mice in Dial-street. He was requested by an officer to get away home, but instead of doing that, he ran towards the police- man and struck at him in a wild and furious manner. The officer got hold of the prisoner, but Was at once set upon by a number of young women, and he did not succeed in securing Backe until assistance arrived to repel his feminine assailants. Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, or 14, days' imprisonment fur having been drunk and disorderly ; and 203„ including costs, for the assaults, or in default of pay- ment, another 14 days's imprisonment. AN UNGRATEFOL GEssr : CLEVER CAPTURE Or • TIIIIIP—At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday. before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Mr. John Fairclough. a yomog and respectably dressed female named Eliztheth Hayes, who was described as a carder from Ashton-under-Lvne, was charged on remand from Saturday with stealing 43 ea in money from the dwelling house of William Morris, Brook-street, on the previous Friday,—Tne Clerk (Mr. White) said thit there Has another charge against the prisoner of stealing from a dwelling-hoase at Appleton. He also read a letter showing that he had been sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment at the Manchester Assizea—At three o'clock on the afternoon of the Friday in question the prisoner went to the house of Mr. Morris and desired to know where she could obtain lodgings, say- log that she was tired and would like a cap of tea, as she bad come front Manchester in search of work, which she had obtained. Mrs. Morris went out and procured lodgings for her, and the prisoner then left the house avowedly with the intention of fetching her box from the statism After she had left it was ascertained that 4a rid bad been taker out of a waistcoat. pocket in a bedroom in the house a Mr. Morris. Information was given to the police, and Inspector Spinks succeeded in apprehending the prisoner at the rail. way Station as she was about to take train to Manchester. When she observed him, she endeavoured to elude him by getting into a London train, but failed to effect her object. —She pleaded guilty, and was :west to gaol for two months with hard laboar.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT. A sitting of this Court was held on I hursday before Mr. W. W'ynne-Iffonikes, Judge. The only case of public interest was one in which John Barnes, master p tinter, Dallarn-lane,Warrington, sued Daniel Rose, master builder, Manchester, for a sum of LI 1155., part of an amount due to the plaintiff' from the defendant on a contract for painting Capt. Braybrooke's farm at Orford. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff. t. and defendant was not represented, be' a solicitar.—lt appeared that the plaintiff Rent in a tender to do the work • required at the farm in question, the amount of the tender be- ing £8 2a Of, extras amounting to 9,k brig afterwards added. Plaintiff proceeded with the work, but not receiving any money from defendant, he stopped work. He had received 55 on account, and the amount of work that ha had exe- cuted he valued at IC, the claim tiding for the balancer £1 15s. Daring the examination of the plaintiff by the defendant, the former made use of improper oxpresetonsr end was sbarply reprimanded by the judge, who told him that he had not come to the court to enter into,a, wrangle, but to speak the truth. The son of the plaintiff, wbrr was called in support of the case, also made an, indiscreet remark, whereupon his Honour again delivered a repri- mand, tie was not, his Honour s miii, surprised at what the witness had said, after the example that had been set hint by his father, but he must tell witness that he would have to behave and caution him to act properly.—The defendant disputed the account on the ground that the plaintiff had taken instructions from a Mr. Smith, which took the matter out of his (defendant's) hands.—His Honour said that be had nn doubt that the defendant was liable upon the con- tract.
